California now has AB 493 (interest on held proceeds), a July 2026 order on holds over 10 days and an Oct 15 2026 reporting order; DFPI has 160+ complaints; 16,000+ structures were destroyed and fewer than a dozen rebuilt one year on. Disputes over percent complete are the stated cause.
ideas.solution: (1) Digital multi-party endorsement; (2) a custodial FBO account per claim at a partner bank, interest passed through; (3) release rules encoded from the servicer's policy and checked against permit-status feeds, dated geotagged photos, contractor licence and insurance, and statutory lien waivers; (4) contractor fast-pay on approved draws at 1-2% (assumed); (5) later, a completion guaranty and a soft-cost bridge secured on the proceeds. Legal premise to check: money transmission (use a bank partner), security-instrument terms (restore if feasible), state inspection-before-release rules, California lien-waiver forms.
ideas.why_now: Oct 15 2026 DFPI order, AB 493, hurricane Isaias (Oct 10, $2.5-4.5B insured), and the March 2026 GSE letter accepting ACV roofs, which widens depreciation gaps on hail claims.
ideas.wedge: California fire loan books: median days from check receipt to homeowner disbursement under 10, with an interest ledger and a DFPI-ready export; then monitored claims nationally.
ideas.path_to_100m: Direct losses about $102B (61.59% of $165.2B) x 60% mortgaged x 50% monitored (assumed) = $30.5B of proceeds a year (if monitored is 30%, the pool falls to about $340M). Servicer fee: about 305k files x $600 = $183M. Contractor fast-pay: $21B of draws x 1.5% = $320M. Float spread 0.5% on about $12.7B average balance = $64M. Pool about $567M; add a completion guaranty (about $80M) and bridge interest (about $100M) for about $750M. $100M is 13-18% blended share. Heroic, but three payers stack.
ideas.who_does_it_today: iink (check capture and multi-party payments; $14.8M raised; self-reports 162,029 claims and $2.3B of proceeds), DIMONT (loss-draft service), National General/Assurant LPI claims, servicers' own loss-draft teams, The Hub/CORE (nonprofit escrow oversight in LA), Built Technologies and title-company disbursers (construction lending, not insurance money).
ideas.why_they_lose: iink moves checks but does not decide releases, has no contractor credit and is small. Servicers cannot underwrite contractors or hold interest-bearing accounts cheaply under AB 493. The Hub is local and philanthropic.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (servicer integrations, DFPI audit trail) and process power; contractor draw history becomes credit data (cornered resource).
ideas.earned_secret: The money is not slow because servicers are lazy; it is deadlocked: the inspector's percent-complete is a judgment call and nobody will pre-fund the contractor. Replace the judgment with evidence and release becomes mechanical. Outside California servicers also earn float on these balances, so expect resistance until other states copy AB 493 (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign two CA lenders with open fire files; process 200 draws at cost; connect LA County permit data; sign one bank partner; agree fast-pay terms with 20 rebuild contractors.

ideas.title: Closing Desk: outcome-priced total-loss claim operation with a regulatory warranty
ideas.one_liner: Take a carrier's major-loss and total-loss files end to end (contents, ALE, debris, dwelling scope, mortgagee) for a fixed fee per closed file, with a cap-limited warranty on statutory clocks.
ideas.customer: VP Property Claims at mid-size carriers, reciprocals, Florida domestics and residual plans. First 10: 100 open LA total-loss files at a mid-size carrier or the FAIR Plan; a Florida domestic after Isaias.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Claims Officer from the outsourced LAE budget (adjusting and TPA fees); the compliance officer co-signs because the warranty reduces exam exposure.
ideas.problem: Total losses run as separate queues (dwelling, contents, ALE, debris, mortgagee), each with a different adjuster; reassignment resets clocks. CDI listed repeated adjuster reassignment, late status letters and underpayments among 398 violations in a 220-file sample of State Farm; penalties are small ($10,000 per willful violation) but a one-year licence suspension is sought. State Farm is about 78% closed after roughly 20 months. SB 495 (effective Jan 1 2026) requires a 60% contents advance without inventory in declared emergencies.
ideas.solution: One case owner per file, a clock engine for every statutory deadline, templates for status and ALE-extension letters, SB 495 advance workflow, contents valuation, vendor routing, and an indemnity for penalties up to a cap. Surge mode with pre-credentialed adjusters on retainer. Priced per closed file with a cycle-time bonus.
ideas.why_now: CDI Accusation (May 4 2026), LA County suit (Aug 31 2026), ALE ends Jan 7 2027 for many survivors, and the Sept 2026 mitigation rule add clocks; State Farm's closure rate gives every carrier a public benchmark.
ideas.wedge: Contents plus ALE workflow on open Palisades/Eaton files, priced per closed file.
ideas.path_to_100m: Outsourced adjusting about $11.7B (IBISWorld, all lines) x 35% property (assumed) = $4.1B; x 40% major/cat/total-loss (assumed) = $1.6B; $100M is about 6%. Cross-check: about 150k major-loss files a year (assumed) x $6,000 = $900M; $100M is about 11%. No homeowners LAE ratio was found, so these shares are assumptions.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Sedgwick (property split into five product lines, desk outsourcing accepted), Crawford ($1.27B 2025 revenue), Pilot, Frontline, Engle Martin, Alacrity; policyholder-side Claim Architect; AI newcomers (Curant.ai $3.1M seed, Sprout.ai); carriers' own major-loss units.
ideas.why_they_lose: IA firms bill by the hour or file, so automation shrinks their revenue; their adjusters are 1099s shared across firms; none sells a compliance warranty.
ideas.moat: Process power and switching costs (delegated authority, carrier-system integration); scale economies in surge capacity.
ideas.earned_secret: Total losses are slow because five queues restart each other, not because estimating is hard. One owner and a clock engine cut reassignments, and the warranty is only priceable once the clocks are automated (insider hypothesis, unverified). Cliche flag: 'AI claims' is on the cliche list; the differentiators are the warranty and total-loss scope, not first notice of loss.
ideas.first_90_days: Take 100 open files at fixed price; measure reassignments, days to ALE decision and days to contents payment; get an E&O carrier to quote the warranty.

ideas.title: Soft-Landing Exchange: outplacement for non-renewed policyholders, sold to the carrier that is leaving
ideas.one_liner: Sell the leaving carrier a consent-based service that moves its non-renewed policyholders to quoted, bindable offers from other carriers, and keep the resulting agent-of-record commission.
ideas.customer: Carriers cutting exposure in CA, FL, TX, CO and LA, and regulators who want softer exits. First 10: State Farm General's slated nonrenewals for 2027 (about 72,000 announced in 2024, unverified), plus Travelers, Chubb, Nationwide, USAA, Farmers and Allstate, all reported as having pulled back in high-risk California areas.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Exiting carrier (signer: VP Customer/Regulatory Affairs; budget: nonrenewal handling, call centre, complaint and regulatory-risk cost, assumed about $30 a policy); buyer carriers via commission (about 12% of premium, assumed).
ideas.problem: A non-renewal is legally a termination, not a referral. The captive agent cannot place elsewhere, the carrier cannot recommend a competitor, and the policyholder starts from zero inside roughly 75 days (unverified). About 2.03M policies a year are non-renewed; most dissolve into the market and the buyer carriers' acquisition value (about $500 a policy, assumed) is never captured.
ideas.solution: The notice carries an opt-in link; on consent the desk becomes agent of record, pre-qualifies the home against 5-10 appetites using the carrier's own data, shows bindable offers within 24 hours and handles BOR and mortgagee changes. The exiting carrier gets a regulator-ready harm-mitigation report. Legal premise to check: policyholder data-sharing consent (California Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act), nonrenewal notice content rules, any CDI view on carrier-paid referral services, agent licensing.
ideas.why_now: State Farm's no-nonrenewal stay ends Dec 31 2026; NAIC data show nonrenewals up 96-216% since 2018; CDI and the Governor are publicly measuring harm to homeowners; FAIR growth slowed to 1.9% as it tries to depopulate.
ideas.wedge: One carrier's 2027 slated cohort handled as a managed transfer; free pilot on 5,000 policies.
ideas.path_to_100m: 2.03M nonrenewals x 60% re-placeable (assumed) = 1.22M a year. At 15% share that is 183k placements a year; with 85% retention (assumed) the in-force book after five years is about 678k policies. At $2,400 premium x 12% commission x 70% after local-agent splits = $200 a policy, revenue is about $135M in year five. Needs about 15% of the flow; the exiting-carrier fee adds only about $5M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No service sold to the exiting carrier was found. Adjacent: Policygenius, Insurify and The Zebra (leads), Matic (origination), Young Alfred, Bridge Specialty (agents), the FAIR Clearinghouse, retail agents.
ideas.why_they_lose: Aggregators are paid per lead by buyers and have no access to the exiting carrier's data or notice. Captive agents are contractually stuck. The FAIR Clearinghouse serves only FAIR policies.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (a service no carrier or aggregator can offer), cornered resource (carrier-originated cohorts) and recurring commission that accumulates.
ideas.earned_secret: Carriers lose more from the exit story than from the exit: complaints, legislators, press. They already pay for outplacement of laid-off employees; the same logic applies to customers (my inference, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Offer one carrier a free pilot on 5,000 non-renewed policies; measure rebind rate and time to bind; get an informal CDI view.

ideas.title: Draw and Price Oracle: the conflict-free percent-complete and paid-invoice price standard (weakest, flagged)
ideas.one_liner: A neutral percent-complete and paid-invoice price standard that servicers, insurers, contractors and appraisers can all accept, built as the data layer of the Proceeds Desk.
ideas.customer: Servicers (draw approvals), insurers (RC holdback and ALE evidence), public adjusters, contractors and appraisal umpires. First 10: the lenders from the Proceeds Desk plus two PA firms.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Servicer loss-draft head (inspection line), carrier property-claims VP (reserving and disputes), PA principal, litigation counsel.
ideas.problem: Xactimate's list is the de facto price standard, and contractors and advocates say it lags real costs after a surge (advocacy sources). Verisk sells to carriers and contractors and agreed to buy the roofer CRM AccuLynx for $2.35B; Delaware ordered it to perform on Aug 7 2026, and the FTC's reported theory is that Verisk could build an exclusive pricing integration that forecloses rivals. Nobody neutral can say what a line item cost or how complete a job is.
ideas.solution: Photo, permit and invoice ingestion scores percent complete and flags overbilling; a paid-invoice index by line item, ZIP and month; auditable evidence packets for supplements, RC-holdback releases and appraisals.
ideas.why_now: Verisk/AccuLynx ruling and FTC review; LA price disputes; reinsurers and regulators asking about demand surge.
ideas.wedge: Use the Proceeds Desk's draws as the data source; sell evidence packets to LA public adjusters.
ideas.path_to_100m: Servicer inspections: about 305k monitored files x 3 x $100 = $92M at 100% share. Contractor/PA seats: 100k x $600 = $60M. Carrier benchmark licences: 25 x $1M = $25M. Packets: about $15M. Pool about $190M, so $100M needs over 50% of it. It does not reach $100M alone; treat it as a data layer whose value shows up as higher release rates in the Proceeds Desk.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Verisk Xactware (Xactimate; Xactware says 22 of the top 25 US insurers use its tools), Symbility/Cotality, in-house price lists, expert witnesses.
ideas.why_they_lose: Verisk cannot publish a price that contradicts its own list or undercuts its carrier customers; Cotality has the same customer mix.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (paid-invoice data), but only if the Proceeds Desk wins first.
ideas.earned_secret: Disputes are rarely about the dollar amount of a line; they are about the date of the price and the percent complete. A dated paid-invoice index ends the argument (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Load 500 LA invoices; compare to the Xactimate list for the same month; publish the gap.

ideas.title: Rebuild Velocity: an insurer-paid owner's rep priced on ALE months saved
ideas.one_liner: A neutral, homeowner-trusted rebuild coordinator (permits, design, bids, code upgrades, draw readiness) paid a share of the ALE months it saves for the insurer carrying the meter.
ideas.customer: Carriers with open total-loss files in LA and later hurricane, tornado and hail total losses. First 10: three carriers with at least 100 open LA files, plus the FAIR Plan.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Property Claims (budget: ALE and indemnity), with servicers contributing for draw readiness and homeowners paying a small fee.
ideas.problem: The meter runs on the carrier: fewer than a dozen homes rebuilt one year on; 1,153 permits issued of about 2,900 applications by Jan 2 2026; ALE ends Jan 7 2027 for many survivors, extendable up to 12 months on reasonable diligence; NBC LA (July 2026) says 38% have run out or soon will; LA County's suit alleges ALE caps. Survivors are first-time builders; soft costs are $200k-350k+ before a shovel (marketing source, unverified); insurers cannot manage construction and servicers will not release money without progress.
ideas.solution: A neutral coordinator takes the homeowner from payout to permitted start, produces dated progress evidence that satisfies the 'reasonable diligence' test, and lines up draws with the servicer. Paid 40% of ALE months saved (ALE assumed at $5,000 a month; no ALE data found) plus a homeowner fee. Legal premise (decisive, unverified): whether an insurer paying this is steering, an inducement or unlicensed contracting under California rules; the cleanest structure is an opt-in benefit tied to ALE extension.
ideas.why_now: Jan 7 2027 ALE cliff, the LA County suit, and the state's focus on payouts; insurers face a 12-month extension liability on thousands of households.
ideas.wedge: 500 LA households with the longest-open ALE; guarantee four months saved or no fee.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 13,000 homes destroyed x 55% insured primary residences needing extension (assumed) = about 7,150; a 12-month extension at $5k a month is about $430M of insurer cost. Saving four months is $20k a household; at $10k revenue a household (insurer 40% share plus homeowner and servicer fees) LA is about $70M, spread over two to three years. Nationally about 60k major rebuilds a year (assumed) x $10k = $600M; $100M is about 17%. Heroic, and LA is a one-time pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Homebound (design-build with permitting and insurance advisors), The Hub/CORE (project management and escrow oversight), LA County One-Stop Permit Centers (free), Habitat plus Foothill Catalog (pre-approved plans), Samara/Steadfast and Cover (modular), Claim Architect (policyholder-side estimates), RockRose (mitigation). No insurer-funded programme was found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each is paid by the homeowner or by charity; none is paid by the party carrying the meter, and none is neutral enough to certify diligence.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (permit and contractor throughput data) and process power; weak until an insurer signs.
ideas.earned_secret: The biggest controllable cost in a total loss is time to rebuild, not the dwelling number, and nobody owns it; the insurer wants it owned but cannot own construction (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Offer three carriers a no-fee pilot on 100 files; measure months from payout to permit; get counsel's view on the payment structure.

ideas.title: Defensible-Space Network: annual, verified, route-dense fire-hardening subscription
ideas.one_liner: A route-dense subscription that keeps the 0-5 ft and 100 ft zones compliant every year and produces an inspection-grade record that insurers and fire departments accept.
ideas.customer: Homeowners in very high fire zones and state responsibility areas; HOAs; insurers that want fewer high-risk renewals. First 10: 500 homes in one local-responsibility-area city with an active fire-department inspection programme (LA County charges $151 a parcel).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Homeowner (subscription, assumed $1,000 a year); HOA board (signer: president or treasurer); insurers may co-fund for high-score policies (unverified, to be tested).
ideas.problem: The 100-ft defensible-space law has applied since 2005. Zone 0 emergency rules were adopted Aug 19 2026 for close to 2M homes, with existing-home deadlines of 3-5 years (earliest about 2029; sources conflict). CAL FIRE can fund only 129,206 inspections a year against a 250,000 goal. Insurers must credit mitigation and offer free inspections (CDI FAQ rev. Sep 4 2026). Compliance decays within a year and no one sells upkeep with proof.
ideas.solution: Annual or quarterly crews, goats and chippers on routes, with before-and-after geotagged evidence stored for the fire department and insurers; certificate packet for sale and rating credits; add Zone 0 conversions when deadlines bite.
ideas.why_now: Zone 0 adoption, the Sept 4 CDI FAQ, the inspection capacity gap, and unfunded state loans (SB 894 signed Sep 29 2026 with no appropriation) mean homeowners pay and need proof.
ideas.wedge: One city, 500 homes, a letter from the fire department accepting the evidence format.
ideas.path_to_100m: 100,000 homes x $1,000 a year = $100M, which is 5% of the roughly 2M Zone 0 homes (assumed price and uptake). Needs multi-state expansion for safety. Zone 0 retrofit spend is upside, not the base case.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Local tree and landscape firms (thousands), goat grazers, RockRose (roll-up of tree-trimming and roofing firms; $12.5M Series A; considering a $30-40M credit facility), BurnBot (Mercury-backed), private fire-defence contractors hired by insurers (unverified), Fire Safe Councils, CAL FIRE and local fire departments.
ideas.why_they_lose: Local firms cannot document to an insurer's standard or build routes across towns. RockRose is a carrier/broker first and early.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (route density), switching costs (the compliance record) and a possible standard if fire departments accept the evidence format.
ideas.earned_secret: Compliance is an annual re-grow problem, not a one-time retrofit, so it is a subscription; a homeowner who clears once drifts out of compliance within 12 months (insider hypothesis, unverified). Whiplash flag: Zone 0 existing-home deadlines may slip, so the business should stand on the 2005 law and insurer credits first.
ideas.first_90_days: Agree the evidence format with a fire department; run 100 homes; test whether two insurers will credit or co-pay; price at $75-100 a month.

verdicts.title: Custody Mutual: jail-health liability program priced on clinical process data

competitors_found.name: County risk pools (e.g. Association of County Commissioners of Oklahoma pools)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Pool jail and law-enforcement liability for member counties; created because commercial cover was unavailable
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Cover most Oklahoma county jails; pool-level premiums in the hundreds of thousands per county

competitors_found.name: Correctional Risk Services (via Montana Association of Counties)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Administers catastrophic inmate medical insurance and claims administration programs for state county associations

competitors_found.name: E&S jail insurance wholesalers (Complete Markets storefront)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Place jail liability, professional liability and excess limits for counties and private jails in the surplus-lines market
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Mature brokerage channel; no funded jail-specific insurtech found

competitors_found.name: Maine statutory county jail-medical pool
competitors_found.what_they_do: State law lets 5+ counties self-fund a pool covering 80% of jail medical expenses over $10,000 per prisoner

verdicts.substitutes: Taxpayer self-insurance (Multnomah-style self-funding), county pools and joint-powers authorities, vendor-purchased professional liability with the county as additional insured, higher deductibles (Rockingham NC deductible rose from $10k to $200k), and counties simply dropping or reducing limits.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea assumes 1,200 deaths x 30-40% claim rate x $2-3M = $0.7-1.4B. Observed settlements are lower and selection-biased (Cuyahoga $1.35M across 4 suits, San Bernardino $3.23M across 4; the $9-20M cases are the news). At about $0.75M per claim the loss pool is nearer $0.5B, premium-equivalent about $0.7B, insurable share about $0.3-0.4B. Real whole-package county premiums are $0.35M (Rockingham NC) to $0.7M (Camden GA). $100M GWP is 25-30% share, and an MGA keeps only about 15-20% of it, so $100M GWP is about $15-20M revenue. Booking $100M of revenue means becoming the risk-bearing carrier (about $60-70M surplus, long-tail reserving).
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Vendors hand over EHR timestamps despite discovery risk: low plausibility. (2) Process indicators actually separate bad from average outcomes in 50 closed claims: unknown but cheap to test. (3) A fronting carrier and reinsurer back a first-of-kind program: plausible. (4) 15-20% share of insurable jail liability in 6 years via pools: low-to-moderate. Reaching $100M of revenue additionally requires converting to a risk-bearing carrier with 25-30% share: not credible.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: PSQIA protects only patient safety work product reported to a PSO, never original medical records; in Crawford v. Corizon (jail death) the court ordered most documents produced because the vendor could not show they were assembled for a PSO. I found nothing on whether sharing with a liability insurer waives privilege. Deliberate indifference turns on what officials knew, so a dashboard showing notice creates the exhibit it claims to prevent. Punitive damages are barred against counties under Newport v. Fact Concerts (background knowledge), so that gate is narrower than the idea says. The Wellpath indemnity-gap premise is real (self-insured retentions up to $8M per incident, Cobb County fraud suit) but the cover counties actually need is mostly bought via additional-insured status, not a new MGA.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Insurable pool is about $0.3-0.4B; $100M GWP is 25-30% share and only about $15-20M of MGA revenue; the data and privilege premises are fragile.

verdicts.title: Outside Care Plan: the DOC's own off-site health plan

competitors_found.name: Prime Health Services / Prime Corrections
competitors_found.what_they_do: Savings-share bill review and repricing of off-site inmate medical bills for county sheriffs (NC sheriffs plan since 2011, Florida, Wisconsin); no risk, no access guarantees
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Flagler County alone saved $1.05M in a year; idea cites $88M cumulative documented savings

competitors_found.name: Heritage Health Care Solutions (Polk County FL TPA sole-source)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Third-party administrator adjudicating and paying off-site inmate medical and pharmacy claims for a county

competitors_found.name: Centene / Centurion
competitors_found.what_they_do: Medicaid-plan parent running full-service state prison health contracts, incl. hospital networks and risk (Maryland $1.7B prisons plus $723M pretrial)

competitors_found.name: CDCR/CCHCS provider network and prior authorization (RFP SD25-00019)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Largest state's off-site specialty network and prior authorization procured as a TPA-style contract
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Five-year term plus five one-year extensions; value not stated

competitors_found.name: State university and state-paid models (Texas, Iowa, Connecticut, Georgia, NC corrections hospitals)
competitors_found.what_they_do: 17 states deliver care directly and 4 use a university model; they pay off-site claims from their own budget, usually at Medicaid or Medicare-based schedules

verdicts.substitutes: State-set fee schedules (Mississippi 200% of Medicaid; South Carolina 135% of Medicare; Utah and NC lower rates for non-contract hospitals; California receiver caps), Medicaid inpatient claiming for expansion-state stays, carve-out of inpatient care in 5 states, repricing TPAs, and the state simply replacing the failed vendor (Alabama to NaphCare, Maryland to Centurion).
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Off-site is 20-27% of about $11B = $2.2-3.0B headline (Pew confirms 27% Virginia, 23% New York). But Pew shows Medicaid expansion moved most inpatient stays to Medicaid at the lowest rates, 5 states already carve out inpatient care, and 17 states plus 4 university-model states already pay off-site directly. My haircut: about $1.4-2.0B reachable. As a risk-bearer revenue is premium, so $100M is about 5-7% of that (one large state or 2-3 mid-size), at 5-8% margin = $5-8M gross profit. Prime's $88M in cumulative savings over about 14 years shows the non-risk repricing fee pool is tiny.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) 2-3 states restructure a vendor or in-house arrangement to carve hospital payments out to a third-party risk-bearer: no 2026 precedent (every shock produced a vendor swap), low plausibility. (2) Hospitals accept Medicare-plus rates for 15-day payment and 5-10 year volume: plausible. (3) Insurer or health-plan licensure and stop-loss are workable in target states: unknown, unverified. (4) Georgia-style unpaid-provider fallout makes a 'payer of last resort' valuable to DOCs: plausible but not yet a procurement trend.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Assuming risk for hospital claims on a prepaid basis likely triggers insurance or HMO licensure in many states; not verified per state. Federal precedent (Marshals/BOP Medicare-based pricing) is real but state rate caps already capture much of the repricing. HHS-OIG is auditing improper Medicaid capitation payments for incarcerated people (report due 2026), a regulatory flag for the Medicaid-match piece.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real budget line and pain, but states already hold carve-outs, Medicaid rates and TPAs, 2026 buyers replaced vendors instead of restructuring, and risk-bearing needs licensure and capital for a 5-8% margin.

verdicts.title: Clinical Corps: pre-cleared nurse and tele-psychiatry pool

competitors_found.name: AB Staffing Solutions
competitors_found.what_they_do: Correctional travel nurse and clinician staffing since 2002; clients include ICE, US Marshals, federal, state and county facilities

competitors_found.name: North Carolina DAC competitively bid nurse vendors (21)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Twenty-one bid vendors supply 13-week contract nurses to NC prisons
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: NC prison health spend $400M in FY2024; RN vacancy about 48% (July 2026)

competitors_found.name: CDCR/CCHCS Mental Health Registry Network (RFP SD25-00031)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Single contractor runs California's statewide temporary and relief mental-health staffing registry; 3-year firm-fixed price from 2027-01-01, 80% fill-rate target (aggregator listing, unverified)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Rates confidential; incumbent probably Management Solutions (unconfirmed)

competitors_found.name: Generic per-diem marketplaces and travel-nurse firms (AMN, Cross Country, ShiftKey, Clipboard Health)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Place nurses into any setting; corrections share not verified
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Public and venture-scale; corrections share unverified

verdicts.substitutes: State overtime and float pools, civil-service hiring with raises (NC gave 5.5%), vendors' own recruiters, and the CDCR-run telepsychiatry hubs under the Coleman stipulation.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea's $0.9-1.3B agency-labor pool (8-12% of state-prison health budgets) is not sourced. The 2.5x contract versus state hourly gap ($64 vs $25.40) is from a 2023 DAC table, while NC Health News (July 2026) says contract nurses cost about 30% more, so the pilot saving ($54 vs $64) is probably overstated. $100M would be 8-11% of an unverified pool at 20-25% gross margin. Staffing revenue is gross billing, so $100M is reachable in principle but not with a copyable product.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Clearances and training are portable across 15-20 states: low plausibility, each state has its own background and key-control rules. (2) States let contractors pay above civil-service scales: plausible. (3) Win the California registry or its tele-psychiatry gap: the RFP is already bid, so low for this cycle. (4) Margin survives once rivals copy the credential in 6-12 months (the idea's own estimate): low.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: W-2 versus 1099, staffing licensure and contracting-out rules are untested. The idea's own moat rating is 'weak'.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Corrections staffing already exists and is bid competitively; the idea itself rates the moat weak and copyable in 6-12 months.

verdicts.title: Piggyback Prime: the first cooperative contract for jail medical services

competitors_found.name: NaphCare TechCare on NASPO ValuePoint (MA #LS5009, Utah lead)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Cooperative vehicle for a corrections EHR (SaaS) only, purchasable without RFP from 2026-09-16 once a participating addendum is signed
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: TechCare in 220+ facilities; NaphCare also took Alabama's prisons on emergency basis

competitors_found.name: NASPO ValuePoint correctional supplies (Bob Barker, South Carolina lead)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Cooperative contract for correctional products and supplies, not medical services

competitors_found.name: Full-service vendors acting as primes (NaphCare, Centurion, CFG, Mediko)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Already hold the prime role and emergency sole-source awards after failures (Alabama to NaphCare, Polk to CFG)

verdicts.substitutes: Emergency sole-source procurement (already used in Georgia 2024 and Alabama 2026), interlocal agreements, and incumbents extending their own contracts to neighbouring counties.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea's own math: $100M gross is $8-12M net (8-12% prime take); $100M net would need about $1B gross, about 20% of an estimated $5B jail pool, which the idea calls heroic. Recognised revenue could be gross if the prime is principal, but then it carries all the clinical liability on a thin margin.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) A cooperative accepts a professional-services solicitation for clinical care with indemnity: unproven, none found. (2) Rival operators subcontract to the prime: low plausibility. (3) Sheriffs give up local procurement control: low. (4) Emergency buyers choose the pre-papered vehicle over the best-capacity vendor: plausible but unproven.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: No cooperative contract for jail medical services found (supplies, EHR and generic staffing only). Piggyback rules for clinical services and prime licensure vary by state and were not checked. A prime holding the indemnity is the exact structure that failed with Wellpath and YesCare.
verdicts.deciding_reason: A prime that holds the contract and the liability is just a new thin-margin Wellpath; $8-12M net on $100M gross by its own math, and operators will not subcontract to a rival.

verdicts.title: Day 91: reentry care organization that starts inside the walls

competitors_found.name: FQHCs and county health systems (e.g. Peach Tree Health with Partnership HealthPlan)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Run the jail-to-plan warm handoff with case managers and community health workers, billing the state's reentry bundles and ECM
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Existing Medi-Cal providers; California first year: 159,000+ billable services, 24,000+ enrolled pre-release

competitors_found.name: CalAIM PATH-funded CBOs and ECM providers
competitors_found.what_they_do: Justice-involved capacity-building grants to community organizations; ECM providers contract with plans
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: PATH is a five-year $1.85B initiative, $1.66B+ awarded

competitors_found.name: Total Reentry Solutions
competitors_found.what_they_do: Detroit healthtech platform linking health systems, payors and social services for people leaving custody

competitors_found.name: Cityblock Health (adjacent risk-bearing Medicaid model)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Risk-bearing care for high-need Medicaid members; no reentry contract found
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Series D 2021 at about $5.7B (aggregator); revenue undisclosed

competitors_found.name: Wellpath, NaphCare, CFG reentry offerings and Medicaid plans' in-house teams
competitors_found.what_they_do: Custody vendors and plans already offer reentry coordination under the 1115 waivers
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Waivers now in 22 states plus DC

verdicts.substitutes: Plans' own care managers, FQHC and CBO ECM teams, nonprofit Transitions Clinic Network, and county reentry offices.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea: 33,000 members x $3,000 = $100M, about 7% of 500,000 high-need releases. But jail stays under 90 days cannot use a 90-day pre-release benefit, so the reachable high-need cohort looks like 100-200k a year (my estimate), making 33,000 members 17-33% share. California's pre-release bundles pay per claim (about $256 health risk assessment, $199 care plan, $167 warm handoff), so pre-release is a small pool; the idea's '$16M reimbursed' and '42,000 eligible' did not verify. I could not find a published post-release ECM PMPM. Full-risk $16-20k per member-year needs plans to delegate total cost of care, which I did not see anywhere in reentry.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Plans sub-capitate 12-month total cost of care for released members to a specialist: not yet seen in reentry, low-to-moderate. (2) 4-5 states keep funding the benefit through 2031: plausible (CMS approved 3 more on 2026-09-23) but Michigan withdrew for lack of appropriation. (3) Release-date data feed stays proprietary: weak, the waivers build it in. (4) Outcome data (ED, overdose) is strong enough to move plans: unproven.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: CMS reentry framework confirmed live (22 states plus DC, approvals Oct 2026 to Sept 2031) and I found no rescission. Wrong-payer risk is real (Connecticut study put savings in the justice budget). Federal Medicaid cuts and work requirements from 2027 are a flagged risk.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real Medicaid-paid benefit, but FQHCs, CBOs, plans and vendors already deliver it, the release-date pipe is built into the waivers, and the payer and federal funding can walk.

verdicts.title: Cure Carve-Out: high-cost drugs out of the per-diem

competitors_found.name: Louisiana subscription model (Asegua/Gilead)
competitors_found.what_they_do: State-run capped-spend subscription for hepatitis C cures covering Medicaid and about 1,500 incarcerated people by 2022; prison price was about $10k a patient before the deal
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: State program; NBER found it more than pays for itself

competitors_found.name: Federal Cure Hepatitis C Act (H.R. 9682 / S. 1941)
competitors_found.what_they_do: HHS five-year subscription purchasing with correctional opt-in; $5.5B appropriation proposed

competitors_found.name: Vendor pharmacies, manufacturer-direct deals and state in-house programs
competitors_found.what_they_do: Existing drug supply routes for prison hepatitis C treatment

verdicts.substitutes: Court-ordered treatment under settlements (Colorado, Indiana, Kentucky), state subscription deals, and the DOC simply paying per cure at a falling net price.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea assumes 100-170k infected prisoners. A 2019-2023 survey of all state prison systems found 15.2% antibody-positive and 8.7% viremic, about 91,090 people. At about $10k net (Louisiana's prison price) that is about $0.9B one time, not annual, mostly drug pass-through; the operator's net fee is 6-10% of it. Even adding HIV and long-acting MOUD, an operator net of $100M a year is not reachable, and the idea itself says it is probably a feature of Outside Care Plan.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Needs states to mandate pass-through and the federal subscription bill to fail, while the operator keeps a fee on HIV and MOUD volumes too. Each is plausible alone; together they still cap near $25M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: 340B patient-definition eligibility for people in custody was not found. H.R. 9682 would put the drug purchasing layer in HHS, and the 2025 Senate version (S. 1941) makes correctional populations eligible. Louisiana already proved the subscription mechanism without an intermediary.
verdicts.deciding_reason: A finite, mostly pass-through $0.9B one-time pool with a 6-10% fee that a pending federal subscription bill would bypass.

verdicts.title: Day 21: forensic capacity for court-ordered competency restoration

competitors_found.name: Wellpath Recovery Solutions
competitors_found.what_they_do: Forensic, civil-commitment and jail-based restoration programs for states and counties (Florida Treasure Coast 224 beds, Kern 60 beds, Washington 30 beds, Colorado RISE)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $425M revenue, about 3,000 patients, 70 facilities, 10 states; now owned by Wellpath's creditors

competitors_found.name: Liberty Healthcare (San Bernardino jail-based program)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Jail-hosted restoration treatment for California DSH; $17.98M over three years for 96 beds (about $170 per bed-day), later expanded to 126

competitors_found.name: HHSC private contracted beds (747 beds/day)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Texas already buys private inpatient forensic capacity; vendors not named in sources
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Roughly $120-190M a year at $450-700 per day (my arithmetic)

competitors_found.name: County jail-based programs (Hays County with Hill Country MHDD; Harris County JBCR)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Counties launch their own jail-based restoration, Harris at about $261 per patient-day versus about $412 at state hospitals
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: County and HHSC grant funded; HHSC says earlier JBCR programs barely moved wait times

competitors_found.name: GEO Group, Universal Health Services, Acadia
competitors_found.what_they_do: GEO ran Florida forensic hospitals (2008 OPPAGA); UHS and Acadia are large private psychiatric operators, current competency contracts unverified

verdicts.substitutes: State-built hospital beds (HHSC: 175 new and 540 replaced by 2027, about $2.5B for 680 state-owned beds, roughly $3.7M per bed), county jail-based programs, outpatient competency restoration and diversion (Colorado), and simply paying fines.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M is about 600 full-service beds at $450 a day (600 x 450 x 365 = $98.6M). Price matters: jail-hosted treatment slots are $170 (Liberty) to $261 (Harris), while full-service beds are $412-$800 and Wellpath RS earns about $388 per patient-day, so the core must be full-service secure beds. Texas: 1,626 on the wait list in June 2026, 175 net new state beds by 2027, HHSC told lawmakers it would still be short; I estimate a 1,000+ bed gap worth $160M+ a year. National unmet 3,000-4,000 beds (idea's estimate, unsourced) makes $100M about 15-20% share, at the edge of heroic. Margin is thin and exit multiples low (Wellpath RS sold to creditors at about 0.9x revenue).
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Fifth Circuit upholds Ward v. Muth (permanent injunction 2026-07-07, 21 days, four years): uncertain, the state is appealing and a 2012 21-day order was paused. (2) HHSC meets it partly by contracting rather than only building, which its $3.7M-per-bed build cost and 747 private beds/day support: plausible. (3) Win 300-400 Texas full-service beds plus 150-200 in Washington/Oklahoma/other states over 5-6 years: plausible for top-decile execution. (4) Licensure and psychiatric/RN staffing hold up on a 6-12 month timeline: moderate. (5) Incumbents with owned beds do not win everything: moderate.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Verified: Ward v. Muth, W.D. Tex. No. 1:16-CV-00917, Judge Ezra, permanent injunction 2026-07-07, 21 days from commitment order, four years to comply, state asked the Fifth Circuit to postpone benchmarks and argues the remedy was never constitutionally required (no ruling found). Texas law lets inpatient competency restoration occur only in HHSC-operated or HHSC-contracted facilities, and SB 528 (89R) requires cost-comparison reporting. Colorado's decree runs through 2027-12-01 and Colorado has paid $55M in capped fines ($242M uncapped); Oklahoma paid $928,400 in its first month; Washington was fined about $100M in 2026. Idea's $400M Washington figure did not verify.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Court mandate, an existing HHSC private-bed budget line, proven category scale and a state build cost far above a contracted bed; thin moat and Fifth Circuit risk are the open issues.

verdicts.title: Open-Book Health Authority: fee-only management for counties that lost their vendor

competitors_found.name: Wellpath management-services-organization model (Oswego County NY)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Already sells a management-fee MSO with pass-through costs: $500,000 fee on a projected $3.07M budget

competitors_found.name: County in-house and public-hospital models (Allegheny, Barnstable, Alameda Health System proposal)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Counties run jail care themselves or via a public hospital; Allegheny paid Corizon about $12M a year and estimated $2-3M to manage in-house

competitors_found.name: Washington County OR and Putnam County TN hybrid cost-reimbursement contracts
competitors_found.what_they_do: Existing fixed-fee-plus-pass-through and true-up structures in county contracts

verdicts.substitutes: County in-house teams, public hospital districts, consultants and RFP advisers, and vendors' own cost-plus or MSO options.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 6-10% fee on a $10-19M county contract is $0.6-1.9M per county; Oswego's fee is about 16% of a tiny budget. $100M of fee needs 50+ large counties sold one at a time. The idea's gross $100-180M 'including employer-of-record payroll' contradicts its own structure, where the county is the employer and licensee, so payroll is not company revenue.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Needs 20-30 counties converted in 5-6 years through emergency bridges (low, county procurement is slow), plus data and software revenue layered on (unproven), plus a hospital-district partner willing to scale across counties (low).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: County employment, pension, sovereign-immunity and Medicaid/340B eligibility for a county-employed clinic were not verified. The demand signal is real (Barnstable, Monterey, Shasta switched) but buyers mostly chose another vendor, not a fee-only authority.
verdicts.deciding_reason: The model already exists inside Wellpath, the fee pool is a small percentage of each county budget, and county-by-county sales cannot reach $100M of money the company keeps.

picks.from_title: Day 21: forensic capacity for court-ordered competency restoration
picks.title: Day 21: multi-state operator of full-service forensic restoration beds
picks.one_liner: An operator that adds licensed secure forensic beds in 6-12 months, paid per available bed-day by state forensic agencies under court deadlines, starting with Texas.
picks.sharpened_pitch: A multi-state operator of full-service secure competency-restoration beds, sold on 5-year availability-based contracts to state forensic agencies, delivered in leased and modular licensed units next to existing campuses, with an owned clinical staffing pool and an outpatient restoration track for low-risk defendants. Do not make jail-hosted treatment-only slots the core: Liberty's San Bernardino contract works out to about $170 per bed-day (county supplies the bed) and Harris County's program about $261, while full-service beds price at $412-$800 and Wellpath Recovery Solutions earns about $388 per patient-day. $100M needs about 600 full-service beds at $450. Texas is the anchor: the wait list was 1,626 in June 2026, HHSC adds only 175 net new beds by 2027 and told lawmakers it will still be short, and a state-built bed costs about $3.7M against about $164k a year for a contracted one. Then replicate under the same kind of pressure in Washington, Oklahoma and Colorado. Use jail-based units only as a door opener with counties that are already suing. The edge is speed, outcome data (days to competency, restoration rate) and a staffed, licensed footprint, not a technology moat.
picks.payer_and_signer: Payer: Texas HHSC's private inpatient competency-restoration bed line (about 747 beds a day already contracted), plus equivalent forensic lines in Washington DSHS, Oklahoma ODMHSAS and Colorado CDHS. Signer: HHSC deputy executive commissioner for state hospitals and procurement; the legislature appropriates (next regular session starts January 2027), and the federal court monitors benchmarks.
picks.path_to_100m: 600 beds x $450 x 365 = $98.6M. Example mix by year 6: Texas 350 beds, Washington 150, Oklahoma/Colorado/next-wave state 100. Texas alone is a 1,000+ bed gap I estimate at $160M+ a year; the national unmet need is 3,000-4,000 beds per the pool file (unsourced), so $100M is roughly 15-20% share, at the edge of heroic. Requires 5-year take-or-pay or availability payments to finance leased units. Revenue per full-service bed is about $164k a year; exit multiples are low (Wellpath RS sold at about 0.9x revenue).
picks.competitors_and_edge: Wellpath Recovery Solutions ($425M revenue, 3,000 patients, 70 facilities, creditor-owned), Liberty Healthcare, GEO Group, and likely UHS and Acadia (unverified); HHSC's current private-bed vendors are not named in public sources. Edge: deployable in 6-12 months versus years for state construction ($2.5B for about 680 beds), a price below HHSC's own cost per bed ($412 at Harris's state-hospital comparison, $697 at North Texas State Hospital in 2016), and a clean restoration-outcome record. Edge is thin and copyable by incumbents with buildings.
picks.why_now: Ward v. Muth permanent injunction on 2026-07-07 requires admission within 21 days with four years to comply; HHSC says beds will still fall short; Washington fined about $100M in 2026; Oklahoma began paying $100-$500 a day per waiting person in Oct 2025; Colorado has paid $55M in capped fines through a decree that ends 2027-12-01; Wellpath RS is now creditor-owned, loosening an incumbent.
picks.moat: Thin: licensed and permitted beds, site and lease agreements, 3-5 year contracts, a credentialed staff pool and a restoration-outcome record. A rival with owned buildings can copy it; the defence is speed to first contract and track record.
picks.biggest_open_risk: The Fifth Circuit narrows or reverses Ward v. Muth (the state has asked it to pause benchmarks, argues the Constitution never required the remedy, and an earlier 2012 21-day order was paused), removing the urgency that moves Texas from building to buying.
picks.cheapest_next_test: File a Texas Public Information Act request to HHSC for every private inpatient competency-restoration contract (vendor, per diem, beds, term, occupancy) and the SB 528 cost-comparison report; read the benchmark order and any Fifth Circuit stay ruling on the docket; get three modular or leased-unit quotes and staffing plans for a 60-bed unit; call the Dallas and Bexar sheriffs and HHSC contract management.

result.pool_note: The vendor-bankruptcy shock produced vendor swaps, not new structures, so ideas needing buyers to restructure stalled. Gross pass-through revenue (primes, drugs, fee-only, MGA premium) hid small net revenue. The survivor had a court mandate, an existing budget line and physical capacity. Round-1 pattern repeated: thin moats everywhere.

ideas.title: Werkhof
ideas.one_liner: A net-lease landlord that buys the owner's privately held operating building at the moment the company is sold and leases it back to the successor for 15-20 years, so the owner exits clean and the buyer needs about a third less financing.
ideas.customer: Owner-managers aged 58-68 who hold the Betriebsimmobilie personally or in a Besitz-KG and rent it to their own GmbH, and the successors who cannot fund company plus building.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The successor's operating company pays rent from operating costs (it replaces debt service). Signers: the retiring Inhaber (sale) and the successor Geschaeftsfuehrer (lease); the Steuerberater recommends. Capital side: a Pfandbrief or insurer lender's credit committee plus equity LPs.
ideas.problem: The building is the second-largest asset and the hidden deal-killer. A building a shareholder rents to his GmbH is usually a Betriebsaufspaltung (BFH treats it as an essential operating asset). When the shares go to an unrelated buyer the link ends and hidden reserves in the building can become taxable (CMS Law, Steuerschroeder). The owner is left with three bad choices: sell building with company (successor cannot fund both), cash it out taxed, or stay landlord to a stranger.
ideas.solution: A standardised, notarised sale (of the building, or the Besitz entity where that is tax-better) to Werkhof at closing, with a triple-net 15-20 year indexed lease to the new owner and a tenant buy-back option. The first product is a tax-first term sheet built with the owner's Steuerberater, not a price quote.
ideas.why_now: KfW Jan 2026: prices are up 34% since 2019 to an average EUR 499k, while the 077 loan funds only 35% of costs up to EUR 500k and only for natural persons, so the building is the cheque that breaks the financing stack. 119,000 short-term successions are already agreed or in talks. E&Y found 11.6% of Mittelstaendler could imagine selling real estate.
ideas.wedge: Standardised sale-and-leaseback of buildings worth EUR 0.5-2.5M (Handwerk, light industry, wholesale) tied to an identified successor. First 10 customers via 10-15 Steuerberater kanzleien in Bavaria and NRW (largest absolute handover counts per IfM).
ideas.path_to_100m: Rent of EUR 87M ($100M) at a 7% net initial yield (my assumption for thin-credit single tenants) = EUR 1.24B of buildings. At EUR 1.2M average that is about 1,030 assets, built at 225 a year over 4.6 years. If 25% of the 37,200 actual handovers a year (IfM) have an owner-held building (my assumption; no national statistic found, only that Mittelstand firms own about 75% of used property), that is 9,300 a year, so Werkhof needs about 2.4% of them. Capital: about EUR 370-430M equity plus EUR 800-870M secured debt, so it needs a real-estate sponsor, not a seed round.
ideas.who_does_it_today: DAL Deutsche Anlagen-Leasing (Sparkassen-Finanzgruppe) markets Immobilienleasing for succession; Nord Leasing does machinery sale-and-rent-back; Sparkassen sell Immobilien-Leasing (a leasing executive says they are often called 'as an emergency anchor' late). Free substitute: the owner keeps the building and rents it to the successor, which is the default today. I did not find DAL's minimum ticket.
ideas.why_they_lose: Leasing arms are project-driven and sold at the Berater's discretion, not a standard small-ticket product with a Steuerberater channel. Sparkassen want the building loan and the deposits, not a buyer that removes both. Nobody owns the tax-first workflow.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (cost of capital, standard documents) plus switching costs (15-20 year leases); counter-positioning against bank-owned leasing arms.
ideas.earned_secret: In small-company sales the argument is rarely about price. It is about what happens to the building after tax. A buyer of the building that lets the owner pick the cheapest tax path unlocks deals that otherwise die in the Steuerberater's office.
ideas.first_90_days: Get a written tax memo on the three exit paths from two Steuerberater firms. Sign 10 kanzleien for a free Immobilien-Check. Underwrite 5 live buildings. Get one Pfandbrief-bank term sheet on a pooled facility. Draft the notarial template. Kill risks: lender appetite for small single-tenant assets, tax structure too expensive for most owners, yield above 7% for weak tenants.

ideas.title: Verkaufsreif
ideas.one_liner: A 6-24 month 'make it sellable' programme for owners 58-66 that is paid only at closing (about 9-10% of price), producing audited normalised earnings and the first price database for sub-EUR 2M firms.
ideas.customer: Owner-managed firms with 3-30 employees, 1-3 years before the planned exit.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The seller-owner, from sale proceeds at closing (a transaction cost netted from the price). Signer: the Inhaber, introduced by the Steuerberater. Later buyers (holding vehicles, lenders) pay for data access.
ideas.problem: Deals die 24 months before the negotiation: owners stop investing (KfW: about -32% investment in firms with short-term plans), the owner is the only relationship holder, books are tax-minimised so buyers cannot see earnings, and expectations meet reality only at LOI (owner median 0.6x revenue versus a Bau/Handwerk market range of 0.25-0.50x). KfW itself says there is no generally accepted pricing scheme. The 42% of closure planners who cite bureaucracy never start.
ideas.solution: A fixed programme: normalised-EBITDA package; install a Prokurist or Betriebsleiter and move key customer relationships into the firm; e-invoice/GoBD/ERP clean-up; capture the owner's tacit knowledge; then run a buyer process into a pool of pre-qualified buyers (Meisterwerk and Teamkauf below, PE platforms, strategics, individuals). The platform fronts the cost and is repaid at closing.
ideas.why_now: Closures exceed successions for the first time (KfW Jan 2026); 186,000 firms plan to hand over by end-2026; 11% see modernisation cost as a hurdle; nexxt-change 2.0 will make listings free and commodity, so paid value moves to readiness and certainty.
ideas.wedge: Handwerk and small trade/wholesale firms with EUR 0.8-4M revenue. First 10 from a Steuerberater panel and an HWK Nachfolgemoderator in one region.
ideas.path_to_100m: 9-10% of an average EUR 450,000 price = EUR 40,500-45,000 a closing. EUR 87M needs 1,930-2,150 closings a year = 5.2-5.8% of the 37,200 actual handovers a year (about 2x the roughly 1,100 a year nexxt-change has initiated). Staffing: about 300 transaction managers at 7 closings each. It needs a 45-55% close rate; it is the only fee model in this pool that gets near $100M without heroic share.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Unternehmensmakler and M&A boutiques (e.g. Nachfolgekontor), IHK/HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren (free), nexxt-change (free, 431 regional partners), Steuerberater with DATEV Vermoegensnachfolge and wevalue valuation on the DATEV Marktplatz, Sparkassen advisers.
ideas.why_they_lose: Brokers are paid only at closing, so they cannot fund 12-24 months of preparation. Chambers are free and cannot operate. Steuerberater are barred from referral shares (section 9 StBerG, 'sonstige Vorteile') and from most success fees (section 9a, narrow exceptions, from memory), and the sale may cost them the client. DATEV's valuation is a tax valuation, not a market price.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the only dataset of normalised earnings to realised prices below EUR 2M) plus process power.
ideas.earned_secret: The price gap and the owner-dependence are curable, but only if someone is willing to work for free for two years and be repaid out of the closing. Nobody in the chain has that incentive.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 10 owners with 24-month exclusivity and a tail clause (to stop disintermediation). Build the normalisation template with two Steuerberater. Price 20 closed comps from advisers. Recruit 5 buyers. Get counsel on the fee premise. Kill risks: disintermediation after the free work; programme cost per closing above EUR 15k.

ideas.title: Meisterwerk
ideas.one_liner: A steward-owned, permanent-capital buyer of micro Handwerk and technical-service firms (electrical testing, fire protection, heating and water service, lift maintenance), priced below what private equity can touch, with a Meister equity ladder for the people who run them.
ideas.customer: Owners 58-68 of firms with EUR 0.8-2.5M revenue and recurring inspection and service contracts.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The customers of the firms (building owners, property managers, small industry) pay from maintenance budgets. Capital comes from permanent-capital LPs (Versorgungswerk or family office CIO). Signer on each deal: the seller-owner.
ideas.problem: A-trades in Germany need a Meister as owner or Betriebsleiter on the Handwerksrolle (from memory, HwO section 7; verify). When the owner retires, the licence leaves with him. PE platforms want EBITDA above EUR 1M and a sale in 4-6 years; micro firms are below that and sellers fear a flip.
ideas.solution: Buy at 0.25-0.50x revenue (FINANCE range) with half deferred against retention of service contracts. The old Meister stays 2-3 years as Betriebsleiter (a Ludwig-Froehler-Institut finding). The firm sponsors a Geselle to Meister, who earns equity in the local firm over 5 years. Central back office, procurement, compliance scheduling and insurance. No AI claim.
ideas.why_now: HWK Dortmund spring 2026: 33% of Handwerk firms plan a handover within 5 years. About 100,000 unfilled Handwerk positions (KOFA 7/2026). KfW: owners value continuity (EBO 28%, MBO 24% considered). BMJV/BMF key points for a GmbH mit gebundenem Vermoegen (Feb-Mar 2026), though no draft bill is confirmed.
ideas.wedge: Elektro and SHK firms with periodic-inspection books in two regions; the first 10 acquisitions from HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren.
ideas.path_to_100m: 60 firms x EUR 1.5M revenue = EUR 90M ($103.5M). Purchase price EUR 22-45M in total (0.25-0.50x revenue) plus working capital; 12 deals a year over 5 years. This needs about 0.03% of handovers, so the limit is Meister supply and integration, not market share. Revenue is bought; expect a 6-9% operating margin. This is the least original idea here and the surest path to $100M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: HWP Handwerkspartner (Adiuva to Goldbeck Robens), Builtech Group, Konzmann Gruppe, TBS Brandschutz (DBAG's Fire Holding), FOGTEC (Deutsche Private Equity), svt (Ergon). Free substitute: the owner closes.
ideas.why_they_lose: Fund economics cannot buy EUR 100-200k EBIT firms or promise to hold forever. Banks cannot hold equity. Steuerberater cannot take a commercial role.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against PE (a hold-forever promise), scale economies in back office and procurement, and a Meister pipeline as a cornered resource.
ideas.earned_secret: In Handwerk the Meister is the asset, not the building or the customer list. Whoever solves Meister succession can buy the rest cheaply.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign term sheets with 3 sellers. Line up EUR 15M of seed permanent capital. Draft the Meister-equity ladder. Check contract recurrence on real customer books (DGUV V3 intervals are risk-based, not fixed). Kill risks: customers drift away on the owner's exit; PE moves down-market.

ideas.title: Netzplan
ideas.one_liner: A group of retiring owner-led planning, survey and permit offices that sells fixed-price 'planned and permitted kilometre of route' to distribution-grid operators and Stadtwerke.
ideas.customer: Distribution-grid operators and municipal utilities with rate-base-funded grid expansion.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The DSO's approved investment budget (capital costs recognised in the revenue cap). Signer: head of grid construction or of procurement; the municipal Tiefbauamt for Sondervermoegen work.
ideas.problem: The bottleneck of the money is planning and supervision, not shovels. IW: about 10,000 planning and supervision experts missing; 81% of planning vacancies unfilled (Oct 2025); Tiefbau needs about 18% more capacity. BDEW: DSO investment rises from EUR 8.6B (2024) to EUR 15.4B a year by 2030. Small owner-led offices that hold local permit knowledge are retiring.
ideas.solution: Buy the offices and keep the owners as employees (Aktivrente is tax-free to employees, not to the self-employed). Install one toolchain (digitised route data, standard permit packs). Sell per-route-kilometre or per-connection-batch fixed prices instead of hours.
ideas.why_now: The BDEW grid-investment path; the EUR 500B Sondervermoegen (about EUR 30B a year of construction orders per IW); Aktivrente from 2026; the planner shortage.
ideas.wedge: Hausanschluss and Trassen planning for 3 mid-size Stadtwerke; the first acquisitions are 2 offices with EUR 2-3M revenue.
ideas.path_to_100m: Planning/survey/permit/supervision at about 10-12% of grid capex (my assumption) = EUR 1.5-1.85B a year by 2030, plus about EUR 1.9B on Sondervermoegen Tiefbau. EUR 87M is 5-6% of the DSO pool alone, or about 2.5% of both. Build: 25-30 offices at EUR 3M revenue each, bought at 0.56-1.03x revenue = EUR 50-80M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Triton's formicon (Jan 2026), XPartners (Axcel, employee-majority; bought Corall Ingenieure in Aug 2026), large engineers (Sweco, Arcadis, Ramboll, from memory) and DSO in-house teams.
ideas.why_they_lose: Generalist engineering roll-ups sell hours across all building types; none is organised around DSO outcome units. DSOs are rate-regulated and want predictable unit costs.
ideas.moat: Process power (standard toolchain, permit templates) and switching costs through framework contracts.
ideas.earned_secret: Permit knowledge sits in the head of a 62-year-old. It is the scarce input, and the DSO will pay for certainty.
ideas.first_90_days: Hold 3 DSO pilot conversations; identify 10 retiring offices through Ingenieurkammer listings; test unit-price quotes on 5 past projects. Kill risks: an Aug 2026 survey says the Sondervermoegen barely arrives at engineering offices; a VKU poll says only 8% think the DSO target is reachable under current rules; PE is already buying.

ideas.title: Teamkauf
ideas.one_liner: A packaged team buyout for 3-8 employees, using the 100% state-guaranteed 077 loan per partner, a vendor note and a regional participation, plus a shared back office that stays with the firm for a fee on revenue.
ideas.customer: Retiring owners who want continuity, and teams that lack equity, collateral and management bandwidth.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The firm pays a service fee out of operating costs; the origination fee is financed inside the purchase. Signers: the seller-owner (mandate) and the lead Geschaeftsfuehrer of the team.
ideas.problem: KfW says EBO (28%) and MBO (24%) are considered by many but get little attention. Hausbanken lend against collateral and personal guarantees; the Steuerberater cannot take equity or a commercial role; chambers cannot charge; PE cannot do the tickets; 077 is per natural person and covers 35% of costs. Nobody assembles the stack, or stays on as the finance function afterwards.
ideas.solution: A standard vehicle (a holding of employee-partners), a template financing stack (077 per partner as a 'taetige Beteiligung', Buergschaftsbank-backed bank loan, MBG participation, vendor note), governance covenants, and a back office (invoicing, dunning, payroll prep, e-invoice compliance, purchasing, insurance, financing) for about 1.2% of revenue. Right of first offer on partner exit.
ideas.why_now: KfW Jan 2026 (closures exceed successions; EBO and MBO rising). 077 live since Nov 2024. BMJV/BMF key points for a GmbH mit gebundenem Vermoegen in Feb-Mar 2026 (no draft bill confirmed).
ideas.wedge: Firms with 6-20 employees and a clear No. 2 and No. 3 in the team. First 10 via HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren and Steuerberater who already see the employee option.
ideas.path_to_100m: Origination 2.5% of a EUR 400k price (EUR 10k) plus 1.2% of EUR 1.8M revenue (EUR 21.6k a year). A portfolio of about 3,900 firms gives EUR 87M of recurring fees: about 650 closings a year for 6 years = 1.7% of the 37,200 actual handovers a year. Honest caution: only 123 applications for 077 were logged at Buergschaftsbank Baden-Wuerttemberg in 2025, and applicants stay personally liable, which is the real reason employees say no.
ideas.who_does_it_today: I found no dedicated German EBO packager in this run. Pieces exist: Hausbank + Buergschaftsbank + MBG + KfW 077, Steuerberater, and steward-ownership investors (Purpose Evergreen Capital, from memory). UK EOT advisers and US ESOP administrators are analogues.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each incumbent holds one piece and a conflict: collateral culture, no equity role, no fee mandate.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (embedded back office, covenants, right of first offer), scale economies in shared services, counter-positioning against Steuerberater.
ideas.earned_secret: Employees do not fail at buying; they fail in the 18 months after, when nobody is the finance function.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 5 sellers with a visible No. 2; write the stack with one Buergschaftsbank and one MBG; draft the legal template; price the service fee against a part-time Buchhalter. Kill risks: personal liability keeps employees out; demand behind 'considered' is thin.

ideas.title: Aufloesungsboerse
ideas.one_liner: An orderly-closure service that sells the bundle a closing firm leaves behind (its staff, customers, equipment and premises) to neighbours who are short of all four.
ideas.customer: Owners of the roughly 114,000 firms a year that plan to close with no successor; on the other side, growing firms with open positions.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The owner pays a wind-down fee; hiring firms pay placement fees from their personnel budget; buyers pay for customer books and equipment. Signers: the closing owner and the Inhaber of the hiring firm.
ideas.problem: No incumbent earns anything on a firm worth under EUR 100k. M&A boutiques have minimum fees, Steuerberater bill hours, chambers are free and cannot operate, Sparkassen see no credit, and nexxt-change matches going concerns. Yet Handwerk has about 200,000 open positions (ZDH) and roughly 100,000 unfillable ones (KOFA 7/2026).
ideas.solution: A fixed wind-down package (Schlussbilanz and archive with a partner Steuerberater, Gewerbeabmeldung, notices, GoBD archive, run-off cover) that the owner can fund from selling the bundle. Selective hiring of staff by neighbours (not an entity transfer, to stay outside section 613a BGB), customer-by-customer consent for the customer book, and an equipment and vehicle auction channel.
ideas.why_now: 2026 is the first year planned closures exceed planned successions; KfW says 47% of closure planners cite no family interest and 42% cite bureaucracy.
ideas.wedge: Handwerk closures in regions with the most open positions. First 10 via HWK Betriebsberater and Steuerberater who tell clients 'it is not worth anything'.
ideas.path_to_100m: Per client: EUR 2.5k wind-down fee (all clients) plus, for the 45% with a bundle, about EUR 13.5k (1.8 hires x EUR 5k, EUR 3k customer-book commission, EUR 1.5k equipment) = about EUR 8.6k average. EUR 87M needs about 10,100 clients a year = about 9% of the 114,000 planned closures (about 12% of the 80,000 that actually close, my assumption). That is close to heroic: it works only with strong software and as the feeder for Meisterwerk and Teamkauf.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody as a bundle. Pieces: nexxt-change, HWK Betriebsboersen (from memory), Surplex/Troostwijk machinery auctions (from memory), Kleinanzeigen, the Arbeitsagentur, Steuerberater for the wind-down.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each earns nothing on its piece and none can sell the whole.
ideas.moat: Network economies (closing supply meets hiring demand in the same region) plus regional vacancy data.
ideas.earned_secret: A closing firm's value is not on its balance sheet. It is its Gesellen and its customer list, and the buyers are the neighbours who cannot hire.
ideas.first_90_days: Run 20 closures end to end in one region; get a labour-law opinion on selective hiring versus section 613a; sign 15 hiring firms. Kill risks: the 613a reading; customers don't follow; most closers are solo operators with no staff (I found no headcount data for closers).

ideas.title: Zulieferwerk
ideas.one_liner: An acquirer-modernizer of owner-led precision-machining shops that qualifies them as second-source suppliers for defence primes.
ideas.customer: Primes and tier-1s that need machined parts (Rheinmetall says it has about 23,000 suppliers).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Strategic procurement at the prime, through multi-year framework supply contracts. Signer: head of purchasing or supply chain. On acquisition: the seller-owner.
ideas.problem: The constraint is qualification, not orders (quality systems such as AS/EN 9100, security clearance, traceability, first-article approval, export controls). A 58-year-old Zerspanungsunternehmer with idle 5-axis capacity cannot afford 18-36 months of qualification and has no successor.
ideas.solution: Buy the shop at 0.38-0.69x revenue, fund the qualification, bring the prime's framework contract before closing where possible, and keep the owner on.
ideas.why_now: German rearmament, the auto-supplier job losses, VW Osnabrueck in talks with defence firms, Rheinmetall selling its auto division to Aequita for EUR 350M to focus on defence, and IHK Stuttgart procurement seminars up from a few to 300-400 attendees.
ideas.wedge: Turned-part and 5-axis shops with EUR 4-8M revenue and an existing prime as customer.
ideas.path_to_100m: 15 shops x EUR 6M = EUR 90M. Cost EUR 35-50M to buy plus EUR 10-15M qualification. Execution-limited, not share-limited.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mutares (turnarounds, defence units such as Magirus), Pinova Capital (industrial tech, EUR 10-75M revenue), Aurelius, Rheinmetall itself.
ideas.why_they_lose: Mutares and Aurelius buy distress, not healthy owner-led shops. Primes cannot buy suppliers without a conflict. Banks hesitate on defence exposure (from memory).
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (qualified capacity) and switching costs once qualified.
ideas.earned_secret: Spare capacity is worthless until it is certified. Certification is what the buyer adds.
ideas.first_90_days: Sit with 3 primes' purchasing teams; get a qualification-cost estimate from a lead auditor; find 5 shops. Kill risk: sources do not show Mittelstand gains yet (produktion.de: value distribution not clear before 2027; Stuttgarter Zeitung: auto jobs are not absorbed). This fails the digest's gate unless a prime commits.

ideas.title: Anschluss
ideas.one_liner: Buy the sites of closing Mittelstand plants whose value to the owner is a building but to a battery, charging or data-centre developer is an existing grid connection.
ideas.customer: Closing manufacturers, bakeries, cold stores and workshops with a medium-voltage connection; on the other side, storage, truck-charging, light-industry and defence tenants.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Tenants and developers from their site budgets. Signer: their head of grid or real estate.
ideas.problem: E.ON reports more than 10,000 large-battery connection requests (about 500 GW) and more than 500 data-centre projects (about 70 GW). Oldenburg IHK reports delays of years. The cabinet adopted the Netzpaket on 29 Jul 2026 (priority and reservation rules). An existing connection is the scarce input, and the closing owner prices only a building.
ideas.solution: Buy or option the site at a price above building value, secure the Anschlussnutzung, and re-let or develop.
ideas.why_now: The Netzpaket, the connection queue, and 114,000 planned closures a year.
ideas.wedge: Sites with 0.4-2 MVA connections in grid-constrained regions. First 10 via HWK, IHK and local Steuerberater.
ideas.path_to_100m: 150 sites a year at EUR 1.2M = EUR 180M a year; after 6 years about EUR 1.08B at 8% yield on cost = EUR 87M. Assumption: 3-5% of the 114,000 closers have a connection of 400 kVA or more, so 150 a year is 3-4% of that group.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Developers buy land directly; DSOs; real-estate developers. I found no one systematically buying closing SMEs for connection rights (a negative result, not proof of a gap).
ideas.why_they_lose: Developers look at greenfield; closers don't know what they have; DSOs cannot trade capacity.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (connection rights) and speed.
ideas.earned_secret: The queue is long, and a closing neighbour has already waited in it.
ideas.first_90_days: Get a written opinion from a grid lawyer on whether capacity survives owner change and change of use under the Netzpaket; survey 50 closures for connection size; sign a battery developer for 3 sites. Kill risk: if capacity lapses on closure or change of use, the idea is dead. It overlaps with Werkhof as a real-estate model.

ideas.title: Signed-Off: the QA-accountable AI engineering house
ideas.one_liner: Sell nuclear plants finished, signed, Appendix B-compliant engineering deliverables at a fixed price per deliverable, produced by an AI pipeline that sits inside a qualified quality program, instead of selling another AI tool or more hourly engineers.
ideas.customer: Design and fleet engineering organizations at the ~25 owner-operators. Start with single-site and restart operators with thin benches (EUCG counts 10 'one plant' operators; e.g. Energy Northwest, Evergy/Wolf Creek, Ameren/Callaway, Holtec/Palisades, Constellation/Crane, NextEra/Duane Arnold; names from background knowledge).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Contracted engineering and supplemental-staff lines in O&M plus project engineering inside the $7.59B 2025 capital budget (NEI/EUCG, Aug 2026). Signer: Director of Design Engineering or VP Engineering. Supply Chain adds the firm to the Approved Supplier List and the QA director must accept the quality program.
ideas.problem: Capital spend jumped 24% in 2025 and ~30 uprates, three restarts and 20+ license renewals queue behind a shrinking engineer pool. The work product (50.59 screenings and evaluations, calculation revisions, engineering change packages, license-amendment sections) must be traceable, independently verified and issued by an organization under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B. AI tools exist (Nuclearn lists an 'Engineering AI' product) but a tool's output cannot be used on safety-related work until a qualified organization owns it, so engineers redo it by hand and overflow goes out hourly to Sargent & Lundy-class firms.
ideas.solution: An engineering supplier with (a) its own NQA-1/Appendix B program, listed on customers' Approved Supplier Lists after a NUPIC-style joint audit; (b) a version-locked AI drafting and checking stack verified under NQA-1 software QA; (c) nuclear-qualified engineers who review and sign every output; (d) a fixed price per deliverable with a rework guarantee. Over time the verified calculation and evaluation templates per plant design become a reusable library, then new-build and licensing work.
ideas.why_now: Capital +24% in 2025 and uprate capex up from $66M (2022) to $365M (2025) meet a thin engineer bench. A DOE/INL/ANL/Microsoft/Everstar test turned a 4-6 week license-application drafting task into one day (208-page draft). Hyperscaler-priced power lets owners afford capital but not engineers.
ideas.wedge: 50.59 screenings and calculation revisions (high volume, bounded) for 2-3 single-site operators, with the plant's own engineer signing the first pilots (quality-related scope) while the QA program and ASL listing are built. Faster route: buy or white-label a 30-100 person ASL-listed engineering boutique and run under its QA program. First 10 customers: single-plant operators plus the three restarts.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION (no published figure found): outsourced nuclear engineering is ~10% of capital ($0.76B) plus ~5% of non-labor operating ($0.37B), about $1.1B/yr; add the uprate/restart wave (2.3 GW x ~$4.8k/kW is ~$11B, 8-10% engineering is ~$1B over 5 years, ~$200M/yr). Pool ~$1.3-1.4B/yr by 2028-30. $100M is ~7% of it (~400 billable-engineer equivalents at ~$250k); because deliverables are priced at a discount to hourly, volume share is ~10-12%. Upside: ~25 funded reactor developers spend tens of millions each on engineering and licensing. A software-only subscription across ~70 facilities (Nuclearn-style) caps at ~$35-70M (my arithmetic at $0.5-1M per site), which is why the service model is the path.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Hourly engineering firms: Sargent & Lundy (ENR #1 in nuclear plants, eight times in a decade), Enercon (self-described top 3), Jensen Hughes (ENR #4), Framatome, Westinghouse, Bechtel, Aptim; owner in-house design engineering. AI tools: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, 'over 70 facilities', annual per-product subscription), Atomic Canyon ($7M seed, Diablo Canyon), Everstar ($4M pre-seed, Gordian, DOE drafting test). No one found selling QA-accountable deliverables.
ideas.why_they_lose: Hourly firms cannot cut hours without cutting revenue. Tool vendors do not carry QA accountability or an engineer's signature. Frontier labs will not hold an Appendix B program. Owners will not accept unowned output on safety-related work.
ideas.moat: Switching costs plus process power: ASL status takes 12-24 months of audits, each owner's QA acceptance and per-plant verified templates lock in; counter-positioning against hourly billers. Reached by passing the first supplier audits and accumulating a signed-deliverable history.
ideas.earned_secret: Nobody in nuclear buys AI; they buy a name on the signature block. The binding constraint is who is accountable under Appendix B, not model quality, which is why every AI product stays stuck on search and screening. The business is the QA program. (Hypothesis from the insider persona; validate in first 15 interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 15 design-engineering directors and QA managers and 2 ASL-listed boutiques (acquire or white-label). Write the NQA-1 software-QA plan. Run a paid pilot of ~20 50.59 screenings with 1-2 single-site operators, plant engineer signing; measure hours saved and rework. Schedule the supplier audit. Legal gate: Appendix B Criterion VII makes the licensee responsible for suppliers; state PE rules apply; no NRC rule found barring QA-controlled AI-assisted analysis (confirm with counsel).

ideas.title: Dose Ledger: the nuclear traveler network
ideas.one_liner: A W-2 employer-of-record network of radiation-protection technicians, welders, pipefitters, NDE and I&C techs that chains workers across every outage in the country, with a portable credential and dose-headroom ledger, so plants get badged crews in days and workers get ~40 weeks of work a year.
ideas.customer: Outage managers and site-support directors at ~55 nuclear sites, plus the integrated outage primes (Westinghouse, Framatome, GE Vernova Hitachi) that subcontract labor; later restarts and new-build owners.
