ideas.payer_and_signer: Supplemental-labor lines in outage O&M. Signer: Outage Manager or Director of Site Support; Supply Chain executes the MSA; merchant CFOs care because outage days are worth ~$1.6-2.4M each.
ideas.problem: A refueling outage brings 1,000-1,400 temporary workers (Entergy ANO 1,300; Columbia Generating Station 1,400 for a 40-day outage; Davis-Besse 1,000+). Outage seasons cluster, so every plant bids for the same people at once; the senior contract RP technician pool shrank ~37% in three years (Health Physics, 2022); travelers idle between seasons and quit; each site re-badges a worker (background, fitness-for-duty, training, dose history), which sits on the outage critical path.
ideas.solution: Employer-of-record payroll; a credential vault (certifications, training, access status, respirator fit); a dose-headroom ledger showing remaining annual dose so planners see who can take a high-dose job; a scheduler that chains workers across plants' outage calendars; pre-clearance workflows so site badging takes days. Expand to training pipelines (Navy nukes, veterans), housing/per diem, and a senior-expert bench for restarts and new builds.
ideas.why_now: Hyperscaler-priced power raises an outage day to ~$1.6-2.4M for a 1.1 GW unit at $60-90/MWh (arithmetic), so labor readiness is the cheapest lever. Palisades, Crane and Duane Arnold restarts and new builds compete for the same people. NRC's July 2026 ALARA proposal keeps dose limits unchanged but may reduce RP hours (risk).
ideas.wedge: Senior RP technicians, the scarcest trade, for spring 2027 outages (March-May) at 2-3 single-site operators or one integrated prime. First 10 customers: single-site operators plus one OEM outage organization.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~50 outages/yr (inference from 94 reactors on 18-24 month cycles) x 1,000-1,400 temporary workers = ~50-70k worker-outages. At ~300-350 hours x ~$75/hr blended bill rate (Vogtle outage posting: senior RPT $39.52-44.72/hr), ~$22-26k per worker-outage, so outage temp labor is ~$1.2-1.6B/yr (cross-check: older trade figures put direct outage cost at $300-800k/day x ~38 days = $11-30M per outage). $100M of billings is ~4,000-4,500 worker-outages, ~7% share. Gross margin only ~15-20%, so this is a $100M-revenue business, not a $100M-profit one, unless the ledger, training, payroll and housing layers earn more.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Integrated outage primes: Westinghouse (10-year integrated outage contract with Xcel), Framatome (integrated outage services for FENOC), GE Vernova Hitachi (>$70M Browns Ferry outage services); Westinghouse direct-hire outage technician postings; NukeWorker job board; a long tail of regional craft and RP staffing firms (not individually verified). No funded startup found doing nuclear credentialing or outage staffing.
ideas.why_they_lose: Staffing firms are paid per head per outage and see only their own customers' schedules. Merchant rivals do not share outage calendars, so nobody can chain a worker into 40 weeks. Badging is rebuilt site by site.
ideas.moat: Network economies (two-sided: workers and plants) plus cornered resource (the best few thousand travelers' loyalty and their dose/credential histories). Commodity staffing is the failure mode.
ideas.earned_secret: The shortage is a synchronization and paperwork problem as much as a headcount problem: outage windows cluster so travelers idle and quit, and a worker's remaining annual dose headroom and badge status, not skills, decide who can take a job. Whoever sees every schedule sells continuity and speed. (Hypothesis; validate in first 20 interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 outage managers/RP supervisors and 30 travelers. Build the credential and dose-ledger MVP with ~100 RP techs. Sign an LOI with one single-site operator or integrated prime for spring 2027. Register as employer of record (W-2, workers' comp, staffing licensing). Legal gate: 10 CFR 73.56 access authorization and Part 26 fitness-for-duty stay licensee-run programs; Part 20 dose-record rules; worker classification must be W-2.

ideas.title: Certified Cell: Hadrian for nuclear (the automated NQA-1 parts factory)
ideas.one_liner: Transfer the defense neo-prime playbook (Hadrian-style automated precision-machining factories selling into supply-constrained primes) into nuclear: a factory whose machine-control and inspection systems write the Appendix B/NQA-1 paper trail as they cut, so certified capacity becomes the product.
ideas.customer: Westinghouse and its AP1000 supply base, BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, Flowserve-class valve/pump OEMs, reactor developers (TerraPower, X-energy, Kairos), and fleet owners' supply chains (replacement internals, fasteners, supports, instrument fittings).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Supply Chain Officer or VP Procurement at the OEM/developer, from component procurement in capital budgets. Fleet side: Director of Supply Chain with engineering acceptance.
ideas.problem: Few shops hold ASME N-type certificates or NQA-1 programs, so a new-build and uprate wave hits a thin sub-tier. DOE conditional loans of $17.5B (June 2026; up to five loans of two reactors each) pull long-lead buying forward by up to three years. Valar and Radiant are hiring supplier-quality engineers because the qualified base is small. April 2026 Section 232 changes (25% on full value for most metal derivatives, 50% for near-all-metal) push buyers toward domestic content.
ideas.solution: A high-mix, low-volume automated machining and inspection factory: material heat traceability, in-process inspection and certificates generated by the system; ASME certification and an NQA-1 certificate; pre-dedicated stock of fleet long-tail parts; anchor customer offtake before building.
ideas.why_now: First sustained nuclear order book in ~40 years, federal loans financing long-lead buys, tariffs, and defense-tech investors who proved the automated-factory model but have not looked at nuclear.
ideas.wedge: Fasteners, valve and pump internals, supports and instrument fittings for AP1000 and developer orders, qualified through one anchor customer; fleet long tail follows. First 10 customers: Westinghouse tier-1s, BWXT, 3-4 reactor developers, and OEMs short of capacity.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION: 8-12% of the $17.5B long-lead value is machined/fabricated sub-tier content outside the big forgings: ~$1.4-2.1B over ~6 years, $230-350M/yr. Add the fleet long tail: parts are ~25% of ($7.59B capital + ~$7.5B non-labor operating), ~$3.8B, of which 20-25% is OEM-unsupported (Rolls-Royce study), ~$0.8-0.9B. $100M is one large factory (~150-200 cells) and ~15-20% of the combined flow; capital need ~$50-100M. Honest verdict: big only with an anchor offtake from Westinghouse, BWXT or a developer.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Dedicators/distributors that do not make parts: Park Nuclear (Oak Ridge dedication facility), ATC Nuclear, Nuclear Logistics. OEM aftermarket: Curtiss-Wright (commercial nuclear a stated growth driver; ~$300M base unverified), Flowserve, Velan, Crane. Family-owned qualified machine shops. Kairos built its own U-stamp vessel shop. Hadrian is defense/aerospace only.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs prioritize new-build and cannot add capacity fast. Family shops cannot fund automation plus QA overhead. Dedicators and distributors do not manufacture.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (certified, audited capacity that takes 18-24 months to replicate) plus process power (automated records) plus scale economies; reached via ASME/NQA-1 certification and an anchor offtake.
ideas.earned_secret: The scarce thing is not machine time but certified, auditable lots: the paperwork twin of a safety-related part costs more than the metal, so a factory that generates the paperwork automatically turns a compliance tax into a moat. Caution: 10 CFR 50.69 can move up to 75% of safety-related components (EPRI pilot result) out of special treatment, so target Class 1/2, pressure-boundary and new-build content, not the whole fleet tail.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick the 50 part families with the most backorders from two Westinghouse-qualified suppliers and one developer. Secure an anchor LOI. Identify a state with an existing ASME-certified shop to partner with or acquire. Draft the NQA-1 program. Apply for state/DOE incentives. Legal gate: ASME Section III/NCA-3800 certification, Part 21 reporting, customer ASL audits, Buy-American/domestic-content rules.

ideas.title: One Audit: a supplier-paid shared accreditation for nuclear (Nadcap for nuclear)
ideas.one_liner: Aerospace solved duplicate supplier audits in 1990 with Nadcap (suppliers pay once, every prime accepts). Do the same for the nuclear supply chain across competing primes and ~25 funded developers.
ideas.customer: Subscribers: Westinghouse, Bechtel, Fluor, BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, TVA, X-energy, TerraPower, Kairos. Accreditation payers: the suppliers themselves (machine shops, foundries, welders, test labs).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Supplier President/QA Manager pays fees; subscribers' Chief Supply Chain Officers pay annual subscriptions from supplier-quality budgets.
ideas.problem: Every developer builds its own supplier-quality team (Valar and Radiant job posts list supplier qualification, audits and dedication protocols) and re-audits the same shops. NUPIC (utility-run joint audits, formed 1989, relied on by the NRC) covers utilities, not competing OEMs, EPCs and developers.
ideas.solution: A neutral registry plus audit program: one standard checklist mapped to NQA-1, ASME NCA-3800 and ISO 19443; accredited auditors; a shared eAuditNet-style database; a 'QA program in a box' for aerospace and oil-and-gas shops converting to nuclear; optional dedication testing labs.
ideas.why_now: DOE-financed AP1000 long-lead buying and ~25 funded developers racing DOE and NRC clocks all need qualified suppliers at once.
ideas.wedge: Sell the 'QA program in a box' and shared assessments to 3-5 founding subscribers (one OEM, one EPC, two developers) who pay for the first 25 supplier assessments; convert to accreditation when a utility QA organization accepts it as survey input.
ideas.path_to_100m: Nadcap precedent: >1,350 accredited suppliers by 2007, >6,900 active accreditations and 53 subscribing OEMs by 2015-16, ~40% fewer audits (PRI-commissioned survey). ASSUMPTION (no published count found): 2,500-3,500 US and allied nuclear-qualified or aspiring suppliers x $20-30k/yr = $50-105M, plus ~60 primes/developers x $250k = $15M, plus QA-in-a-box services. Stretch: needs near-universal adoption and non-US scope (Canada, UK, Poland).
ideas.who_does_it_today: NUPIC (utility joint audits), ASME N-stamp and NQA-1 certificate programs, DOE's own consolidated audit program, third-party inspection firms (not individually verified), and each developer's in-house supplier-quality team.
ideas.why_they_lose: NUPIC's members are utilities that cannot extend audit liability to competing vendors; competing primes will not share audit findings with each other; ASME certifies capability but not ongoing process performance. No incumbent has a neutral position.
ideas.moat: Network economies and switching costs once primes require the accreditation; counter-positioning against each prime's in-house audit team. Reached by signing founding subscribers who commit to accept it.
ideas.earned_secret: The fix is not technology but a neutral party two competing primes both trust, with the supplier paying once. Boeing and Airbus both subscribed to Nadcap for exactly that reason.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 3 founding subscribers. Recruit 6 ex-NUPIC lead auditors. Run 10 pilot assessments. Ask 1 utility QA organization to confirm acceptability as survey input. Legal gate: antitrust review of shared-audit information exchange (Nadcap/PRI precedent) and licensee acceptance under Appendix B Criterion VII.

ideas.title: Day Rate: the performance-priced outage prime
ideas.one_liner: A challenger outage prime that earns a base fee plus a bonus or penalty per outage day against a P50 baseline, backed by its own critical-path dataset; incumbent primes cannot copy it because they earn on emergent work.
ideas.customer: Site VPs and fleet outage directors, starting with single-site and mid-size operators whose integrated outage contracts come up for renewal.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Outage O&M and capital budgets. Signer: Chief Nuclear Officer or Site VP; for merchant owners the CFO cares because a day of a 1.1 GW unit is ~$1.6-2.4M (arithmetic at $60-90/MWh).
ideas.problem: Outage contracts are typically fixed-price for baseline scope and time-and-materials for the rest (BWXT 10-K language), so emergent work is the incumbents' profit center. Average outage length was ~38 days in an older NEI figure while individual operators showed 19-26 day outages in 2008-2011 SEC filings. Trade figures put direct cost at $300-800k/day plus ~$1M/day replacement power; hyperscaler pricing pushes that higher.
ideas.solution: A fixed-fee-plus-days-saved integrated outage contract, outage control software (critical path, work-package readiness, mobilization, laydown), a dataset of schedule actuals, downside beyond a cap reinsured or capitalized. Pairs with the traveler network (idea 2).
ideas.why_now: Hyperscaler-priced power roughly doubled the value of a day while incumbents' contracts are long-term and fixed, so owners have a reason to look at renewals.
ideas.wedge: Offer a 'critical-path logistics' sub-scope (containment access, laydown, mobilization) with gain-share on days saved for spring 2027, then expand to full prime at renewal.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~50 outages/yr x ~$25-30M each = $1.3-1.5B/yr of outage spend; four outages a year as prime is $100-120M of mostly pass-through revenue at a 10-15% fee (~8% of outages). The prize: fleet outage-days ~1,750/yr (50 x 35); pulling the slow half from 40 to 28 days saves ~300 days x $1.6-2.4M = $480-720M/yr; a 20% performance fee is $95-145M. The two stack.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Westinghouse (10-year integrated outage services contract with Xcel), Framatome (integrated outage services for FENOC), GE Vernova Hitachi (>$70M Browns Ferry outage services), BWXT-type fixed-scope contractors, Day & Zimmermann (background knowledge, not verified), plus owners' own fleet outage organizations (e.g. Constellation).
ideas.why_they_lose: T&M emergent work is margin; fixed-price scope is already priced against risk; the OEMs are not balance-sheet risk takers on schedule and none will pay penalties for days.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning plus cornered resource (a critical-path dataset incumbents will not build) plus scale; reached by winning the first one or two guaranteed outages.
ideas.earned_secret: Outage length is mostly decided before the outage starts (work-package readiness at T-12 weeks, labor mobilization, tooling, crane and laydown constraints), not during execution. (Hypothesis from the insider persona; I found no source for it, validate in the first 10 interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Build a duration model from NRC's daily Power Reactor Status reports (public, 30 years). Interview 10 outage managers. Pitch a critical-path-logistics gain-share pilot to 3 operators for spring 2027. Legal gate: liquidated damages in a services contract are not insurance; avoid cash-for-lost-generation structures that could be classified as insurance (round 1's NY DFS lesson).

ideas.title: Second Source: HEICO for nuclear plants
ideas.one_liner: An OEM-neutral second source for the long tail of obsolete safety-related parts, with the reverse-engineering, test and dedication package built once and sold to every plant; OEMs cannot do it because sole-source aftermarket is where their margin is.
ideas.customer: Procurement engineering and supply chain at ~55 sites.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Materials and parts lines in O&M and capital. Signer: Director of Supply Chain with Site Engineering acceptance.
ideas.problem: A Rolls-Royce study estimates 20-25% of nuclear plant components are no longer supported by the original equipment provider, and a plant relies on >100,000 parts. The same commercial item is dedicated separately by each plant that buys it. OEMs have no reason to fix that.
ideas.solution: Reverse-engineer and test equivalents for obsolete I&C cards, relays, transmitters, valve and pump internals; build one dedication package per part, accepted across the fleet through engineering equivalency; hold pre-dedicated stock; sell at 30-40% below OEM; keep the library of qualified alternates as the data asset.
ideas.why_now: License extensions toward 80 years plus uprates increase parts demand, and AI-assisted reverse engineering and additive manufacturing cut engineering cost per part.
ideas.wedge: The 200 most common obsolete part numbers across the top 8 plant designs, starting from two operators' obsolescence lists. First 10 customers: operators with active obsolescence programs.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION: parts are ~25% of $15.1B (capital + non-labor operating), ~$3.8B/yr; OEM-unsupported 20-25% is $0.75-0.95B. A second source priced at ~65% of OEM needs $154M of OEM-equivalent volume for $100M of revenue, ~16-20% of the exposed pool. Stretch. Existing proof that $100M+ is possible in this space: Curtiss-Wright's commercial nuclear unit (reported ~$300M, unverified).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Park Nuclear (dedication, seismic and material testing, reverse engineering, new Oak Ridge facility), ATC Nuclear, Nuclear Logistics, Curtiss-Wright, Westinghouse and Framatome dedication services, Nuclearn 'Parts AI', Nuclear Utility Obsolescence Group, USA Inc. co-op, PIM pool and the rapidpartsmart network.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs will not release drawings or price at cost; co-ops are non-profit and carry no inventory or liability; mid-size dedicators are sub-scale on engineering.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against OEM aftermarket plus cornered resource (qualified-alternates library with accepted dedication packages); reached by the first ~200 accepted part numbers.
ideas.earned_secret: The dedication package, not the part, is the product. Caution: 10 CFR 50.69 can move up to 75% of safety-related components (EPRI pilot) out of special treatment, shrinking the nuclear-grade premium where adopted; the surviving premium is Class 1/2 and pressure boundary.
ideas.first_90_days: Get 20 obsolete part numbers from two plants, produce dedication packages, have 3 CGD engineers confirm acceptability, take counsel on OEM drawing/patent/trade-secret exposure. Legal gate: Appendix B, Part 21, engineering equivalency; reverse engineering faces IP and contract limits. The aviation PMA analog (HEICO) is background knowledge, not verified here.

ideas.title: Uprate Kit: the fixed-price uprate integrator
ideas.one_liner: Become integrator-of-record for hyperscaler-funded uprates: productize standard uprate kits per plant type and sell megawatts delivered at a fixed price and date.
ideas.customer: Owners with uprate pipelines in NRC's expected-applications table: Constellation, Duke (Brunswick, McGuire, Catawba), PSEG (Salem), Southern (Hatch), Vistra.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Uprate capital project budgets (hyperscaler-backed). Signer: VP Nuclear Engineering/Projects and the CFO; DOE LPO is the lender where loans exist.
ideas.problem: Uprate capex went from $66M (2022) to $365M (2025) and is heading to billions. NRC expects 30 uprates / ~2.3-2.4 GW by 2030-32 against 3-8 GW of potential. Constellation's $4.3B for 890 MW is ~$4.8k/kW versus Browns Ferry's $475M for 14% over 3 units (2018-19) at roughly $1,000/kW. Not like-for-like, but the spread suggests sole-source pricing, scope creep or both. Main turbines, generators, pumps and transformers carry long lead times.
ideas.solution: Feasibility screen for each of 94 reactors, standard retrofit kits by plant type, LAR plan, competitive procurement of long-lead items, reserved equipment slots, and a fixed price per MW delivered with schedule guarantees; optional revenue share on incremental MWh.
ideas.why_now: First large uprate money since 2012 (Google-Constellation 890 MW across 11 units, Meta-Vistra, Amazon-Constellation Calvert Cliffs). The first projects will set the template.
ideas.wedge: A paid feasibility and cost-review package for 3-5 owners built on public data (172 prior uprates), which converts into engineering and procurement for the cheapest 2-3 units.
ideas.path_to_100m: 2.4 GW x $4.8k/kW is ~$11.5B through 2032, about $1.6B/yr; at 8 GW it is ~$38B, $4-5B/yr. As engineering and licensing only (~11%) the base case is ~$180M/yr, so $100M needs ~55% share: not viable. As fixed-price integrator-of-record (revenue gross of equipment) $100M is 2-6% of capex flow: the only version that works. Capital need and warranty risk are high, and owners must give up OEM sole-source relationships. Stretch.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEM uprate packages (Westinghouse, GE Vernova Hitachi, Framatome), turbine OEMs (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi), engineers (Sargent & Lundy, Bechtel, Burns & McDonnell), owner in-house programs (Constellation). No funded startup found.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs bundle uprates with fuel and services at sole-source prices and will not standardize across competitors' designs. Engineers bill hourly. Owners' in-house teams are the bottleneck.
ideas.moat: Process power (repeatable kits) plus scale economies (reserved equipment slots) plus switching costs (licensing basis); reached by delivering the first two uprates on time.
ideas.earned_secret: Uprate cost sits in a handful of long-lead secondary-side retrofits and licensing analyses, not reactor physics. (Unverified; test with the first three cost reviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Build the public-data headroom screen. Contact the 5 owners on NRC's expected-uprate list. Sell 1-2 paid feasibility and cost reviews. Legal gate: NRC LAR process, OEM IP licenses, DOE domestic-content guidance (INL, March 2026).

ideas.title: Clock Keeper: pay-on-approval licensing for the 12- and 18-month NRC clocks
ideas.one_liner: Executive Order 14300's clocks (18 months for new reactors, 12 for renewals, enforced through fee-recovery limits) move the bottleneck to the applicant; sell a fixed-price, pay-on-approval licensing submission and RAI-response service with a schedule guarantee.
ideas.customer: Reactor developers (~25 funded), restarts, and fleet owners filing uprate and license-renewal amendments.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Regulatory affairs and licensing budgets plus project capital. Signer: VP Licensing or Chief Regulatory Officer.
ideas.problem: With reviews capped, the NRC's defense against a missed clock is early requests for additional information (RAIs) and strict docketing. The applicant's critical path becomes completeness at docketing and RAI turnaround. Preparing applications takes tens of millions and months.
ideas.solution: A licensing factory: structured regulatory building blocks, a library of RAIs and accepted responses by topic from the NRC's public ADAMS record, former NRC reviewers for mock docketing, and a RAI-response SWAT team. Priced per submission and paid on approval within the clock.
ideas.why_now: EO 14300 (May 2025), NRC reorganization due by end of September 2026, a cluster of final rules September-November 2026, TVA Clinch River approved in 14 months (2026-09-29), rising application volume, and the DOE/INL/ANL/Microsoft/Everstar drafting test.
ideas.wedge: Free mock docketing reviews for 3 applicants due in 2027, converting one to pay-on-approval. First 10 customers: developers and restarts with 2027 filings.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION: ~10 new-reactor applications per year x $30M outsourced preparation = ~$300M/yr; fleet licensing actions ~6 uprate LARs/yr x $20M, ~5 renewals/yr x $25M, plus ~80 smaller actions/yr x $1.5M = ~$365M/yr. Total ~$0.65B/yr; $100M is ~15% of it. Stretch, concentrated in ~35 applicants per year. NRC's own estimate of industry savings from licensing reform is only $15-22M/yr, so the market is applicant preparation spend, not NRC savings.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Licensing consultants (Enercon, Sargent & Lundy, Jensen Hughes, ERIN, Framatome, Westinghouse), law firms (Morgan Lewis), in-house licensing. AI tools: Everstar (Gordian, $4M pre-seed, DOE test), Nuclearn, Atomic Canyon.
ideas.why_they_lose: Consultants and law firms bill hourly and will not take approval risk. Tool vendors sell software, not accountability. Reference-design owners (Westinghouse, GE Vernova Hitachi, TerraPower) keep their own adaptation kits.
ideas.moat: Process power only; all RAIs are public so there is no data moat. Weak. Best treated as an extension of idea 1.
ideas.earned_secret: The NRC clock is enforced through fee-recovery caps, so speed is set by completeness at docketing and the days an applicant takes to answer RAIs, and most RAIs repeat recurring topics (to be validated against ADAMS). It is a process-and-accountability business, not a data business.
ideas.first_90_days: Ingest the ADAMS corpus of RAIs and responses for uprates, renewals and construction permits. Build a topic-level RAI predictor. Offer 3 free mock docketing reviews and convert one to pay-on-approval. Legal gate: 10 CFR 50.9 completeness and accuracy, fee-sharing limits if lawyers are involved, and the practice-of-law boundary.

verdicts.title: Second Look: independent per-case SNAP accuracy layer

competitors_found.name: Maximus Accuracy Assistant
competitors_found.what_they_do: AI case-prep review before authorization, error-risk scoring, dashboards, training insights (launched 2026-01-27)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Maximus, public multi-billion-revenue contractor in all 50 states

competitors_found.what_they_do: Monthly risk scores on SNAP determinations; Nevada flagged $130k/month of overpayments in two months
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: SAS, large private analytics firm; Nevada contract value not disclosed

competitors_found.name: Deloitte SNAP payment accuracy
competitors_found.what_they_do: Accuracy consulting plus verification hub; claims error reductions up to 35% (self-reported)

competitors_found.name: Public Consulting Group
competitors_found.what_they_do: SNAP accuracy improvement consulting; Maine rapid assessment $241,800

competitors_found.name: Carahsoft (Nevada) and KPMG (Virginia)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Nevada $2.1M anomaly-flagging and income-tracking services; Virginia $1.7M six-month KPMG engagement

competitors_found.name: Code for America SNAP Policy Navigator with Anthropic
competitors_found.what_they_do: Free nonprofit AI policy guidance for caseworkers

verdicts.substitutes: State QC units and supervisory case review; FNS and APHSA technical assistance; USDR and Code for America free tools; states building in-house analytics on existing eligibility-system data.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $660M pool at $30 per household-year does not match observed behaviour. States spend 0.4% (Florida, $4M against about $1B exposure) to 4.2% (Nevada, $2.1M against about $50M) of one year's exposure. At 1-4% of roughly $9-10B exposure the whole vendor pool is $90-400M shared with SAS, Maximus, Deloitte, PCG, KPMG, so $100M is 25-100% share. Florida at $30 per case would be about 10x its appropriation. The 'CA alone $76-133M' line is not credible.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (a) Cost share survives to FY2029-30 (about 60%); (b) states spend 2-3% of exposure, 5-10x today (plausible only after first bills); (c) a new entrant wins 15-20 states against SAS, Maximus and Deloitte as the trusted independent measurer (low, about 15%); (d) Medicaid eligibility assurance becomes a second line from FY2030 under the 3% threshold (rolling PERM eligibility rate 4.42%) (plausible, but CMS measures PERM on a 3-year rotation). Joint probability roughly 5-8%.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Tier math confirmed (0/5/10/15% at 6/8/10; FY2025 national 10.62%, $10.1B). FL, MD, MA, NJ, NY lost delay eligibility. FY2025 and FY2026 rates are locked for FY2028; FY2027 sample year (began 2026-10-01) is the controllable window. Senate delay bill is stalled/contested. The OIG consultant finding is from an FY2011-12 audit and the Wisconsin contingent-fee consultant was Julie Osnes Consulting, not PCG. Contingent pricing correctly avoided (DOJ settlements).
verdicts.deciding_reason: Best idea in pool: hard-dollar dated cliff and named signer. But SAS, Maximus and Deloitte are already in states, and observed state contracts are $0.4-4M, so median misses $20M and the $100M upside needs 5-10x current spend.

verdicts.title: Medicaid-Pending Bridge for nursing homes

competitors_found.name: PointClickCare Revenue Cycle Management
competitors_found.what_they_do: Outsourced SNF revenue cycle including Medicaid eligibility specialists who run the application with families

competitors_found.name: Optum eligibility and enrollment outsourcing
competitors_found.what_they_do: Outsourced Medicaid eligibility and enrollment (case: 15,000 patients, 96% approval)

competitors_found.name: Nursing-home-referred application firms and elder-law attorneys
competitors_found.what_they_do: Prepare Medicaid applications for families for roughly $2,500-5,000

verdicts.substitutes: Operator in-house business offices; free help from facility staff; county caseworkers; state bills to pay facilities while applications pend (NJ bill not found enacted).
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Volume of 600-800k applications a year is unverified; my estimate from about 1.2M residents, about 60% Medicaid and multi-year stays is 300-400k new Medicaid starts a year. $100M of fees at $1,000 needs 100k filings, 25-30% share. The financing leg needs $0.6-0.8B of advances; revenue there is yield not margin and carries credit risk.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Fee-for-filing displaces PointClickCare and Optum inside chains (low), and a balance sheet is raised to advance against pending applications despite Medicaid anti-assignment constraints and receivables-lender wariness after NCFE (low-moderate).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: The retro cut is one month, not a cliff: non-expansion applicants go from three to two months, expansion adults to one, and coverage keys off the application month. A facility filing in the admission month loses nothing. Factoring needs an approved billed receivable, so financing against a pending application is awkward.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Why-now is thin (one month of retro reach-back), PointClickCare and Optum already sell the service, and even the upside is under $50M.

verdicts.title: Continuity Manager: PMPM carve-out for the top Medicaid plans

competitors_found.name: Fortuna Health
competitors_found.what_they_do: Medicaid enrollment and recertification platform sold to payers, providers and states; claims 15% churn reduction (company-reported)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $18M Series A (a16z, YC); payer clients cover 25M+ Medicaid lives

competitors_found.name: Reema Health
competitors_found.what_they_do: Community-worker-led Medicaid member outreach

competitors_found.name: Conduent work requirements and community engagement suite
competitors_found.what_they_do: End-to-end work-requirement reporting, verification and compliance for states

verdicts.substitutes: Plans' in-house engagement and care-management teams; state-led outreach; Maximus and Conduent outreach on state contracts.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $480M pool at $30 per member-year overstates plan willingness to pay. A retained expansion member contributes roughly $250-350 a year after medical costs. Retaining 3.75% (25% loss x 15% relative reduction, Fortuna's own claim) is worth about $11 per enrolled member-year; 8% (Manatt loss rate x 20%) about $25. Realistic plan budget $8-15 per member-year gives a $130-240M pool shared with Fortuna and in-house teams.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Two or three of the Big Five sign outcome-priced PMPM contracts (plausible, plans buy NEMT/dental managers this way); a neutral cross-plan utility solves the free-rider problem (low, needs state buy-in); outperforms Fortuna on measured retention (unproven).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: The statute bars states delegating compliance determinations to plans with a financial relationship; Crowell reads it as reaching financially affiliated contractors. Outreach and evidence support remain allowed, so a plan-paid vendor can do exactly what Fortuna already does. Section 438.58 citation not confirmed from the CFR text.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real buyers and a funded rival already selling to plans; price per member-year exceeds the contribution margin of the members it retains, so the pool is half the claim and the upside tops out near $60M.

verdicts.title: Hours Marketplace: verified shifts for the 80 hours

competitors_found.name: Better Impact CE Hours
competitors_found.what_they_do: Coordinator-validated volunteer-hour records sold to state Medicaid and benefit programs

competitors_found.name: Helper Helper
competitors_found.what_they_do: Volunteer platform marketing Medicaid community engagement hour verification

competitors_found.what_they_do: Automated 80-hour verification and state-owned tracking tools

verdicts.substitutes: State-owned hour trackers (free to clients), paper verification letters from hosts, court-ordered and probation hours that already count, existing SNAP E&T providers.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The 12-15% of 20M needing non-job hours (2.4-3.0M) is unsourced and probably 3-5x too high: KFF finds most expansion adults already work 80+ hours and many of the rest are in school or disabled. Georgia Pathways enrolled about 6,500 in 18 months. Serving 0.3M member-years is 10-15% of the idea's own need and needs about 290M hours of unpaid host supervision.

FLSA and workers' compensation treatment of compelled service unresolved; workfare participants were held to be FLSA employees in Stone v. McGowan (TANF) and Oregon and Ohio treat SNAP workfare as covered.
