verdicts.title: Open Verification Exchange with a cheapest-first router

competitors_found.name: Argyle
competitors_found.what_they_do: Consent-based income and employment verification for state agencies; Washington State contract 10925 and GSA MAS schedule; claims up to 90% below The Work Number (vendor claim)

competitors_found.name: SteadyIQ
competitors_found.what_they_do: Missouri DSS Income Passport for gig and self-employment income, optional for applicants; 18-minute average report

competitors_found.name: Equifax Workforce Solutions (Work Number, TotalVerify)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Incumbent income verification used by about half of states; per-query price hikes of 69-126% in four states
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Government revenue growing but fell about 4% in Q2 2026; about $300M ACV signed mostly with states

competitors_found.name: Deloitte NextGen360 Verification Hub
competitors_found.what_they_do: Multi-source verification hub bundled with state eligibility work
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Free first year under CMS pledge per the idea

verdicts.substitutes: NDNH (SNAP agencies must query it at certification), state UI wage files, the federal Data Services Hub (student and veteran checks now carry Emmy functions), integrators' own source orchestration.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $800M Equifax government figure is not in any filing I could open (Q4 2025 8-K gives growth rates only). A savings-share router taking about 30% of savings on a book that includes SSA and non-state revenue yields roughly $30-60M even if half of an assumed $500-800M book moves at a 40-50% discount. The 19% share arithmetic is unverified.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Antitrust discovery forces payroll providers to open data (plausible, but the case is brought by mortgage lenders and is slow); states mandate a waterfall (moderate); Argyle, Truv and SteadyIQ choose to sell through a router instead of directly to states (low, they already hold state contracts).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Antitrust case is real (E.D. Pa., motion to dismiss denied Feb 2025; direct-purchaser lenders). The senators' letter confirms price hikes and 'about half of states' but names no exclusive partners (ADP and Intuit not confirmed). Truv state contract not confirmed.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Consent-based competitors already hold state contracts (Washington, Missouri) at lower prices, states and integrators already orchestrate cheap sources first, and a router is a thin layer with a ceiling near $50M.

verdicts.title: Renewal Autopilot priced per auto-completed case

competitors_found.name: CMS vendor pledge group: Accenture, Acentra, Conduent, GDIT, Deloitte, Gainwell, Maximus, Curam, Optum, RedMane
competitors_found.what_they_do: Pledged about $600M of free or discounted services to states for work requirements and redeterminations
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Incumbent state eligibility-system and operations vendors

competitors_found.name: Maximus
competitors_found.what_they_do: Eligibility operations contractor; says growth in U.S. Services returns with Medicaid and SNAP requirements

competitors_found.name: Conduent work requirements suite
competitors_found.what_they_do: Determinations, reporting and compliance for community engagement

verdicts.substitutes: State staff; existing ex parte rules inside state eligibility systems; CMS free toolkit and Hub; Clarity Solutions-style mail-processing contracts.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 55M renewals and recertifications at $12 per auto-completed case: $100M is 8.3M cases, which the idea itself puts at 30% of national volume at 50% auto-completion. No published per-renewal or outcome-based pricing or state RFP found. Savings logic ($55 per case) is plausible but the 2027 start is January 1 not July, and the vendor must integrate with systems owned by the incumbents.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: States sign outcome contracts against a measured baseline (no precedent found); incumbents allow third-party access to their eligibility systems (low); 10-15% national volume captured (heroic).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Six-month renewals for expansion adults from 2027 confirmed (CMS guidance March 2026; two transition options). Staff-decides model is consistent with the rule. State procurement of outcome-priced operations is the untested premise.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Ten incumbents already pledged free or discounted help on the same systems the vendor needs access to; no outcome-pricing precedent; the idea's own $100M path needs heroic share.

verdicts.title: Exemption Evidence Utility, starting with medical frailty

competitors_found.name: Gainwell medically frail identification tool
competitors_found.what_they_do: AI tool and 2,000+ clinical-code logic across medical, behavioral and pharmacy claims; offered to every state at no charge
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Gainwell, major MMIS vendor, announced 2026-03-31 under CMS pledge

competitors_found.name: Milliman Frailty Framework
competitors_found.what_they_do: Claims-based medically frail identification with risk adjustment and policy considerations

competitors_found.name: Wipro MCAID360
competitors_found.what_they_do: Work-requirement compliance platform covering exemptions and good-cause determinations

verdicts.substitutes: State analytics teams on MMIS data; CHCS data and analytic guidance; health information exchanges; self-attestation until 2028.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The idea's own total is $77-111M at near-total adoption of both halves. The code-set licence ($0.8-1.2M x 40 states) is undercut by a free equivalent. The clinician packet at $45 for 1.0-1.4M claimants is a thin-margin services network. Realistic median a handful of states.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: States prefer a paid audited code set over free Gainwell logic (low); a clinician network reaches a million completions at $45 with margin (moderate-low); self-attestation limit from 2028 forces documentation (plausible).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: IFR (June 2026) confirms the frailty definition requires a qualifying condition plus significant functional impairment, a state-maintained code list, and limited self-attestation from 2028 (KFF). CMS sub-regulatory frailty guidance issued 2026-09-08. A lawsuit over the exemption was mentioned but unconfirmed.
verdicts.deciding_reason: A free product from the vendor states already pay covers the code-set half, the clinician half is a thin-margin services network, and the idea's own total is only about $100M at near-total adoption.

verdicts.title: Rules Twin: versioned rules and a caseload digital twin

competitors_found.name: PolicyEngine
competitors_found.what_they_do: Open-source microsimulation of US tax and benefit programs, expanding to all 50 states

competitors_found.name: Nava PBC
competitors_found.what_they_do: Public benefit corporation building state benefits systems and rules-as-code experiments

competitors_found.name: Alluma rules engine
competitors_found.what_they_do: Decision-model rules engine built from CFR and program applications

verdicts.substitutes: Urban Institute TRIM3 and state-rules microsimulation, Milliman/Manatt/Mercer forecasting, integrators' proprietary engines, Beeck Center Rules as Code community.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $107M needs about 70% of states plus 25 plans; the idea itself says to kill if four states will not share de-identified caseloads. Buyers are policy and IT directors with project-sized budgets; no machine-readable rule set exists from any government, so the library is reverse-engineered and easy to copy.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: States share caseload data (unproven); CMS/courts require forecasts as routine (speculative); open-source PolicyEngine does not commoditise the rules layer (low).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: IFR volatility and 26-state litigation are real, but the premise that nobody simulates rule effects is false (TRIM3, PolicyEngine, actuarial firms). Integrator change-order claim is unverified.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Open-source and nonprofit rules-as-code already exist, buyers have project budgets not recurring lines, and the idea's own path needs about 70% of states.

result.pool_note: Forced state spend is real but incumbents (Maximus, SAS, Deloitte, Gainwell) and CMS free pledges absorb it. Observed state contracts run $0.4-4M against $50M-$2.5B of exposure. Value to states is huge; money they actually spend is small. Near miss: SNAP accuracy assurance (median ~$12M, upside ~$85M).

ideas.title: Badge-to-Bill: pre-payment hours integrity for T&M and cost-type labor invoices
ideas.one_liner: Reconcile every labor-hour invoice to independent evidence of work (badge, login, ticket, commit) before the agency pays, and hand the CO a decision-ready package instead of a post-hoc audit.
ideas.customer: Civilian agency CFO shops, senior procurement executives and OIGs with large T&M or cost-type services (civilians put 11% of obligations in T&M vs 1% at DoD, GAO-22-104806). Second customer for the same neutral ledger: primes, as False Claims Act defense and incentive-fee evidence. First 10: ten large T&M orders at agencies with a prior IG finding (IRS, GSA, HHS and DHS components, VA, State, SSA).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Deputy CFO or senior procurement executive, from contract-administration and payment-integrity funds (31 U.S.C. 3352(i) requires recovery audits on every program spending $1M+ a year where cost-effective, contract payments included). Contractor side: VP contracts or general counsel at primes. Fixed annual fee per covered contract, not contingency.
ideas.problem: With T&M the invoice is hours x rate and the only control is a collateral-duty COR checking timesheets. TIGTA's sample found $394,430 of $1M of invoiced IRS labor hours (39%) unsupported on one procurement; FCA recoveries hit a record $6.8B in FY2025 but arrive years later; DCAA cleared its backlog by sampling, so it is not full coverage. Cost-type consulting was $120B in FY2024 and every dollar is hours.
ideas.solution: Read-only connectors to invoices (WAWF/IPP or contractor feed), to presence evidence (PIV badge logs, directory logins, ticketing and commits inside the agency boundary) and to timesheets. Flags hours billed with no presence evidence, labor-category mismatches against resumes, duplicate hours across contracts and idle-time patterns. Output is an evidence package the CO decides on inside the Prompt Payment return window (7 days, unverified). The product never decides an overpayment.
ideas.why_now: April 30, 2026 EO forces a top-10 non-fixed-price review and twice-yearly OMB reporting; GSA's $23.3B savings claim needs verification; FCA at a record; existing T&M task orders run off over 2027-29 so the exposed pool does not vanish on conversion.
ideas.wedge: Fixed-fee retrospective on 12 months of invoices for one large T&M order, offered to an OIG or CFO who already has a finding; convert to an annual per-contract subscription.
ideas.path_to_100m: Labor-based pool is about $28B/yr of T&M (GAO $139B over FY17-21) plus ~70% labor share of the EO's $120B cost-type consulting, roughly $110B (A). Fee 0.4% of covered spend, below the 1-2% of contract value a COR function costs (A). Agency side $55M needs $13.8B covered, about 12-13% of the pool; contractor side 300 accounts x $150k = $45M. Heroic: it works only if OMB or a CFO council points to it as a standard control.
ideas.who_does_it_today: DCAA (sampled, after the fact), agency OIGs and TIGTA (episodic), CORs (collateral duty), DOJ and qui tam relators (years later), commercial recovery auditors that work commercial payables, Big 4 forensic teams. No productized continuous control for federal labor invoices found in my searches.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each owns one piece (invoice in finance, badge log in security, judgment in the program office) and none is paid to join them before payment.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (agency-granted data access plus a labeled dataset of billed vs evidenced hours by labor category and contract type) and switching costs once embedded in the payment workflow.
ideas.earned_secret: The proof of an hour already exists inside the agency; a 2025 Booz Allen settlement ($422,557) was built by comparing invoices and timesheets to badge-swipe data. The gap is organizational, not technical: nobody owns the join. Legal premise: contractors may identify but not finally determine an overpayment (31 U.S.C. 3352(i)), and the 2020 amendment removed express contractor-payment language, so never price as contingency.
ideas.first_90_days: Hire an ex-OIG auditor and an ex-COR; offer a no-cost retrospective to one agency via an OIG referral; build badge and directory ingestion in the agency environment; draft CO decision memos; run one contractor-side pilot on a contract where the agency is not also a customer (hard firewall).

ideas.title: The subcontract rail: Textura for federal services
ideas.one_liner: The workspace where a prime and its subs exchange flow-downs, status, timesheets and accepted milestones, report to the government, and move money within days of the prime being paid.
ideas.customer: Subcontracts and contracts managers at mid-tier primes ($100M-$1B revenue, 20-100 subs) and the small-business subs they depend on. First 10: mid-tier primes that lost 8(a) subs to suspension (1,091 suspended, ~800 in termination) and must re-verify every small-business credit.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Prime's VP of subcontracts or contracts, from subcontract administration (allowable indirect, assumption); subs pay for early payment. Platform fee plus payment take on both sides.
ideas.problem: Primes reported a record $86.4B of small-business subcontract awards in FY2023, and the plumbing is email and spreadsheets: flow-downs that now differ by agency FAR deviation, small-business status that can flip overnight, subaward reporting (threshold now $40k), timesheet collection, pay-when-paid terms. CPARS rates primes only, so subs have no portable past performance, and services subs have no Miller Act or lien protection like construction. Two shutdowns in 12 months (43 and 76 days) left subs unpaid.
ideas.solution: Sub onboarding with live SAM and SBA status feeds, flow-down generation, sub timesheet and milestone submission with evidence, prime acceptance, automatic payment to the sub from the prime's own account on a fixed schedule after the prime is paid, eSRS and FSRS report generation, limitations-on-subcontracting dashboards. Each accepted milestone becomes a prime-signed entry in the sub's portable performance record.
ideas.why_now: Fixed-price milestone billing under the April 2026 EO, the 8(a) wave, RFO clause churn, higher reporting thresholds, and repeated shutdown payment shocks.
ideas.wedge: Status monitoring plus eSRS and FSRS report generation for mid-tier primes (compliance only, no money moves), then the pay rail.
ideas.path_to_100m: Platform fee 0.15% + payment/early-pay take 0.30% = 0.45% of flow (A). $100M needs ~$22B/yr of flow: about 26% of the $86.4B small-business sub flow, or ~10% of all subcontract flow if the total is near $220B (unverified; no governmentwide total found). Heroic share; credible only if portable sub performance records become the thing primes ask for.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Exostar (defense supplier credentialing/collaboration), Deltek and Unanet (GovCon ERPs with subcontract modules), Oracle Textura and Procore (construction only), Coupa/Jaggaer (corporate procurement), supplier-diversity software. For money: Blackstar Capital (works with primes to fund subs, $1B facility reported), X-Caliber, factors. No two-sided services workspace with an acceptance-linked pay rail found.
ideas.why_they_lose: ERPs are the prime's cost-accounting books, not a shared workspace; Exostar handles credentials, not acceptance and payment; factors fund after the invoice exists and do not control when the prime pays.
ideas.moat: Network effects (a sub works with many primes and keeps one history) plus a cornered resource in the portable, prime-signed performance record.
ideas.earned_secret: Subs do not lose because they cannot win work; they lose on cash timing and on having no past performance of their own. Late payment is mostly manual invoice matching and acceptance, not a cash shortage at the prime. A ledger of prime-signed accepted milestones is the first portable credential a sub has.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 3 mid-tier primes on the free compliance tier; wire SAM and SBA feeds; pilot with 30 subs; get a sponsor bank for ACH pay-outs from the prime's own funds (avoids money-transmitter status, assumption). Check FAR 52.232-40 accelerated-payment duty and CUI handling (FedRAMP Moderate) before any DoD work.

ideas.title: The Acceptance Rail: per-event verification for outcome-priced federal contracts
ideas.one_liner: A neutral measurement standard that checks each milestone or metric against objective evidence and gives the CO a signed evidence package, priced per verified event.
ideas.customer: COs, CORs and program managers on fixed-price, performance-based services above $10M (the EO's agency-head approval line), plus contractors with profit at risk. First 10: ten IT-operations contracts whose acceptance criteria are already numeric (ticket resolution time, backlog burn-down, uptime) at agencies restructuring their top-10 contracts.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Program office, from the contract's own surveillance/QASP line (COR labor is typically 1-2% of contract value, assumption); signer is the CO with a chief acquisition officer sponsor. Contractors pay for evidence that protects performance-tied profit and CPARS ratings.
ideas.problem: The April 30, 2026 EO ties profit to performance metrics and penalizes weak results, which needs a metric both sides accept. CO/COR capacity is collapsing (GSA acquisition attrition 39%). CPARS is late and weak (a DoD IG sample: 83 of 238 assessments late by 73 days on average, 200 of 238 non-compliant). IV&V is episodic and only for big IT. AI-delivered work produces thousands of small outputs nobody can review by hand.
ideas.solution: Machine-readable metric definitions for ~30 common service outcomes attached to the contract at award; connectors to systems of record (ServiceNow, Jira, GitHub, logs); a signed time-stamped event ledger; CO dashboard and CPARS-ready evidence summary. The CO accepts; the rail never does (inherently governmental).
ideas.why_now: EO; RFO batch 2 adds consumption-based fixed-price solutions that need metering; OneGov moving to consumption pricing normalizes metered billing; CO and COR gaps.
ideas.wedge: Free to the CO for 90 days on ten IT-operations contracts, paid per event afterward; publish the metric spec openly to seed the standard.
ideas.path_to_100m: Outcome-priced services under measurement reach $200-300B by 2028 (A). Fee 0.3% of verified contract value; with 20% of revenue from contractors, the agency side needs $80M, i.e. ~$27B verified, about 9-13% of that spend. Heroic, but measurement standards tend to be winner-take-most once GAO and COFC decisions cite them.
ideas.who_does_it_today: IV&V providers (Booz Allen, SAIC, Leidos, small IV&V shops, NASA's IV&V facility), CPARS/PPIRS (government), in-house QASPs, contract-writing vendors such as Unison PRISM (documents, not evidence), observability tools that do not speak FAR. No productized acceptance-evidence vendor found.
ideas.why_they_lose: IV&V firms sell hours and often also sell delivery, so they are conflicted; contract-writing tools manage paper not data; government cannot hire to build it.
ideas.moat: Network/standard (once COs and tribunals accept the format) plus counter-positioning against conflicted IV&V.
ideas.earned_secret: Outcome disputes mostly come from nobody agreeing at award how the metric is measured, not from bad data. Freeze the definition in the contract and keep a neutral log, and most of the argument disappears. Strict organizational-conflict firewall required: the rail cannot deliver on any contract it measures.
ideas.first_90_days: Co-write five metric templates with two former COs; instrument three contracts; apply to OASIS+ or MAS; get a chief acquisition officer letter of support; hire an ex-GSA FAS acquisition official.

ideas.title: Verified-WIP lender: control the repayment channel for fixed-price federal work
ideas.one_liner: Lend 60-75% against verified, not-yet-billed work in progress on fixed-price federal services, repaid by Treasury directly to the lender under the Assignment of Claims Act or by controlled-account sweep for subs.
ideas.customer: Mid-tier and small GovCons converting from monthly T&M invoices to milestone-billed fixed-price work. First 10: ten firms with milestone contracts at civilian agencies whose bank says unbilled work sits outside the borrowing base (unverified).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Contractor CFO or owner, from financing cost that fixed-price pricing can absorb (interest is unallowable on cost-type work, so this is a fixed-price product).
ideas.problem: Under T&M the invoice follows hours every month. Under milestone billing cost runs ahead of billing and acceptance timing is discretionary. Asset-based lenders typically advance against billed invoices only (unverified). Shutdowns (43 and 76 days in the last 12 months, CR to Dec 11) stop payment altogether, and factors price all of this into a flat fee.
ideas.solution: A non-bank lender that sees progress and acceptance state (contractor ERP and ticket feeds, WAWF or IPP status) and advances against verified WIP, assigned under the Act for prime contracts and sweep-controlled for subs, with shutdown repricing built in. Imports Brazil's payroll-deduction logic: be repaid first from a channel you control.
ideas.why_now: EO and RFO move work to milestones; shutdown frequency; AI investment needs working capital; banks cautious.
ideas.wedge: Verified-progress financing on task orders up to $5M at agencies with fast acceptance history; a $20M facility from a credit fund.
ideas.path_to_100m: At ~12% yield (A), $100M needs ~$830M average outstanding. Fixed-price milestone services reach ~$100B/yr by 2028 (A); unbilled WIP of 1.5 months is $12.5B; mid-tier and small firms hold half, $6.2B; the lender needs ~13% of that plus ~$100M of equity under a warehouse line. Flagged as the weakest of the set.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Blackstar Capital ($1B facility reported; funds prime contractors and subs), X-Caliber GovCon Capital (contract-based advances without factoring), United Capital Funding, Porter Capital, Bay Street Lending, Altline Sobel, bank ABL desks. One lender guide quotes 85-95% advances on approved invoices at 1-2.5% per 30 days. None found underwriting acceptance state.
ideas.why_they_lose: They underwrite the borrower or the submitted invoice; none sees milestone progress or the CO's acceptance history.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in cost of capital plus a cornered data resource (loss history by agency and CO). Thin.
ideas.earned_secret: The lender's real exposure is acceptance timing, not government credit, and acceptance timing is the most predictable variable from a CO's modification and payment history. Legal premise: the Assignment of Claims Act assigns only to a bank or other financing institution with notice to the CO and disbursing officer; a Fall 2026 ABA article says modern credit structures raise unsettled questions.
ideas.first_90_days: Hire an ex-GovCon ABL underwriter; build the progress-evidence feed; sign a credit fund; close 10 facilities; confirm state lending-license needs.

ideas.title: The Evidence Desk: ex-auditors who cannot audit, for the 2028 DoD clean-opinion deadline
ideas.one_liner: An all-ex-auditor firm that never takes an attest engagement and sells audit-ready evidence per Notice of Findings and Recommendations closed, for DoD components and civilian agencies chasing clean opinions.
ideas.customer: DoD component financial-management offices (Army, Navy, Air Force, DLA, DISA, DHA, among 29 stand-alone audits) and CFO Act civilian agencies. First 10: ten recurring NFR families at two components (property accountability and valuation, unliquidated obligations, system access controls).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Component deputy CFO, from audit-remediation funding that already exists (DoD OIG: $4.11B in FY2018-22, government plus contractor). Deloitte holds a Comptroller remediation contract of up to $78.3M ($12.2M obligated, to Nov 2028).
ideas.problem: Eighth failed audit in Dec 2025, 26 material weaknesses, clean opinion promised by 2028 (FY24 NDAA). GAO found the NFR resolution rate fell FY2019-22 and DoD OIG found components managed FIAR contracts poorly. The people who know what an auditor will accept are barred from remediating the entities they audit (auditor-independence rules on non-audit services, unverified), and the firms that remediate sell hours.
ideas.solution: For each NFR, reconstruct the auditor's test (population, sample, evidence request), use AI to tie transactions to supporting contracts, receiving reports and invoices, run mock testing with auditor logic, and close the corrective action plan. Priced per NFR accepted as closed, with a holdback until the auditor closes it.
ideas.why_now: The comptroller publicly said DoD will not reach the goal without a significant acceleration; the Dec 31, 2028 statutory date puts the money in FY2027-28.
ideas.wedge: Tie-out of one recurring finding for one component in 60 days, paid per item resolved.
ideas.path_to_100m: Contractor-addressable remediation about $0.4B/yr now (half of $4.11B/5, A), rising to ~$0.8B on the 2028 ramp (A), plus $0.3-0.5B civilian internal-control and audit-readiness work (unverified): ~$1.1-1.3B. $100M is 8-12% of that. Heroic for a boutique; it scales only if the evidence engine becomes the shared platform.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Deloitte, Booz Allen, Accenture Federal, Guidehouse, Grant Thornton public sector, Kearney; KPMG, EY and other independent public accountants hired for component audits (barred from remediating the same entity, unverified); DoD's Advana data platform; component FIAR teams.
ideas.why_they_lose: Juniors who have never sat across from the auditor; T&M incentives that reward hours, not closed findings; independence rules that keep the best-informed firms out.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (alumni of audit firms and an NFR-by-NFR playbook library reusable across 29 entities) and process power.
ideas.earned_secret: The same few dozen root causes recur across the 29 entities, so a tested remediation at Army is a template for Navy. DoD does not fail for lack of effort but because transactions cannot be tied to supporting documents. Firewall so no affiliate is an independent public accountant for any component served.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit three former audit managers and a former DoD OIG auditor; take one NFR pilot; stand up the independence firewall; confirm clearance needs.

ideas.title: The cost-guaranteed sub that primes buy to reprice their own contracts
ideas.one_liner: Sell primes a fixed unit price per outcome for the automatable 30-50% of their civilian task orders, with a guaranteed price glide path, so they can submit a credible fixed-price restructuring without gutting margin.
ideas.customer: Pricing leads and delivery VPs at primes and mid-tier GovCons whose largest civilian contracts are in the EO's restructuring queue (Booz Allen, Accenture Federal, Deloitte GPS, GDIT, Leidos, SAIC, CACI, Guidehouse, ICF, Peraton-class). First 10: one mid-tier prime with three contracts of $20-80M.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Prime's contracts director with the program manager and pricing lead, from the subcontract line inside the restructured fixed-price offer.
ideas.problem: A prime's revenue is hours x rate. The EO forces fixed price at an assumed 20-30% lower number with the same people (assumption). Leidos reports rising fixed-price mix and margin pressure; Booz Allen's Q4 civil revenue fell 23% and FY27 civil guidance is down high single digits. Internal AI efforts collide with utilization and headcount targets that pay delivery leaders (unverified), and nobody inside can sign a contractual cost-down.
ideas.solution: Per-outcome unit prices (per authorization package, ticket class, case file prepared, report) under the prime's contract, with a scheduled annual price decline, service credits and acceptance tests; operates inside the agency boundary under the prime's authorization. The prime keeps program management, the customer and past performance.
ideas.why_now: April 30, 2026 EO and the July 29 restructuring deadline, GSA's outcome-based push, and civilian IT weakness expected through CY27 (TBR).
ideas.wedge: One slice (security documentation or ticket triage) on one restructured task order, priced at about 60% of the prime's current labor cost with a performance guarantee.
ideas.path_to_100m: EO's $120B cost-type consulting x 70% labor x 30% automatable = ~$25B of cost base (A); at 60% of that, ~$15B addressable sub revenue. $100M is 0.7% of it, or 30 restructured contracts at $3.3M of sub revenue each. Share is easy; trust and cost-guarantee credibility are not.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Primes' own AI programs (Booz Allen, Accenture Federal, Deloitte have internal platforms, unverified), Palantir (platform inside agencies), Ask Sage (BigBear.ai, FedRAMP High), C3 AI and other forward-deployed teams, Kaizen, staff-augmentation firms.
ideas.why_they_lose: Primes cannot contract a cost-down internally against their own headcount incentives; an external guaranteed price converts a hope into a number they can put in a proposal. Honest weakness: after ~18 months a prime can copy the method.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning now; process power (a unit-cost database from every restructured order) and switching costs (inside the prime's authorization boundary) later.
ideas.earned_secret: A prime's pricing lead is not afraid of the technical approach; they are afraid of the minus-25% line in the proposal and of not knowing whether cost will follow. They pay a premium for certainty. Check pass-through limits on cost-type contracts (FAR 52.215-23) and consent-to-subcontract rules.
ideas.first_90_days: Pitch three mid-tier primes with live restructuring; build the unit-price sheet for three work types; offer a first-year guaranteed price; settle the consent-to-subcontract path.

ideas.title: The Outcome Catalog: unit-priced deliverables under the simplified threshold
ideas.one_liner: A schedule vendor that sells a short menu of fixed-price, acceptance-tested deliverables (authorization packages, control-test cycles, information-collection packages, records and accessibility work) that federal offices now buy as hours, each sized to land under $350,000 and obligated with year-end money.
ideas.customer: Program offices and COs at civilian agencies. First 10: ten components at HHS, DHS, VA, Treasury and State, starting with security authorization packages and internal-control test cycles. FOIA surge is a SKU but crowded (FOIAXpress, Seekr, Veritone; DHS reportedly gave Deloitte an AI FOIA build, unverified).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The ordering CO, with program-office O&M funds that used to fund T&M hours. Orders up to the $350,000 simplified threshold need only a reasonable-price determination; a published unit price is the CO's whole analysis (unverified). Micro-purchases up to $15,000 need less.
ideas.problem: These deliverables hide inside large task orders on a 12-18 month cycle or small sole-source orders. The April 30, 2026 EO makes T&M harder to justify (agency-head approval above $10M civilian). COs are leaving (GSA 39% attrition) and cannot write outcome-based requirements quickly; 18F, which used to help, was eliminated in March 2025.
ideas.solution: About ten SKUs with a published unit price, an objective acceptance test and a fixed delivery date, delivered by AI-assisted teams inside the agency boundary and staffed from the largest glut of experienced ex-federal and ex-consultant talent in a decade (Booz Allen alone cut 2,500). Orders go through MAS or OASIS+ BPAs; the top-down route is a OneGov-style enterprise rate card with the GSA FAS commissioner.
ideas.why_now: EO; RFO batch 2's consumption-based fixed price; OASIS+ open on-ramp with no stated cap; simplified threshold raised to $350k; ordering workforce that cannot run long competitions.
ideas.wedge: One SKU (a moderate-impact system authorization package at ~$90-140k, assumption) and ten pilot orders under $50k in the first two quarters; Q4 (July-September) of FY2027 is the first scale test since the FY2027 CR runs only to Dec 11.
ideas.path_to_100m: 400 orders x $250k = $100M by year four (A), which is 0.07% of the ~$148B/yr of T&M plus cost-type consulting. The statutory-deliverable subset is smaller and unsized (unverified), so assume 1-3% of that subset. Capacity about 100-150 delivery staff with AI leverage (A).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Thousands of small MAS holders and the primes; AI-forward entrants Kaizen ($21M), Ask Sage, Palantir forward-deployed teams, Pryzm ($12.2M), C3 AI; compliance software (RegScale, Paramify, Telos Xacta, unverified). No one found that unit-prices accepted outcomes for agencies.
ideas.why_they_lose: Primes cannot make money on a sub-$350k order and their rate cards are contract terms; small shops cannot afford AI or authorization inheritance; software vendors do not deliver accepted outcomes.
ideas.moat: Process power (unit-cost database improving every order) and counter-positioning against T&M books; cornered resource in agency-accepted templates.
ideas.earned_secret: From a GSA ordering official or agency budget officer: COs buy what they can obligate in nine days, not what is best. A non-severable, fully funded, fixed-price deliverable with an objective test is the easiest thing to obligate in a September sprint, and a CO no longer has to defend T&M to the senior procurement executive. Legal checks: bona fide needs and the one-year severable-services rule, inherently governmental line (the AO signs), no requirements-writing for any agency that is also a customer, and size standards (set-asides vanish past the standard, so $100M is a large-business plan).
ideas.first_90_days: Subcontract under eight existing MAS holders as SKU partner while a MAS offer is evaluated; recruit two former COs and two former ISSOs; publish the unit price list; run five micro-purchase and under-$50k pilots; operate only in agency enclaves.

ideas.title: Award Ops: outcome-priced grant operations for offices that lost their staff
ideas.one_liner: Per-unit pre-award packet review, progress-report review and closeout for grant-making offices, with the human grants officer still signing every award.
ideas.customer: Grant-making offices at NIH institutes, NSF, ED, HHS (ACF, HRSA, CDC), DOT, DOE, EPA and Interior. First 10: ten NIH institutes and centers with grants-management shortages (NHGRI fell from 11 specialists to 3).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Deputy director for management or the grants management officer, from program-support funds. Contractors can prepare and monitor; award decisions and obligations stay with a federal grants officer.
ideas.problem: NIH had dispersed $2.3B less than its five-year median by Q3 FY26 and renewals are 90+ days late more often. NPS requires two political appointees to review every grant of $50,000 or more, leaving ~1,400 grants and $362M behind schedule. NSF sits at ~1,300 staff and says that is too low. There are 1,386 grant programs and over $1.2T a year; GAO counted 5,100+ employees significantly involved in grants management at just four agencies.
ideas.solution: Unit prices per application packet brought to award-ready (budget reasonableness, indirect-rate verification, terms and conditions, risk assessment, debarment and audit-status checks), per progress report reviewed, per closeout, per single-audit finding resolved; for politically reviewed agencies the review package is prepared by the desk too.
ideas.why_now: Staff losses, new review layers, a pending Uniform Guidance rewrite (blocked through Dec 11 in the Senate CR text, unverified), and the EO's pressure against hourly contractors.
ideas.wedge: Closeouts and progress-report review first (no award decision), then pre-award packets.
ideas.path_to_100m: Federal-side grants administration labor about $3-6B/yr (0.25-0.5% of $1.2T, assumption); contractor-addressable 20% = $0.6-1.2B; $100M is 8-17%. Heroic, flagged.
ideas.who_does_it_today: GrantSolutions (HHS ACF shared service) and NIH eRA (systems), Salesforce and Oracle grants modules, Euna, SmartSimple and Fluxx (mostly state, local and foundation), integrators such as Guidehouse, ICF, Deloitte and Booz Allen (which hold which grants-operations contracts is unverified), and in-house staff. No outcome-priced AI grants-operations vendor found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Systems vendors sell software but staff are the bottleneck; integrators sell hours that the EO disfavors; hiring is frozen.
ideas.moat: Process power and switching costs (agency-specific term libraries); weak to moderate.
ideas.earned_secret: The bottleneck is not the award decision, it is about twenty mechanical checks before a grants officer can sign (unverified); automate them and three specialists do the work of eleven. Political-review requirements and shifting priorities could remove the work overnight, and research-security checks apply.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit two ex-grants-management officers; pilot closeouts for one NIH institute; build a library of 2 CFR 200 checks; keep a human signature on every action.

verdicts.title: Slot Book: block-booked engine shop capacity for mid-tier operators

competitors_found.name: AJW Group (engine management, shop visit management)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Negotiates shop-visit contract terms and workscope for airlines through a preferred-MRO network; claims purchasing power above many airlines
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Established group; shop-visit management deals such as Donavia and NordStar (2015)

competitors_found.name: StandardAero / AviLease general terms agreement
competitors_found.what_they_do: Lessor-to-shop framework for LEAP and CFM56-7B work; the release describes a GTA, not reserved capacity, and shop terms say it may reject any order
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Public company; AviLease manages ~200 aircraft for 53 airlines

competitors_found.name: OEM power-by-the-hour and closed networks
competitors_found.what_they_do: Bundle priority and limit independent MRO access, per the IATA study
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Industry-wide; IATA calls for removing barriers to independent MROs

verdicts.substitutes: Engine-management firms (AJW, Acumen) and direct lessor framework agreements; large airlines bundle priority in PBH contracts; mid-tier operators can buy cover engines or extend leases. No neutral slot aggregator found in three searches, but the reasons one does not exist (parts, not stands, are the binding constraint; shops decline binding capacity) are the problem.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Pitch assumes ~4,700 narrowbody visits a year; an IBA-sourced figure puts visits near 3,800 a year through 2027 and above 4,000 in 2028 (scope unclear), so the base is plausibly 15-20% high. Corrected: 3,900 visits x 40% mid-tier x $4.5M = ~$7.0B of spend; a 4.5% take is $316M at 100% share, so $100M needs ~32% share. The 10-15% reservation fee is an escrowed deposit, not revenue, and take-or-pay exposure sits on the broker's balance sheet.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Needs: (1) shops sign binding take-or-pay capacity with guaranteed induction windows (the cited StandardAero release does not show this and its terms say it may reject any order; implausible); (2) OEM licenses allow resale or subcontracting of slots (unverified, new-gen engines sit in closed networks); (3) scarcity persists past 2030 while StandardAero, FTAI and others add lines (contested); (4) the broker holds ~12% of mid-tier visits at a 4% take (heroic). Even if all hold, parts shortages, not slots, drive the 180-day turnaround.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Why-now premise overstated: the StandardAero-AviLease release is a general terms agreement 'paving the way' for services, not a capacity reservation. Bain names parts as the main cause of slow turnaround, slots secondary. Take-or-pay is lawful; OEM license assignment limits and buyer-pool antitrust are unverified.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Premise contradicted: no binding capacity product is evidenced, parts rather than slots gate turnaround, and even the pitch's own math needs 26-32% share; upside is about $35M.

verdicts.title: The Repair Library: approved-repair IP for engine piece parts

competitors_found.name: Chromalloy
competitors_found.what_they_do: Independent engine part repair: 50+ DER repairs (25 advanced) on CFM56-5B/7B plus an FAA-approved PMA HPT blade with backlog into 2026

competitors_found.name: HEICO Flight Support Group
competitors_found.what_they_do: PMA parts, repair and overhaul, distribution

competitors_found.name: RTX Pratt & Whitney additive GTF repair
competitors_found.what_they_do: OEM directed-energy-deposition repair of GTF structural cases, cutting process time over 60%
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Projects ~$100M of parts recovered over five years across 20 shops

competitors_found.name: FTAI Aviation with Chromalloy (HPT blade PMA)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Spent 7 years and over $100M developing its own FAA-approved CFM56 blade alternative

verdicts.substitutes: Shops' in-house schemes, CFM repair licensees (CFM committed Jan 2026 that CFM manuals work with non-OEM repairs), DER repairs bought from Chromalloy-type vendors, SFAR 36 route for some holders, and OEM licensing programs. A neutral library competes with every shop's own proprietary data.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $5.6B repair pool and $2.2B independent-addressable slice are the pitch's own multiplications (50.7B x 55% x 20% x 40%), unsourced. A 17.5% royalty is high, and shops with their own schemes are the least likely licensees; licensing alone would need $570M of repaired value, so the plan leans on owned cells ($25-40M per hub). Scale check: Pratt's whole GTF additive program is ~$20M a year of recovered parts, so the model needs several programs that size. $300k per scheme fits simple repairs, not hot-section parts where FTAI spent $100M+ on one blade.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Three or four hot-section CFM56 schemes win DER approval and shop adoption (moderately plausible given Chromalloy precedent); (2) $60-100M of capital for cells, which venture has not funded in this niche (plausible but slow); (3) a lessor writes approved schemes into workscope clauses (speculative, only a 90-day goal in the pitch); (4) shops share post-repair CT and flow data with a neutral party to build the moat (unlikely); (5) LEAP and GTF repair licensing opens (CFM says it will consider requests). Together these are below top-decile odds, and the upside still tops out under $100M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Mechanism is real: major repair data needs FAA approval and DERs approve multiple-use data through repair specifications (FAA N 8110.111, AC 33-6). IATA and Bain both say repair approvals are too few. But approvals are applicant-specific, data is proprietary to developers, and export classification of engine technical data is unverified.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real pain but scaled incumbents (Chromalloy 50+ DER repairs on the same parts, HEICO) and heavy capital; median about $10M, upside about $80M.

verdicts.title: Fleet Buying Group: a Vizient for aircraft maintenance with PMA offtake pools

competitors_found.name: AAR Airvoyant
competitors_found.what_they_do: AI procurement platform for airlines and MROs launched Apr 2026; demand consolidation, vendor optimization and negotiation agents due later in 2026; integrates Aeroxchange's ~5,000 suppliers
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: AAR is a public multi-billion supplier; launch partners include Air Europa, Allegiant, Atlas, JetBlue, Thai, Virgin Atlantic

competitors_found.name: SkySelect
competitors_found.what_they_do: AI sourcing and ordering for airlines, MROs and lessors across 3,000+ suppliers
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $9M raised Mar 2026; $6B cumulative and $1.3B in 2025 transactions; customers JetBlue, Sun Country, Vueling

competitors_found.name: IATP / IATA MRO SmartHub
competitors_found.what_they_do: Airline technical materials pooling (6,600 parts, 350 stations) and inventory visibility, agreed 2026

competitors_found.name: AVIAA (business-aviation GPO)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Group purchasing for business aviation, ~500 aircraft and 70+ suppliers at peak

verdicts.substitutes: Airline-alliance joint purchasing, bilateral bulk deals, distributor contracts, PMA vendors selling direct (HEICO), and airlines' own procurement teams. Free: IATA SmartHub visibility.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $40B+ annual parts spend and $50B excess inventory are SkySelect marketing claims; the 40-50% mid-tier share is unverified. The largest slice of spend is sole-source OEM parts priced by contract, where pooled volume buys less leverage than in healthcare supplies. $4B managed at 2.5% is 20%+ of the mid-tier pool, which the pitch itself calls heroic. At a realistic 5-8% of mid-tier spend the fee is $15-35M.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Needs OEMs and distributors to pay rebates to a brand-new buyer collective (low plausibility while AAR and SkySelect ship pooling), 60+ members with pooled RFPs, and PMA developers committing to offtake letters (non-binding today). Rule-of-reason antitrust exposure after FTC and DOJ withdrew collaboration guidelines in Dec 2024.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: FTC and DOJ withdrew the 2000 competitor-collaboration guidelines on 2024-12-11 with no replacement, so buyer pools are judged case by case; no aviation equivalent of the healthcare GPO fee safe harbor. Vendor-paid fees create buyer-agent conflict and disclosure issues. Not fatal.
verdicts.deciding_reason: AAR Airvoyant and SkySelect are shipping the pitch's year-2 product, the only aviation GPO precedent is dead, and OEM sole-source pricing limits pooled leverage; upside about $35M.

verdicts.title: Graded Parts: authentication, escrow and indemnity for non-OEM parts

competitors_found.name: DUST Identity (Theseus)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Physical diamond-dust marking plus AI document verification so MROs can confirm part identity and provenance; launched Apr 2026, pilots with Airbus (company claims)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: MIT spinout, ~25 staff, $53M+ raised (Kleiner Perkins, Airbus, Lockheed Martin)

competitors_found.name: Aeroxchange eARC with Boeing and Southwest
competitors_found.what_they_do: First digital FAA 8130-3 shipment Oct 2025 using signed encrypted certificates; Boeing rolling out to nine repair centers pending FAA authorization

competitors_found.name: Aviation Supply Chain Integrity Coalition
competitors_found.what_they_do: Airbus, American, Boeing, Delta, GE, Safran, StandardAero, United; recommends digital ARCs and document authentication
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Formed Feb 2024, co-chaired by former NTSB chair Sumwalt

verdicts.substitutes: Shops' own incoming inspection and back-to-birth paperwork audits (now standard after AOG Technics), OEM and distributor verification calls, FAA suspected-unapproved-parts reporting, and free digital-certificate efforts funded by OEMs.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $4B of graded flow is 65% of the pool file's $6.2B used-serviceable-material figure. The '$20B non-OEM-direct' base halves an unverified $40B claim. At a still-generous 5% of a $20B base, a 2.5% fee yields $25M. AOG Technics involved ~70-86 documents and ~50 part numbers: rare but severe, which is hard to price into a 1.0% premium without actuarial data.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Needs lenders, insurers and the airline coalition to mandate this grade as the standard (the pitch itself says that is the only path; low plausibility while OEM-backed digital certificates and DUST are being rolled out), an admitted insurer willing to underwrite consequential AOG loss (no product found), and sellers accepting a buyer-paid fee.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Grader cannot issue return-to-service documents unless a Part 145 holder, so inspection is subcontracted. I found no aviation-parts indemnity or counterfeit-coverage product, so insurer appetite is unproven; escrow and MGA licensing unresolved. No FAA or EASA mandate for digital certificates (pitch searched; consistent with my finding).
verdicts.deciding_reason: Authentication layer is occupied and funded; indemnity layer has no evidenced insurer or loss data; realistic fee base is a few percent of a small USM pool.

verdicts.title: Kit-First: induct the kit, not the engine

competitors_found.name: FTAI Aviation (module factory and materials)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Refurbishes CFM56 modules (757 in 2025, 1,200 targeted 2026, capacity 3,000 a year across six sites) and increasingly sells to third parties; says CFM56 is supply-constrained
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Aerospace Products revenue $1.6B in 2025, Q4 EBITDA margin 35%

competitors_found.name: CFM Materials LP (GE and Safran JV)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Used CFM56 and LEAP material for shop visits, material services agreements, customer-owned material and set management

competitors_found.name: AAR (Cebu Pacific surplus material agreement)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Supplies CFM56-5B surplus material across 30 planned shop visits, sourced via its FTAI partnership

competitors_found.name: AerSale
competitors_found.what_they_do: Builds engines from its own material inventory; bought Sanad parts including quick-engine-change kits
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Public; consumes its own USM, so outside USM sales fell in Q1 2026

verdicts.substitutes: AJW 'full engine material solution' per shop visit, StandardAero and shops' own material purchasing, lessors' own teardown stock, and customer-furnished material, which is already normal practice.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Pitch arithmetic holds: 300 visits x $2.5M = $750M revenue, $90-112M gross profit at 12-15%. But 300 visits is 6-8% of narrowbody visits and needs $120-150M of inventory capital, while FTAI earns ~35% EBITDA on similar activity, so a 12-15% margin entrant is underpricing or sourcing worse. Teardown feedstock is shrinking (retirements tracking 1.5-2% versus 3-4% forecast, per coverage of FTAI). Forecast-fee-only ceiling is ~$20M, as the pitch admits.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Net revenue (gross profit) basis; gross billings median ~$35M and upside ~$150M. Needs: privileged teardown and USM supply against FTAI, AAR, AerSale and CFM Materials (low plausibility); $100M+ of inventory financing (plausible); shops accepting induction gating that cuts their utilization metric (the pitch concedes this); and a findings-data forecast edge that is an unverified insider hypothesis. Revenue passes $100M easily, gross profit does not.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Customer-furnished material is normal in shop contracts and USM needs full traceability; no legal blocker. Premise error: the scarce input is the part, not the forecast, and the holders of parts are the incumbents.
verdicts.deciding_reason: FTAI already runs this as a profitable module factory and sells to third parties; the entrant has the forecast but not the parts. Gross profit upside is about $22M.

verdicts.title: Shop-Floor Ledger: evidence capture the MRO ERPs cannot do

competitors_found.name: EmpowerMX (acquired by IFS)
competitors_found.what_they_do: MRO records, EMX Vision AI module for planning and execution
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: About $11M raised; acquired by IFS July 2024

competitors_found.name: Soji AI
competitors_found.what_they_do: Agentic AI that reads and structures technical records for MROs, lessors and airlines; Active Partners deal May 2026
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Founded 2023, Airborne Capital backed; amount undisclosed

competitors_found.name: Amygda
competitors_found.what_they_do: AI maintenance data observability for aerospace and rail

competitors_found.name: Ramco Systems (aviation MRO software)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Incumbent MRO ERP including Korean Air engine maintenance deployment

verdicts.substitutes: Incumbent ERPs (Trax, Ramco, AMOS, Veryon, IFS) adding native capture, Lufthansa Technik AVIATAR (absorbed flydocs and AMOS), and shops' existing paper-plus-scan workflows.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M needs 55,000 paid seats, 7% of an estimated 800,000 technicians (technician total is the pitch's estimate), for an add-on that sits beside the system of record. Ramco's entire company reports ~$80M. The ~$7B 'MRO software market' analyst figures lump in ERP and are not a budget line for a capture add-on. Per-seat value ($7-9k saved vs $1.8k price) is plausible; seat count and adoption speed are not.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: ~30,000 seats at a lower effective price, lessors and insurers accept the evidence package for reserve claims (speculative, unverified), and no ERP vendor bundles a native version (they sell to the same shops). Adoption inside regulated shops is slow.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Maintenance records need a human certifier's signature, so AI drafts are not releases; electronic records rules (AC 120-78A as cited by the pitch) and EASA Part-145 apply. Not a blocker, but liability and data-ownership terms are open.
verdicts.deciding_reason: A $100M outcome would exceed Ramco's whole revenue; the space is funded and consolidating under IFS and AVIATAR; matches the generic AI copilot cliche. Upside about $20M.

verdicts.title: Engine Lifeline: flexible-term spare-engine cover pool for institutional owners

competitors_found.name: Shannon Engine Support (AerCap and Safran 50:50)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Short-term spare engine cover for CFM56 and LEAP operators; claims 500+ TRUEngine qualified spares
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: AerCap/Safran JV; AerCap Engines lists CFM56-7B and LEAP-1A with short-term leases

competitors_found.name: Willis Lease Finance and Willis Aviation Capital
competitors_found.what_they_do: Engine lessor and third-party asset manager; Blackstone fund targeting $1B+ over two years
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: AUM $4.4B, WAC platform $1.4B (up ~80% y/y), $1.3B dry powder, Q2 2026 lease rent $77.1M

competitors_found.name: Bridgepoint, AIP Capital and GFH engine platform
competitors_found.what_they_do: Institutional engine leasing platform buying LEAP-1B spares; 11 more ordered Jul 2026 for 2027-29 delivery
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $1B+ portfolio target, raising from institutional and private wealth investors; AIP ~$4B AUM (June 2025)

competitors_found.name: Engine Lease Finance Corporation (AerCap)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Spare engine lessor with 200 CFM spares and a 50-engine LEAP spare agreement

competitors_found.name: Aero Engine Leasing (new platform)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Newly launched CFM-focused engine leasing platform

verdicts.substitutes: Extending a 3-year lease, CFM's own lease pool (TRUEngine benefits), airlines holding their own spares, and pools like Willis's historical CFM56-7B pool shared by American, Southwest, WestJet, Alaska and Delta. Teardown-sourced serviceable engines.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Pitch: 450 engines, ~$3.9B, rent ~$630M (16% of asset value), fee 12% of rent = $75M plus 1,170 swaps x $40k = $47M. Willis earns ~$77M of rent a quarter on ~$3B of owned assets, about 10% a year; ISTAT shows long-term LEAP rent of $130-150k a month (13-15%) with short-term quotes of $6-7k a day in 2025. A 16% pool-wide yield assumes nearly every engine earns the short-term premium; at 10-14% the fee line is $47-66M. The $47M swap line is weakest: the pitch says a swap costs $150-300k, so a $40k fee is pass-through or loss-making. $4B of third-party AUM is ~3x Willis's whole third-party platform.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Fee-basis net revenue. Needs: (1) $3-3.5B of third-party engine AUM within 7 years, with a $300-500M anchor LP (plausible, GFH just did this for Bridgepoint); (2) engine supply by secondary purchase because OEM spares go to CFM's leasing arm and SES (plausible but expensive); (3) rents stay high to 2030 (contested; SMBC Aero Engine Lease's CEO warned in Feb 2026 that rents will collapse if spare ratios normalize, and ELFC warns of premature part-outs); (4) the standardized swap protocol really cuts the $150-300k per-swap cost (unverified insider hypothesis); (5) no warranty or TRUEngine friction from installing third-party engines (unverified). On a principal-lessor basis revenue passes $100M with ~$0.9B of owned engines, but that is a financing business with no edge over Willis or Blackstone-backed rivals, so it is not counted.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Cape Town registrations, customs and VAT on temporary imports, and OEM warranty or LTSA effects of third-party engines are unverified but standard issues. Premise claim that no one offers short-term or multi-owner cover is false: SES, AerCap Engines and ELFC sell short-term cover and Willis and AIP already manage third-party engine capital.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Cleanest payer and fee pool in the pool, but short-term cover and third-party engine capital already exist at scale and the why-now is the crowding signal; median about $12M, upside about $75M.

verdicts.title: Certifier Capacity: portable-authorization travel certifiers

competitors_found.name: LAUNCH Technical Workforce Solutions
competitors_found.what_they_do: Self-described largest aviation workforce firm; 500,000-candidate database, PlaneTechs acquisition, eLAUNCHNow technician matching platform
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Private; third-party revenue estimates range $69M-$460M, unverified

competitors_found.name: Aerotek (Allegis)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Contract and contract-to-hire A&P mechanics at $35-48 an hour in current postings
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Part of a large private staffing group

competitors_found.name: Job Aire Group
competitors_found.what_they_do: Aviation mechanic and technician staffing to US maintenance facilities

competitors_found.name: VP Aviation Technical Services
competitors_found.what_they_do: Technician staffing for MROs, OEMs, airlines and repair stations

verdicts.substitutes: Direct hire with retention bonuses, employer pathways (SkyWest AMT, Bombardier apprenticeship), Part 147 schools, and the MRO's own authorization onboarding. Free: hosts already authorize contractors under their own manuals.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Spread $22 an hour (bill $65, pay $43) is a 34% gross margin; typical staffing guidance puts net margin at 5-15% of bill rate. $100M of gross profit needs ~2,400 FTE and ~$300M of billings; $100M of revenue needs ~800 FTE. The pitch's own moat line calls this the least defensible idea.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Net revenue (gross profit) basis; gross billings median ~$25M and upside ~$120M. Needs ~1,000 placed FTE via two or three large MRO accounts (plausible for a strong tech-enabled roster), hosts accepting a portable record in place of their own authorization process (unlikely, since the FAA authorizes per station), and working capital for payroll. Revenue clears the bar but at staffing margins and against an incumbent with a matching platform.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: 14 CFR 145.157 requires each approving person at a US station to be an appropriately certificated mechanic or repairman, and 145.151 keeps the station responsible for qualifying them, so authorization is per station and per manual. A 'portable authorization' is a faster onboarding checklist, not a legal status hosts must accept. 145.217 (contract maintenance) not retrieved; W-2 versus 1099 and visa limits unverified.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Aviation staffing is already done at scale; revenue can pass $100M but net economics are staffing-grade with no moat; upside net revenue about $25M.

result.pool_note: Real $100B pool, but scarcity profit sits in physical supply (parts, repairs, engines) held by balance-sheet incumbents (FTAI, HEICO, Chromalloy, Willis, AerCap). All eight ideas are intermediaries or information layers on that bottleneck. Information-layer ideas cap near $20-35M; supply-creating ideas need hundreds of millions of capital against scaled rivals.

verdicts.title: Last Mile: a locate-first, net-recovery operator for the default chain

competitors_found.name: Primeritus Financial Services
competitors_found.what_they_do: Locate, recover and remarket for lenders through a national agent network; titles, liens, redemptions
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Kinderhook-backed since 2012; revenue estimate about $134M (weak aggregator estimate, growjo)

competitors_found.name: Servicing Solutions
competitors_found.what_they_do: Skip tracing, asset recovery, remarketing, loss mitigation and backup servicing for auto lenders

competitors_found.name: Resolvion
competitors_found.what_they_do: Pre-charge-off skip trace, forwarding with automated agent-selection scoring
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: PE-owned; revenue estimates range $14M to $88M, unreliable

competitors_found.name: DRN (Motorola) DRNsights
competitors_found.what_they_do: Lender-direct plate-sighting subscription used in early-stage delinquency to locate vehicles and addresses
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 15B+ sightings; sold to credit unions and Westlake

competitors_found.name: AANGO / Loanbridge.AI-AutoSquared.AI
competitors_found.what_they_do: Small forwarding-technology and AI repossession workflow startups
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Tiny (AANGO six employees); no funding found

verdicts.substitutes: Lenders buy DRN locate data directly, run champion/challenger tests across forwarders, and use in-house recovery at the largest lenders. Forwarders already handle 66% of completed repossessions (CFPB). Borrowers redeem 22-34% of repossessed vehicles and 10-19% of completions are already voluntary surrenders.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Units hold (RDN: 2.42M assignments, 706k repossessions in Q2 2025, about 2.9M a year; Cox 1.73M auction-delivered in 2024) but 22-34% of completions are redeemed, so remarketable units are about 1.8-2.1M. $100M NET at about $650 a unit needs 154k units (7-9% of remarketable units, likely over 30% of the 20-25 reachable non-captive lenders): heroic. $100M GROSS billing with a one-invoice all-in of $1,450-1,700 a unit needs 60-70k units, about 3-4 anchor lenders at 15-25k repossessions: believable but top-decile. The lender value test mixes the RDN 29% unit-completion ratio (which counts repeat assignments, since only 54% of accounts were assigned once) with the 38.2% dollar recovery rate.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Randomized pilot beats the incumbent forwarder and the lender consolidates recovery spend into one invoice: needs 3-5 anchor lenders at 15-25k repossessions each, about 10% chance. (2) Net-proceeds pricing stays a differentiator: weak, copyable once proven, so the moat must be the per-unit outcome dataset and managed-resolution workflow. (3) Outcome pricing does not trigger wrongful-repossession or UDAAP problems: manageable if pay is on net proceeds net of complaints. (4) Plate-data supply stays available: likely, DRN sells to many buyers.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Premise partly false: locate-first is a commodity (DRN lender-direct, Servicing Solutions, Resolvion, Primeritus) and lenders already see assignment and completion counts. Legal checks (UCC 9-609 breach of peace, FDCPA 1692f(6), state agency licensing, right-to-cure notices) are standard forwarder compliance; DPPA and state LPR rules for the locate step not verified. CFPB has linked forwarder use to higher consumer fees and Senate Banking is active on repossessions.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Only idea with an existing budget line, easy bake-off switching and a $100M gross path from 3-4 anchor lenders; but incumbents sell every component except net-proceeds pricing, so upside is borderline and the median is soft.

verdicts.title: Downshift: a lender-approved short-payoff and trade-down exchange

competitors_found.name: Walkaway USA (EFG Companies)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Lender-paid vehicle-return protection; borrower returns the car to a franchised dealer in defined life events
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: About $35-75 per loan to the credit union; traction needed an OEM (Hyundai)

competitors_found.name: Carvana / CarMax lien-payoff buyers
competitors_found.what_they_do: Buy cars and pay off liens, but the borrower covers negative equity

competitors_found.name: Informal BHPH dealer swaps and lender hardship teams
competitors_found.what_they_do: Extensions, deferrals, modifications; unpackaged dealer trade-downs

verdicts.substitutes: Lender hardship programs (deferral, modification), voluntary surrender, and the borrower selling the car privately. Lenders may already run informal assisted-sale handling that is not publicly documented.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 100k cases a year is 3.4-5.6% of repossessions and implies about 100k dealer purchases plus 100k replacement BHPH loans (about 4-5% of the idea's assumed $18-22B BHPH originations). The $1.9k lender gain needs the dealer to pay $8.0k against a $6.9k repossession-path value, i.e. above wholesale; at wholesale the gain falls to a few hundred dollars and the $700 fee is hard to defend. Dealer's profit comes from the replacement loan yield, so the product is a BHPH origination funnel.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Needs several lenders to adopt a pre-authorized short-payoff window as standard policy (ABS consent, 1099-C and credit-reporting treatment solved; moderate plausibility, slow), and dealers to pay above wholesale funded by finance yield (plausible for BHPH, regulatory optics poor). Reaching 100k cases needs about 4% of repossessions funneled through one platform: low plausibility inside 7 years.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Unverified: ABS servicer or trustee consent for a short payoff, 1099-C, state deficiency and notice law, UDAAP and fair-lending risk on the replacement loan. Senate Banking wrote to BHPH dealers and trade groups about repossessions in Feb 2026. No lender policy documents were found, which is not proof of absence.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Most non-obvious idea and a real loss-mitigation insight, but the lender gain depends on dealers overpaying wholesale and adoption is slow; median is far below $20M.

competitors_found.name: Gaya

competitors_found.name: Verifacto and other insurance-tracking / CPI vendors
competitors_found.what_they_do: Insurance tracking and lender-placed (collateral protection) insurance management for auto lenders
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Established vendor; Assurant and National General also sell CPI (not verified)

verdicts.substitutes: Tens of thousands of independent non-standard agents already sell monthly-pay policies with electronic drafts; borrowers can pay the insurer directly; lenders already use force-placed coverage and tracking.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M of commission at an unsourced 12% is about $830M of premium, about 277k policies at $3,000 (unsourced), about 2% of non-prime loans. That is roughly the volume the best embedded channel in the market (Root-Carvana) took years to reach, and non-standard renewals are six months with high churn. competitors_found.name: Paymentus

picks.from_title: Last Mile: a locate-first, net-recovery operator for the default chain
picks.title: Last Mile: outcome-priced recovery operator for non-captive auto lenders
picks.one_liner: A single-invoice, net-proceeds-priced recovery operator that runs locate, voluntary hand-back, forwarding and remarketing for non-captive auto lenders, proven by randomized holdouts and an account-level outcome dataset.
picks.sharpened_pitch: Do not sell 'we locate cars'; plate-sighting data is sold lender-direct by DRN, and Primeritus, Servicing Solutions and Resolvion already sell locate, forwarding and remarketing. Sell accountability for dollars recovered per defaulted account. One accountable operator replaces the lender's separate forwarder, transport, storage, auction-coordination and title vendors with one invoice and one outcome metric. Price: a base fee below today's forwarding bill plus a share of net proceeds above a baseline set by a randomized holdout on the lender's own accounts, with the share reduced by wrongful-repossession and complaint events so the contract cannot reward aggressive repo. The product is the account-level decision (pre-locate, managed voluntary hand-back, dealer-assisted pre-repo sale where the lender has pre-authorized it, repossess, or release) and the route-to-sale choice. Fix the metrics: sell on net dollars per defaulted account and on fewer repeat assignments (only 54% of accounts are assigned once), plus more voluntary hand-backs (10-19% of completions) and redemptions (22-34%), not on the 29% unit ratio. Target the 20-25 non-captive lenders with 8-30k repossessions a year; three to four anchors at 15-25k each is about 60-70k units, or $100M of gross billing at $1,450-1,700 all-in a unit. Wedge via bake-offs, since lenders already split assignments across forwarders. Exit path: the outcome dataset becomes a recovery-pricing engine and an ABS-investor reporting product.
picks.payer_and_signer: SVP Collections/Recovery signs, CFO co-signs; paid from the existing recovery line (forwarder fees, transport, storage, auction and title costs) at about $1,450 all-in per recovered unit today.
picks.path_to_100m: Gross billing basis: one invoice at about $1,450-1,700 per unit x 60-70k units a year = $100M, i.e. 3-4 anchor lenders at 15-25k repossessions each, about 3% of the 1.8-2.1M remarketable units. Net basis ($650 a unit) needs 154k units, which is heroic; present revenue on a gross basis and margin separately. Reachable pool of about $2.6-4.3B of annual recovery cost (1.8-2.95M units x $1,450).
picks.competitors_and_edge: Primeritus, Servicing Solutions, Resolvion, RDN (assignment network), DRN (lender-direct locate), AANGO, Loanbridge.AI. Edge: net-proceeds pricing and single-invoice accountability that activity-paid forwarders cannot offer without cannibalising their own per-assignment revenue, plus a randomized proof per lender. Not an edge: locate data, which is a bought input.
picks.why_now: Repossessions at multi-year highs, non-prime recoveries weak, forwarders consolidating to 66% of completions with higher consumer fees flagged by the CFPB, Senate Banking attention on repossessions, ABS investors asking for recovery reporting, and digital remarketing channels available to plug into.
picks.moat: Weak at first (pricing is copyable). Durable only if the per-unit outcome dataset and managed-resolution workflow create a recovery-pricing engine and switching costs once embedded in a lender's servicing flow; scale economies in dispatch density.
picks.biggest_open_risk: Incumbent forwarders copy the DRN-fed pre-locate and match outcome pricing once a pilot proves the lift, leaving a services business competing on price. Second: the 3-point recovery lift on which the economics rest is unproven and confounded by used-car price swings.
picks.cheapest_next_test: A 2-3 week data-only test: get 12 months of de-identified assignment history (assignment date, days past due, forwarder, outcome, fees, sale channel and proceeds) from 3-5 mid-size lenders or an ex-forwarder ops head, then measure (a) the share of assignments with zero recovery and the fees spent on them, (b) the share of accounts assigned 2+ times, (c) net proceeds by sale channel. If avoidable waste is at least $400 per recovered unit, the $650 net economics hold and a randomized 1,000-account pilot is worth buying.

result.pool_note: P022 is crowded: locate, forwarding, servicing, double-pledge checks and dealer captives all have funded owners. Only the recovery chain showed a real unowned gap, outcome pricing. The 29% recovery ratio is a per-assignment unit ratio, not dollars.

The 2026 Restoration Benchmarking Survey says only about 4% are paid in 1-2 weeks, most wait 3-8 weeks and just over 18% wait over 8 weeks, so a 45-day turn at a likely 2.5% price needs about $4B of advances and about $490M outstanding. The target segment of PE platforms and franchisors is already Rebuild's stated customer base. The 15-25% AR in 'pending supplement' and 5-8 point lift are unverified insider hypotheses.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Outcome pricing at 3%+ of collections holds against software-only substitutes; about 40%. (2) 10-15 PE or franchise platforms with $100M+ of carrier billings outsource rather than build shared services, in a market where Rebuild already sells to the biggest names; about 15%. (3) A measured, repeatable 5+ point collected-rate lift; about 30%. (4) Carrier-side AI invoice review (NovaData) keeps raising the defense burden; about 60%. Joint odds near 5%.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: No licensing barrier for billing and supplement work. Contractors generally may price and supplement but may not negotiate coverage in TX and FL, which limits the service to scope and price disputes.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Largest real wallet in the batch, but the wedge segment is already served by funded software, the percentage-of-collections price is roughly 2x the in-house cost, and median stays under $20M.

Without float, the pool is the 0.4% draw fee on a $30B loss-draft base ($120M at 100% share), and the $30B and $50B mortgage-linked bases are the idea's own assumptions. iink processed roughly $72M a month in 2023, about 2% of the idea's base.

Fannie B-5-01 confirms the 'greatest of $40k, 33% or excess' first release and that no final inspection is required on loans under 31 days delinquent. Escrow-law licensing would apply in California.
verdicts.deciding_reason: The float premise is contradicted by primary Fannie text and AB 493, the servicer remains liable and holds custody by rule, and iink already sits in the workflow; pool without float is at most $120M at full share.

verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M at about $1,200 per claim needs 100k signed claims a year, which needs a fee on the whole settlement (8% of about $15k). The idea's own missing dollars are $1-4k per claim, so the homeowner nets little, and if the fee is limited to the delta revenue is $80-320 a claim, requiring 300k-1.2M claims. The 5.27M total property claims in 2025 (Verisk ClaimSearch, down 19%) is consistent with the 3.5-4.3M homeowners estimate. Claim-size share (55% mid-band) is unsourced.

(2) CAC under about $400 per signed claim without paid contractor referrals, which are restricted; 25%. (3) Licensing in 45 states and compliance with fee caps and solicitation rules; slow but feasible. (4) Carriers do not respond with retaliatory scrutiny or litigation; moderate. Largest unconstrained upside in the batch, but median is far below $20M.

California AB 597 would bar pre-contract-payment fees and cap catastrophe fees at 15% (held in committee Aug 2025). Florida 626.854 caps fees at 10% in the first year after a declared emergency and 20% otherwise, with a 48-hour solicitation ban.

verdicts.substitutes: Insurer-chosen industrial hygienists, homeowner-hired IH firms, CDI certification programs, litigation (LA County v. State Farm), and IH labs.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: LA's $85M assumes the 13,000 smoke files from January 2025 flow into the new regime. One report says neither law applies retroactively, those claims have a 7 Jan 2027 suit deadline, and DTSC's health-based standards are not yet written (emergency regs due 1 Jul 2027 per one source; end of 2028 for lead and asbestos and end of 2029 for heavy metals per another). The $6.5k per file (testing, clearance, 10% of remediation) is the idea's assumption. The national $450-540M pool assumes other states copy California, which is unverified.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) DTSC standard creates an independent clearance role not captured by insurer-selected vendors; the statute text does not say clearance must be independent, 25%. (2) Repeat California wildfires generate smoke volume after 2027; likely but lumpy. (3) Other states copy; unverified, 15%. (4) The insurer pays for the test, so a 'neutral' authority is paid by the conflicted party; structural problem.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: AB 1795 signed 15 Sep 2026 (Ch. 240, Stats 2026), operative once AB 1642 takes effect, creates a rebuttable presumption of fire origin, bars ending ALE until cleared, and requires insurers to pay sampling and testing. Retroactivity unconfirmed. AB 1795 requires CDI training and certification for adjusters and public adjusters on smoke claims.
verdicts.deciding_reason: The clearance standard does not exist until 2027-2029, the 13,000 LA files are likely outside the new law, and the payer is the conflicted insurer; national path rests on other states copying California.

verdicts.substitutes: Default is free: the owner keeps the building and rents it to the successor. After a share sale the Betriebsaufspaltung ends and hidden reserves are taxable unless the owner elects Betriebsverpachtung, so keeping the building is also the tax-cheapest path. Other substitutes: Hausbank mortgage, local family-office buyers, Sparkasse Immobilien-Leasing.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Deal flow was mis-scaled. 37,200 handovers x 46% non-family (IfM: 54% family) x 25% owner-held (idea's own assumption) is about 4,300 a year; with the idea's E&Y 11.6% willingness filter (unverified) about 500 a year. The 225 assets a year needed is 5% of the first figure and 45% of the second. Real-estate transfer tax of 3.5-6.5% (from memory) plus diligence on a EUR 1.2M asset yielding about EUR 84k of rent is a heavy friction. EUR 1.24B of buildings is balance-sheet rent; a sponsor's own income on that AUM would be about EUR 12-20M. The 7% yield on weak-credit single tenants has no source.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Widen from succession to all Mittelstand sale-and-leaseback; the pool is huge (about EUR 2.1T corporate property, 35% light industrial, about EUR 100B institutional), plausibility high. (2) An institutional sponsor commits about EUR 400M equity; plausible only after a multi-year track record, low to moderate. (3) A pooled Pfandbrief or insurer facility finances granular EUR 1M assets; moderate. (4) A 7% net yield holds on weak-credit tenants; unproven. Together these give about $85M, short of $100M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Tax premise partly inverted. BFH: share sale ends personal interlocking, so the Besitzunternehmen is treated as discontinued and reserves are taxable, unless Betriebsverpachtung and the lessor election apply. That makes keeping the building the tax-friendly default and selling it the step that realises tax. Sale of a building also triggers real-estate transfer tax (from memory).
verdicts.deciding_reason: Succession-only funnel needs 5-45% of reachable buildings; tax logic favours the owner keeping the building; specialists start at EUR 10M tickets, so small tickets are capital-heavy with unproven yield and rent is not business-scale revenue.
