verdicts.revenue_math_check: The denominator is wrong. IfM's 186,000 is a 2026-2030 five-year total (37,200 a year), of which about 54% go to family, 17% to employees and 29% to outsiders, so about 10,800 outside sales a year. 1,930-2,150 closings is 18-20% of those, not 5.2-5.8%. KfW price: mean EUR 499k, median EUR 375k, 5% of planners at EUR 50k or less, and realised prices are lower; 9.5% of EUR 375k is about EUR 36k. Funding 12-24 months of work at a 45-55% close rate roughly doubles cost per closing and nearly erases a EUR 36-45k fee.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: About 1,000 closings a year (about 9% of outside sales) at EUR 40k average fee gives about $46M, plus small data revenue. Needs: owners accept 24-month exclusivity with a tail clause (moderate), a 50%+ close rate on firms they help (moderate), a pre-qualified buyer pool (moderate), no disintermediation (low plausibility). $100M would need 2,000+ closings, which is not plausible.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Confirmed: Sec. 9 StBerG bars fee-splitting for referrals and Sec. 9a bars success fees except a narrow single-case rule, so Steuerberater can only refer for free. Exclusivity and tail clauses in standard terms face fairness-review limits (from memory, unverified).
verdicts.deciding_reason: Best fee model in the pool, but capped by about 10,800 outside sales a year and free chamber and exchange substitutes; ceiling around $50M with disintermediation risk after free prep.

verdicts.substitutes: Owner closes (about 54,000 Handwerk closures expected over two years versus 49,000 handovers); family or employee takeover; sale to a PE platform (which prefers firms of about 20 staff and EUR 2M revenue and up); chamber exchanges; individual buyers using KfW 077.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 60 firms x EUR 1.5M = EUR 90M (about $103M) holds. Purchase price is understated: sellers expect a median 60% of revenue (Handwerk about 87%), so likely EUR 45-80M at 0.5-0.87x revenue, half deferred, not EUR 22-45M. Share of sellers is not binding (12 deals a year is a fraction of a percent of reachable A-trade exits). Margin is 6-9%, so $100M revenue means $6-9M EBIT. Existing platforms (Konzmann EUR 180M) prove the revenue path and also mean competition.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) 12 deals a year from year four, reaching about 60 firms: Konzmann and HWP got to 21-40 units under PE, so plausible but top-decile. (2) EUR 45-80M of consideration funded by permanent capital, seller notes and Buergschaftsbank cover: moderate. (3) Old Meister stays two to three years and a Meister ladder keeps the Betriebsleiter requirement filled: moderate. (4) Contract books retain after the owner leaves: unproven until customer ledgers are checked. (5) The Ausbau trades recover from the 2026 slump: moderate.

The GmbH mit gebundenem Vermoegen has key points only and no draft bill. The name Meisterwerk is taken.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Only idea with a proven, named route to $100M revenue, a verified legal premise and abundant sellers; weaknesses are thin margin, a price gap versus owner expectations, and no deep moat.

verdicts.upside_assumptions: Needs thousands of qualifying closures, connection value much larger than the evidence suggests, and rules to keep favouring existing connections. All low plausibility.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Partly verified: under Sec. 2(4) NAV the connection relationship passes to the new property owner. Capacity increases need a separate agreement. No source found on lapse after closure or change of use, which is the idea's own kill risk and remains open. The draft Netzpaket and Reifegradverfahren are still moving.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Small connections are worth little, developers already trade connected land, and the $100M path is just a property fund.

picks.title: Hold-forever Handwerk platform with owned origination (new name needed)
picks.one_liner: A permanent-capital buyer of owner-led Handwerk and technical-service firms below PE's size floor, built as regional hubs with tuck-ins, an owned pre-sale funnel and a Meister-equity ladder.
picks.sharpened_pitch: Buy owner-led German Handwerk and technical-service firms (electrical testing, fire protection, heating and water service, lift maintenance) that PE platforms skip, and never sell them. Five changes from the gate. (1) Buy the contract book, not revenue: target firms with at least half of revenue from recurring statutory inspection or service work, and price against that book. (2) Hub-and-spoke: six to eight hubs of 15-60 staff (EUR 2-4M revenue) in Bavaria and NRW, then tuck in micro firms and the customer books of closing firms around each hub, so deal count stays manageable and routes get denser. (3) Own origination: chamber and Steuerberater referral is shared with HWP, Builtech and Konzmann, so add a pre-sale programme for owners two to three years out with a right of first offer, plus a catch net for the roughly 27,000 Handwerk closures a year. (4) Price the gap honestly: owners expect a median 60% of revenue (Handwerk about 87%), so offer 0.4-0.6x with half deferred against contract retention, keep the old Meister as Betriebsleiter for two to three years, and give a Geselle a Meister-equity ladder. (5) Fund with EUR 15M permanent seed and EUR 45-80M total consideration over five years, using seller notes and Buergschaftsbank cover. Target 60 firms x EUR 1.5M, about $103M revenue at 6-9% margin by year six or seven. Rename: Meisterwerk is a funded Berlin software startup.
picks.payer_and_signer: Customers pay: building owners, property managers and small industrial sites, from maintenance and statutory-inspection budgets. Signers on each deal: the seller-owner (Inhaber). Capital signer: the CIO of a permanent-capital LP (Versorgungswerk or family office).
picks.path_to_100m: 60 firms x EUR 1.5M = EUR 90M (about $103M). Pace roughly 2, 5, 8, 10, 12, 12, 12 deals over seven years. Consideration EUR 45-80M (0.5-0.87x revenue, half deferred), above the original EUR 22-45M. About 27,000 Handwerk closures and about 25,000 handovers a year mean twelve deals is a fraction of a percent of reachable sellers. EBIT at 6-9% would be $6-9M, so this is revenue scale, not software-like value.
picks.competitors_and_edge: Konzmann (21 firms, EUR 180M revenue, KLAR Partners), HWP (30-40 units, about 1,250 staff, GRIP), Builtech (51 firms, 2,000+ staff, merging with VDK) and Purpose Evergreen Capital (minority capital). Edge: they buy firms of about 20 staff and EUR 2M revenue and up and have changed hands within five or six years, so a hold-forever buyer of smaller firms with a Meister pipeline is a real counter-position; the edge is modest.
picks.why_now: KfW Jan 2026: planned closures exceed successions for the first time. In Handwerk about 54,000 firms expect to close within two years against 49,000 handing over, owners are on average 54 and those handing over about 59, and 33% of firms plan a handover within five years (HWK Dortmund). PE platforms get flipped, which makes a no-flip promise credible to sellers.
picks.moat: Thin: scale economies in back office, procurement and compliance scheduling; a Meister pipeline as a modest cornered resource; counter-positioning against PE flips. Mostly execution and cost of capital.
picks.biggest_open_risk: Adverse selection and churn: owners expect about 1.5-2x what a hold-forever buyer pays, so the platform may only get weaker firms or sellers with no alternative, and contract books and Meister may leave after the owner exits. At 6-9% margin one bad cohort of deals can erase equity.
picks.cheapest_next_test: In 6-8 weeks, through HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren get anonymised customer ledgers from 6-8 target firms and measure recurring share and three-year retention; sign three non-binding term sheets at 0.6x revenue or less with half deferred; hold five talks with Versorgungswerk or family-office CIOs on a EUR 15M seed. Stop if recurring revenue is under 40% or sellers insist on over 0.8x in cash.

result.pool_note: The EUR 54B pool is sellers' hope. Fee ideas are capped by about 10,800 outside sales and 6,300 employee takeovers a year, so they top out near $50M. Only a hold-forever Handwerk platform reaches $100M on defensible numbers, and it is capital-heavy with thin margins.

ideas.title: Lab Order Rail
ideas.one_liner: A lab-agnostic ordering layer inside the physician's EHR that checks coverage, eligibility, duplicates and order provenance before a requisition leaves the office, free to the practice and paid per clean order by the lab (the e-prescribing network, transferred to lab orders).
ideas.customer: Ordering practices as free users; the labs that receive their orders pay (6,411 PAMA-reporting labs plus other outpatient and specialty labs).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The lab pays $0.40-0.80 per validated requisition (assumption) from client-services, billing or marketing budget. Signer: VP revenue cycle or CFO at independents; outreach director at hospitals.
ideas.problem: A lab claim is born on someone else's desk. XiFin 2026 (30M+ claims): denials rose 40% to 11.2% in 2025; for non-hospital clinical labs 59.4% of denials are 'procedure not paid separately' and 15% are duplicates; patient responsibility is 30% of claims but patient payments only 9%. Insider view (unverified): lab client-services teams phone practices all day for diagnosis codes and insurance, and no tool sees orders across labs, so cross-lab duplicates are invisible. Since the Schena EKRA ruling (9th Cir., July 2025) and the 2025 DOJ takedown ($14.6B alleged), order provenance is also the lab's own legal risk.
ideas.solution: EHR-embedded panel: real-time eligibility including inpatient/SNF/hospice/home-health episode flags; LCD/NCD/MolDX and major commercial policy checks at order time; diagnosis codes prefilled from the chart; ABN capture; duplicate and frequency checks across every lab on the network; a neutral list of labs with the patient's price by site; clinician-authenticated order tied to the encounter. Labs pay a fee per validated order.
ideas.why_now: Denials +40% in 2025 (XiFin); EKRA enforcement (Schena, Dec 2025 settlements) makes provenance a liability; Transparency in Coverage final rules (issued 2026-10-05) make prices machine-readable; ACA deductibles up 37% make price-at-order matter.
ideas.wedge: Ten independent or outreach labs ($20-80M revenue, denial rate above 10%) run a 60-day lab-side API (eligibility, facility-stay and duplicate check on requisition data they already receive), which needs no practice adoption; then offer the free widget to each lab's top 200 practices and list in two EHR marketplaces.
ideas.path_to_100m: Non-Quest/Labcorp outpatient pool is about $36B (arithmetic from Quest's 2012 segment slide + Kaufman Hall 2016 + Hyde Park $99.7B), i.e. 600M-820M requisitions at $44-60 (Quest: 244M requisitions in 2025, ~$44 each). 167M validated orders x $0.60 = $100M = 20-28% of those orders. Heroic share, but embedded rails behave winner-take-most (Surescripts precedent). Price is defensible: at 11% denials and $5-8 rework per claim the avoidable cost is $0.55-0.90 a claim (assumption). Payer provenance subscriptions ($0.01-0.03 PMPM on 100M lives = $12-36M) are upside.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ELLKAY (vendor claims 770 labs, 58k practices; embeddable ordering portal), Health Gorilla (requisition API/marketplace), Quest and Labcorp captive portals, EHR-native lab modules (Epic, athenahealth), Orchard/Clinisys and XiFin order entry, Concert Genetics (genetic test ordering + prior auth with Availity, Jan 2025). Found no neutral layer combining eligibility, coverage, cross-lab duplicates and provenance, but ELLKAY's integrated ordering may already capture insurance data (not verified).
ideas.why_they_lose: Connectivity vendors are paid per interface, not per prevented defect; Quest/Labcorp portals cannot be neutral; Epic will not favor a lab; none sees orders across labs, which is where duplicates and provenance live.
ideas.moat: Network economies (every lab and practice added improves duplicate detection and provenance); switching costs once embedded in the order workflow; counter-positioning against captive lab portals.
ideas.earned_secret: The cheapest dollar of denial prevention is at the order, and practices will adopt any tool that stops the phone calls; cross-lab duplicates and provenance are only visible to a neutral network, which no single-lab vendor can be.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the facility-stay + duplicate API from eligibility and clearinghouse feeds; sign 3 design-partner labs for a 60-day denial A/B; list in two EHR marketplaces; have counsel review per-order pricing under AKS/EKRA (no e-prescribing-style safe harbor for lab routing exists, unverified) and consider an OIG advisory opinion; fallback is flat SaaS per lab (about 40% less revenue).

ideas.title: Know-Before-You-Bill
ideas.one_liner: Zero-touch claim prevention and recovery for the $5-to-$170 lab claims nobody touches by hand, priced as a share of cash collected on claims it handled.
ideas.customer: Independent labs and hospital outreach programs billing lab claims (6,411 PAMA reporters) and the small billing shops that serve them.
ideas.payer_and_signer: RCM budget (about 4-7% of collections, unverified). Fee 15-25% of incremental cash or 1.5-2.5% of collections. Signer: CFO, VP revenue cycle, or billing-shop owner.
ideas.problem: XiFin 2026: 11.2% denial rate; in clinical labs 'procedure not paid separately' rose from 33% (2018) to 59.4% of denials, duplicates 15.2%. The average successful appeal pays $171 in clinical labs and $48 in hospital outreach (appeals are 0.35% and 0.03% of insurance receipts), so nobody appeals: the money is recoverable but uneconomic to touch by hand.
ideas.solution: (1) Pre-bill status and edit engine learned from remittance outcomes across labs: facility-stay (inpatient/SNF/hospice/home-health) flags, panel/component logic, packaging with same-day hospital encounters, cross-lab duplicates; (2) reroute to client bill; (3) browser-agent resubmission and payer-portal appeals at under $2 an action; (4) contract-rate enforcement from remits using payers' own in-network rate files as baseline where the lab's TIN appears; (5) a January 1 audit of payers' fee-schedule loads after the new CLFS.
ideas.why_now: Denials +40% in 2025 from payer automation; the 2027 cut makes each recovered dollar matter; browser agents make sub-$2 actions possible; Transparency in Coverage files now give a contract baseline.
ideas.wedge: A 90-day look-back at 25% of recovered cash for ten labs on non-XiFin stacks, then switch to prevention at 1.5% of collections; buy 3-5 billing shops for distribution.
ideas.path_to_100m: Pure contingency cannot reach it: a 2% revenue uplift at a 25% fee is 0.5% of revenue, so $100M needs $20B under contract = 56% of the $36B pool. The scaled business is full-service RCM at 3.5% of collections: $100M = $2.9B of collections = 8% of the pool = about 400 labs at $7M each (assumption). If XiFin's customers are out of reach (assume 30% of the pool, unverified) it is 11% of the rest.
ideas.who_does_it_today: XiFin (Empower RCM; says 73% of the largest labs), Sunquest/Clinisys, LigoLab (LIS+RCM), CareCloud, offshore billing shops, Synergen Health with Lighthouse Lab Services, Phytest, Undeniable Health AI ($0.5M seed), AIMA; general RCM startups Candid Health ($120M Series D, July 2026), Silna ($27M), Sift Healthcare; hospital RCM (R1, Waystar) for outreach claims.
ideas.why_they_lose: XiFin's pricing and services are built around the largest labs; general RCM tools are tuned for $200-plus claims; offshore shops cannot fund engineering. Honest risk: XiFin owns the data and could copy this.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in payer-edit data across many labs; switching costs once billing moves; counter-positioning against per-claim/licence pricing.
ideas.earned_secret: Most 'not paid separately' denials are a timing problem, not an appeals problem: the patient was in a facility or hospice/home-health episode, or the test was packaged with a same-day hospital encounter, and the fact exists before billing (inference; XiFin does not define the category).
ideas.first_90_days: Pull 835 remits for five friendly labs; quantify packaging and duplicate denials by payer; build the facility-stay check; run the look-back; sign the first outcome contract.

ideas.title: Telelab
ideas.one_liner: A nighthawk network of US-licensed lab scientists who review digital smears, flagged results and microbiology images remotely under the customer's own CLIA certificate, priced per read and per shift (the teleradiology model applied to clinical labs).
ideas.customer: Community hospitals with 24/7 labs and chronic night/weekend vacancies; independent labs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Lab labor budget (travel/agency premium and overtime). Signer: lab director or CFO.
ideas.problem: ASCP: vacancy 8.6% average in 2018, chemistry 13.1% in 2020, retirements outpacing the pipeline, accredited MLS programs down from 263 to 243. Insider view (unverified): the shortage is the 11 pm-7 am block where one tech covers chemistry, hematology, micro and blood bank; manual differentials and flagged-result verification are the pure-judgement part of that shift. One vendor-promoted single-site study cut weekend turnaround 33-41% and removed an 8-hour backlog shift. The 2027 cut stops labs buying travelers.
ideas.solution: Device-agnostic review workspace (Scopio, CellaVision), LIS integration, state-by-state licence mapping (about a dozen states license lab personnel, unverified), double-read QA by a pathologist medical director, malpractice cover, per-read pricing with shift minimums. Later: remote microbiology plate reading, autoverification exception handling, technical-supervisor coverage. Cytology is excluded by rule.
ideas.why_now: CMS/CDC proposed CLIA rule (2026-10-08, comments due 2026-12-07) would codify remote review of digital lab data, results and images under the primary lab's certificate and drop the six-month on-site director visit; today it exists only as enforcement discretion, which nobody builds a company on. Digital morphology devices are installed; the workforce is shrinking.
ideas.wedge: After-hours smear review and flagged-result verification for ten 100-300-bed hospitals that already own CellaVision or Scopio devices, at $100-150k a year against 1.5-2.5 FTE of shift cost ($150-250k, assumption).
ideas.path_to_100m: Precedent: vRad had about $185M revenue, 350 radiologists and 2,100 clients (~$88k a client) when MEDNAX paid $500M in 2015. Here: 500 hospitals x $120k + 1,000 independent labs x $40k = $100M, about 1,500 clients = 13% of roughly 11,500 hospitals and PAMA-reporting labs (assumption; 5,100 community hospitals unverified).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Found no company selling remote lab-scientist review as a service. Device vendors (Scopio with Beckman distributing; CellaVision/Sysmex) sell hardware; staffing firms (AMN, Cross Country, Aya) sell on-site hours; Quest/Labcorp/Sonic management deals bring their own on-site staff; pathology groups do remote sign-out for anatomic pathology only.
ideas.why_they_lose: Device makers cannot sell a clinical service (liability, conflict with customers); staffing agencies sell bodies at 30-50% markup and cannot hold multi-state licences; Quest/Labcorp want volume in their own hubs.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a multi-state licensed workforce with a QA record); scale economies from follow-the-sun utilization; process power in QA.
ideas.earned_secret: Hospitals already pay agency rates for exactly the part of the night shift that is a picture and a judgement; the licence and QA record, not the software, is the scarce asset.
ideas.first_90_days: File a supportive NPRM comment before Dec 7; recruit 20 ex-hospital supervisors; sign two pilots on existing CellaVision installs; get a malpractice quote; write the double-read QA protocol with a pathologist.

ideas.title: Lab Switch
ideas.one_liner: Make the independent lab free for employees and automatic for their doctors' orders, and bill self-funded employers a share of the savings from hospital-outpatient lab markups (attacking the one thing carriers, hospitals and Quest/Labcorp are each too conflicted to attack).
ideas.customer: Self-funded employers (200-10,000 employees), their TPAs and benefits brokers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Employer medical plan budget (labs are 3-4% of employer medical spend per Quest, vendor). Fee 25% of verified savings or $0.40-0.70 per employee per month. Signer: CFO or head of benefits, usually via a broker.
ideas.problem: HCCI/West Health (2022 claims): hospital outpatient departments were 29% of employer-insured lab use but 60% of spend at about 3x independent-lab prices (comprehensive metabolic panel $51 vs $8.35; interquartile range $116 vs $2). Roughly $18.6B of employer-insured spend in these categories, $11.2B in hospital outpatient, about $7.4B above independent-lab prices (arithmetic from a sample HCCI says is about a third of claims). Same test, same analyzers; orders default to the hospital lab and a deductible-phase employee pays $51 for an $8 test.
ideas.solution: (1) Free hospital-outpatient-lab leak report from claims plus published rate files; (2) plan design: $0 at in-network independent labs on non-HSA plans, price-based incentive plus HRA/wellness credit on HSA plans (HSA members must meet the deductible first, per Anthem's flyer); (3) routing at point of order via text/QR link to a neutral list of nearby labs with the employee's price (shares the Lab Order Rail); (4) direct rates with 2-3 independent networks per region at 120-150% of Medicare with Quest/Labcorp as backstop; (5) quarterly savings attestation for the plan fiduciary file.
ideas.why_now: Transparency in Coverage final rules (2026-10-05); ACA deductibles +37% and bronze/HSA expansion; employer cost pressure. Fiduciary suits over plan overpayment mostly fail on standing (Wells Fargo, J&J) but JPMorgan (Mar 2026) and Northwestern proceeded, so pressure is rising but unproven.
ideas.wedge: Ten employers with 1,000-5,000 employees in metros with dense independent labs; free leak report first, then a pilot with a TPA.
ideas.path_to_100m: Steerable spend = non-emergent outpatient draws, say 40% of the $11.2B (assumption), saving 2/3 of it: about $3.0B, or $19.5 per employer-insured life a year (~$1.60 PMPM, in line with Avalon's $2-3 vendor claim). A 25% fee is $4.90 a life, so $100M needs about 20M lives = 20% of the ~103M self-funded lives (67% of 154M, KFF) or 13% of all employer-insured lives. Heroic; channel via TPAs and brokers.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Avalon Healthcare Solutions (44M members, 30+ plans, Francisco Partners-backed, sold through Blue plans/TPAs, claims $2-3 PMPM), Anthem's site-of-service lab benefit (New Hampshire since 2010, also California), Quest's QuestSelect and Labcorp employer programs (steer only to themselves), Carelon/EviCore lab management; Scan.com does the imaging version. Found no neutral employer-direct lab steering vendor with patient routing; Avalon could extend into it.
ideas.why_they_lose: Carriers hold the hospital contracts and, I believe, all-products/anti-steering terms (unverified), so they steer only where they have leverage; hospitals use lab margin to cross-subsidize; Quest/Labcorp programs are conflicted and employers know it; Avalon sells through carriers.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (every incumbent is conflicted); process power in routing and attestation; switching costs once it is plan design; cornered resource in preferred independent-network rates.
ideas.earned_secret: Fixing the default is cheaper than negotiating the price: nobody chose the hospital lab, the order defaulted there, and the employer never sees the 5x because lab is 3-4% of spend.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the leak report from public rate files and an HCCI-style claims pull; sign three employers with over $1M of hospital-outpatient routine lab spend; design the $0 tier with a TPA; launch SMS routing in one metro.

ideas.title: Outreach Without Selling
ideas.one_liner: The health system keeps its lab and its outreach program; a partner runs the commercial half (independent-lab entity, payer re-enrollment at lab rates, couriers, patient service centers, billing, sales) for a percent of outreach revenue.
ideas.customer: Health-system CFOs and outreach VPs (875 hospital labs filed PAMA data in 2026).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Outreach services agreement: 6-10% of outreach net revenue plus a share of logistics savings. Signer: system CFO.
ideas.problem: Quest and Labcorp are buying outreach: Labcorp-CHS $195M (Dec 2025), Ascension ~$400M (2022), ~$839M of 2024 deals, Parkview pending, Crouse (Mar 2026) with inpatient-lab management, and a 51/49 Quest-Corewell joint venture managing 21 hospital labs. Outreach margins are about to shrink: Quest/Labcorp net revenue per test was ~20% below a typical outreach program's (2016), Anthem's New Hampshire policy shows where payer policy goes, and the 2027 schedule cuts up to 15% on ~775 tests.
ideas.solution: Stage 1 (asset light): create an independent lab entity under hospital ownership (own CLIA, NPI, TIN; Frisbie Hospital did this in New Hampshire to get back in network), enroll at payers' lab fee schedules, run couriers, patient service centers, billing and client services; testing stays in the hospital core lab. Stage 2: route routine overflow to a regional hub when the core lab cannot absorb growth. Stage 3: bundle entities into a payer-preferred network (see Third Lab).
ideas.why_now: 15%-cut year; Quest/Labcorp buying spree; hospital margin pressure (H.R.1 cuts federal Medicaid by $911B over 2025-34 per KFF in the pool file); payers narrowing lab networks (unverified).
ideas.wedge: Five systems with $15-40M of outreach in 2-3 metros; open with a free 'outreach contribution model' built from their own data.
ideas.path_to_100m: 875 programs at about $24.9M average (2016 survey, old) is ~$22B. At an 8% fee, $100M = $1.25B of managed outreach revenue = ~50 programs = ~6% of programs (assumption).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Quest and Labcorp (acquire, joint-venture or manage), Sonic Healthcare USA (A$2.05B US revenue, 0% organic growth, under review), ARUP and Mayo Clinic Laboratories as reference labs, Chi Solutions-type consultants, self-run programs. Found no independent operator that runs the commercial half for a fee.
ideas.why_they_lose: Quest and Labcorp must pull volume into their own hubs and want control (51/49), which hospitals have long resisted; Sonic is stalled; consultants advise but do not operate.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (multi-year operating agreements and payer enrollments in each metro); scale economies in couriers and billing; switching costs.
ideas.earned_secret: Outreach is a contribution-margin business (23-33% in the 2016 survey): the core lab, analyzers and night staff are already paid for by inpatient volume, so an outreach test costs the hospital a dollar or two at the margin. Selling to Quest/Labcorp converts that into a revenue multiple, then moves testing to their hubs, stripping fixed-cost absorption from the hospital's own lab. What the hospital cannot do alone is sales, courier density, lab-specific payer contracting and billing, none of which requires owning the testing.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the contribution model for 20 systems from PAMA and public data; get three CFO meetings; draft the services agreement and entity-conversion playbook with counsel (AKS/EKRA review of a percent-of-revenue fee, Medicare billing rules for non-patient outreach, separate payer contracts per system for antitrust).

ideas.title: Third Lab
ideas.one_liner: Consolidate distressed independent labs into regional automated hubs, keep their physician relationships and brands, and ask the big payers for preferred-network status in exchange for independent-lab prices, because a Quest/Labcorp duopoly cannot be challenged by anyone who depends on them.
ideas.customer: Independent lab owners who cannot fund automation or match patient-service-center and courier density; payers as network buyers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Revenue is test revenue at independent-lab rates; payers pay nothing extra but grant network preference. Signers: lab owners (sellers) and payer network-strategy VPs.
ideas.problem: Quest and Labcorp are ~22% of the pool (about $21.7B of $99.7B) and growing by acquisition; Quest has ~2,400 patient service centers, Labcorp ~2,200 plus 7,000 in-office phlebotomists (company pages); independents have a handful of sites. The 2027 cut (molecular -22/-23%, chemistry -16%) hits routine tests where scale decides who survives. Sonic's US business is flat and under review.
ideas.solution: Buy or merge distressed independents at distressed multiples (0.4-0.8x revenue, assumption), keep brands and sales teams, move routine testing to 2-3 regional hubs, share billing, couriers and procurement, and sign preferred-lab agreements with payers. Operating agreements from Outreach Without Selling feed hubs with hospital overflow.
ideas.why_now: The cut reprices every independent; Quest and Labcorp are absorbing the hospital side; Sonic is stalled.
ideas.wedge: Two adjacent metros: four independents of $8-15M plus two hospital operating agreements, and one payer pilot.
ideas.path_to_100m: Revenue by acquisition is easy: 8-10 labs of $10-12M, about $60-120M of capital (assumption). A hub running 150,000 routine tests a day at $2.50 wholesale is ~$94M a year (assumption). The hard part is becoming 'third national', which needs over $1B and payer commitments; a payer letter of intent is the test of the thesis.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Quest and Labcorp, Sonic Healthcare USA, Aurora Diagnostics (anatomic pathology), Clinical Reference Laboratory (private), NeoGenomics, ARUP and Mayo as nonprofit reference labs, PE-backed regionals.
ideas.why_they_lose: Quest/Labcorp cannot give hospitals or independents control and cannot be neutral; the nonprofits have no commercial outreach engine; independents cannot match density alone; payers cannot build labs.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in hubs and couriers; cornered resource (payer preferred-network contracts); counter-positioning against the two nationals.
ideas.earned_secret: An independent lab's real assets are its physician relationships and payer contracts, not its analyzers. Routine volume belongs in a hub at wholesale cost while the relationship stays local. Payers tolerate a duopoly only until it sets price (my inference, unverified): their only lever is steering and they cannot build.
ideas.first_90_days: Screen 50 independents from PAMA reporters and state licensing data; talk to two payer network teams about a one-metro pilot; line up an infrastructure or PE equity partner. Legal: separate payer contracts per entity (antitrust), Medicare 30% referral rule (hubs must bill as performing lab), AKS in any hospital revenue share.

ideas.title: Hospital Lab Gain-Share Desk
ideas.one_liner: Take over the non-clinical half of a community hospital's lab cost (contracts, send-outs, staffing mix, automation, remote bench) on a gain-share basis, with the hospital keeping ownership, medical director and brand, as the neutral alternative to Quest/Labcorp management deals.
ideas.customer: Community hospitals and small systems with 100-400 beds and lab operating cost of $8-25M.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Lab operating budget; gain-share of 30-40% of verified savings on a three-year term. Signer: CFO and COO.
ideas.problem: Medicaid cuts (H.R.1, $911B over 2025-34) and the lab cut squeeze hospitals; Quest and Labcorp are offering management (Corewell, Crouse, Inspira) and Quest claims 10-20% savings (vendor claim). Hospitals have resisted because they lose control of turnaround and quality. Labor is 57-63% of lab cost in the non-US studies found (unverified for the US).
ideas.solution: Benchmark lab cost per test across client labs; rebid reagent-rental and instrument contracts; rebid send-outs (about 6% of a hospital lab budget per one negotiator, unverified); skill-mix and scheduling; autoverification rules; remote bench (Telelab); ordering nudges (one study found 6.7% fewer routine tests).
ideas.why_now: H.R.1 Medicaid cuts, the 2027 CLFS cut, MLS vacancies, and the Quest-Corewell template showing a path hospitals may not want.
ideas.wedge: A free 30-day lab audit for 20 hospitals; sign five at gain-share.
ideas.path_to_100m: A $12M lab budget saving 12% is $1.44M; a 40% share is $0.58M per hospital. 175 hospitals = $100M, about 6% of roughly 2,750 hospitals of that size (assumption).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Quest, Labcorp, Sonic and consultants; GPOs (Premier, Vizient) for supplies on vendor-paid fees; staffing firms for hours. Found no independent gain-share operator.
ideas.why_they_lose: Quest/Labcorp must move volume into central labs and are paid per test; GPOs are paid by vendors, not by savings; consultants do not operate; staffing sells hours.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in benchmarks and purchasing; switching costs; process power. Weak on its own, hence the low score.
ideas.earned_secret: Hospital labs overspend where nobody owns the line: send-outs, auto-renewing reagent contracts with volume floors, night-shift skill mix and standing orders each sit with a different person (unverified insider view).
ideas.first_90_days: Build the audit from five hospitals' budgets, run it free, convert one at gain-share.

ideas.title: Lab OS for Small Labs
ideas.one_liner: A subscription that gives a physician group, urgent-care chain, dialysis or skilled-nursing operator or specialty clinic a compliant moderate- or high-complexity lab: remote director and technical supervisor, proficiency-testing and QC management, LIS, and a billing hook.
ideas.customer: Multi-site operators with 15-50 moderate-complexity labs each (about 100 such operators, unverified) and independent small labs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Compliance and operations budget; about $33k per site per year (assumption). Signer: COO or the physician owner.
ideas.problem: CMS Sept 2026: 30,756 compliance and accredited labs, 13,361 of them physician-office labs. A lab director is a signature, not a presence; the real work is a few hours a month of QA, proficiency failures and competency files, which small operators do badly.
ideas.solution: One accountable pathologist or PhD group supervising dozens of sites with software for QC, proficiency testing and personnel files; shared LIS and interfaces; billing handled through Know-Before-You-Bill.
ideas.why_now: The proposed CLIA rule (2026-10-08) drops the six-month on-site director visit, codifies remote review and loosens director qualifications. Headwind: the Medicare cut makes owning a lab less attractive.
ideas.wedge: Five urgent-care or specialty groups with 20+ moderate-complexity sites each.
ideas.path_to_100m: 3,000 sites x $33k = $99M, about 10% of the 30,756 moderate and high complexity labs (assumption).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Pathology groups and consultants selling director and compliance services, CAP and COLA education, LIS vendors, lab-management firms such as Lighthouse Lab Services.
ideas.why_they_lose: Consultants sell hours and have no software; LIS vendors sell licences, not accountability.
ideas.moat: Weak: switching costs and process power only. Scored lowest.
ideas.earned_secret: Most of a director's job is paperwork a group can do for thirty sites; the on-site visit was the only thing stopping that, and the proposed rule removes it.
ideas.first_90_days: Comment on the rule; line up a pathologist group; sign five operators for a pilot. Risks: rule may stall, customers may shrink after the cut, director liability.

verdicts.title: Signed-Off: the QA-accountable AI engineering house

competitors_found.name: Nuclearn (Engineering AI, CAP AI, outage planning)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Per-product AI subscriptions sold to licensee engineers for 50.59 screening, corrective action and outage work; the engineer stays accountable
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $10.5M Series A (Sept 2025, Blue Bear); 65+ reactors claimed; investor says profitable

competitors_found.name: Everstar (Gordian), EXCEL Services is an investor
competitors_found.what_they_do: AI licensing drafting; DOE/INL/Argonne/Microsoft test turned a 4-6 week task into one day (208-page draft)
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: $4M pre-seed Feb 2025 plus about $5.5M later round

competitors_found.name: Westinghouse bertha/HiVE AI
competitors_found.what_they_do: In-house gen-AI for design calculations, licensing documents, AP1000 work packages (with Google Cloud)

competitors_found.name: Enercon merged with Pond & Company (Arlington Capital)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Appendix B nuclear engineering and licensing services touching about 90% of US plants
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Bought April 2026, reported $1.25B equity (Bloomberg, unconfirmed); 2,700 professionals combined; add-ons planned

verdicts.substitutes: Owner in-house design engineers using the AI tools above (the real substitute: tools that make plant engineers faster shrink overflow demand); hourly overflow to Sargent & Lundy (ENR #1 nuclear plants), Enercon, Jensen Hughes, Framatome, Westinghouse, Bechtel, Aptim.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Outsourced fleet engineering is a real multi-$B budgeted market (Enercon alone about $200M engineering revenue per an older OCBJ figure and a reported $1.25B equity deal), so $100M is roughly 4-5% of a plausible $2-3B pool, not heroic share. The pool's $1.3-1.4B figure and the NEI/EUCG $7.59B 2025 capital number are unverified (2023 NEI data implies about $5.8B capital). $100M needs about 250-400 billable engineers at about $250k, which is the same shortage the idea sells into, so AI leverage must be real.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (a) Buy or white-label an ASL-listed boutique in year 1: plausible, PE is actively buying nuclear engineering. (b) AI removes 40% or more of hours on bounded deliverables at independent-verification quality: uncertain; Nuclearn's CEO told the NRC that real 50.59 evaluations and complex analysis are hard. (c) Five or more owner QA organizations accept the NQA-1 Subpart 2.7 software QA program within 24 months: moderate. (d) Hiring about 250 qualified engineers: hard. (e) Developer and restart licensing work adds $25-35M: moderate. (f) Enercon/S&L do not match fixed-price AI-enabled pricing for 3+ years: low to moderate.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Premise half false. No NRC rule bars human-verified AI-assisted analysis; RG 1.28 Rev 4 endorses NQA-1 for Appendix B; NRC only has a working group listing AI guidance options. AI vendors already sell to licensee engineers who own and verify output (DOE: experts design, AI accelerates, experts validate). Real gates are customer acceptance of the vendor's software QA and approved-supplier-list status via a NUPIC-style audit.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Best-sized, budgeted market with a testable 90-day pilot and no one found selling fixed-price QA-owned AI deliverables; but QA exclusivity is overstated and Enercon can copy, so the edge is AI-native economics.

verdicts.title: Dose Ledger: the nuclear traveler network

competitors_found.name: TNC Services (The Nuclear Company)

competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 24% organic growth in 2025; parent about $70M raised, 288 open roles

competitors_found.what_they_do: Outage, maintenance and craft staffing, now inside Westinghouse
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 8,500+ peak workers at 130-150 locations; bought 2022, terms undisclosed

competitors_found.name: Day & Zimmermann
competitors_found.what_they_do: Outage workers, maintenance and temp labor; incumbent at 52 of 100 units
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: TVA outage-labor contract valued at $950M over 7 years

verdicts.substitutes: Union hiring halls and local craft, plant-direct hiring (Columbia hired 1,400-2,000 for outages), regional RP staffing firms, NukeWorker job board, licensee-run PADS access-status sharing and NRC REIRS dose records.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Pool overstated: a typical outage is 400-600 contract workers (POWER); Cook says only 30-40% of its 900 added workers are specialty. Specialty-traveler pool is about 175-350 per outage x about 50 outages x $22-26k = about $190-455M, so $100M is 22-50% share, not 7%. Gross margin 15-20% means $15-20M gross profit at $100M revenue.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Wins one integrated prime or one multi-site fleet as anchor (moderate); builds a bench of the scarcest senior RP techs (plausible, pool shrank 37% in 3 years); chains workers across outage calendars to cut idle time (plausible); takes share from D&Z, BHI and TNC without wage inflation eroding margin (low).

W-2 employer of record is fine.

verdicts.title: Certified Cell: Hadrian for nuclear (the automated NQA-1 parts factory)

competitors_found.what_they_do: Roll-up of NQA-1/ASME/Navy-qualified fabrication shops
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Fund IV of a firm with over $1B committed, nuclear-dedicated; 3+ nuclear deals in 2026

competitors_found.name: BWXT (Precision Components Group)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Heavy machining, pressure vessels, ASME fabrication for AP1000/AP300 and naval

competitors_found.name: Oklo (ARMEC) and Kairos in-house shop
competitors_found.what_they_do: Developers buying or building their own certified machining/vessel capacity
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Strategic acquisitions; Kairos holds a U-stamp, working toward N-stamp

competitors_found.name: Hadrian
competitors_found.what_they_do: Automated precision factories; Navy submarine-component factory in Alabama; no commercial nuclear found

verdicts.substitutes: Family-owned qualified shops, OEM sub-tier suppliers (Flowserve, Velan, Crane, Curtiss-Wright), dedicators (Park Nuclear), foreign suppliers (Westinghouse signed UK MoUs), and NEI 22-04 Rev 1 (Aug 2026) which seeks NRC acceptance of ISO 9001 suppliers for safety-related work.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $17.5B is a conditional DOE loan commitment (June 2026) for Westinghouse long-lead items (steam generators, coolant pumps, containment vessels, turbines, instrumentation), repaid from equipment sales, with no FIDs yet; it is not a purchase order and the 8-12% sub-tier machined share is a guess. One large factory at about $100M is plausible (BWXT's acquired shop is a comparable footprint) but needs an anchor offtake and $50-100M capital.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Anchor offtake from Westinghouse, BWXT or a developer before building (moderate); AP1000 FIDs land by 2028 (uncertain, only conditional commitments); automation really cuts cost of the paper trail (uncertain, N-stamp needs human Authorized Nuclear Inspector sign-off); outbid Pelican and BWXT for acquisitions (low to moderate).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: ASME Section III/NCA-3800 and NQA-1 are real gates. 'Qualified capacity is scarce' is true (about 100 US N-stamp holders in an older count) but the DOE loan does not fund sub-tier parts and NEI 22-04 may widen the supplier pool. 10 CFR 50.69 shrinks safety-related scope for the fleet tail.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Good structure but crowded by better-capitalized buyers, demand beyond conditional AP1000 loans unproven, and the pitched pool relied on a loan misread as a parts budget.

verdicts.title: One Audit: a supplier-paid shared accreditation for nuclear (Nadcap for nuclear)

competitors_found.name: NUPIC
competitors_found.what_they_do: Utility joint supplier audits since 1989, results shared across members, relied on by NRC staff

competitors_found.name: ASME N-type certification and NQA-1/ISO 19443 certification bodies
competitors_found.what_they_do: Capability certification of nuclear suppliers

competitors_found.name: Performance Review Institute (Nadcap)
competitors_found.what_they_do: The aerospace analog the idea copies
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: FY2024 total revenue $70.3M across all aerospace programs; 53 subscribing OEMs (2015)

verdicts.substitutes: Each developer's in-house supplier-quality team (Radiant, Oklo, Valar post these jobs), NUPIC, DOE audits, third-party inspectors, and NEI 22-04 Rev 1 which pushes to accept ISO 9001 suppliers.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The nuclear supplier universe is about 250 N-type holders worldwide (2010) and about 100 in the US per an older Power article, not 2,500-3,500. Even aerospace's entire Nadcap administrator earns $70M, so $50-105M of fees from a far smaller industry is not credible; as a non-profit-style neutral party fees are also capped by supplier tolerance.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: All primes and developers accept it as sole supplier evidence (low); utilities accept it as NUPIC input (low to moderate); non-US scope adds volume (moderate); still bounded by a supplier universe about 10x smaller than assumed.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Antitrust review of shared audit information exchange (Nadcap precedent exists). Could not confirm whether NUPIC is closed to non-utility vendors or developers; licensee acceptance under Appendix B Criterion VII is required.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Small even in the upside case: the entire aerospace analog earns $70M and the nuclear supplier base is roughly a tenth of what was assumed.

verdicts.title: Day Rate: the performance-priced outage prime

competitors_found.name: Day & Zimmermann
competitors_found.what_they_do: Outage management, maintenance and mods; markets 130 outages done in 28 days or less via pre-outage planning
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Incumbent at 52 of 100 units; specialty services at 77

competitors_found.name: Westinghouse Integrated Outage Model (BHI Energy)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Single-entity integrated outage contract reducing commercial risk
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 10-year Xcel deal cited in the pool; BHI bought 2022

competitors_found.name: Framatome and GE Vernova Hitachi outage services
competitors_found.what_they_do: Long-term outage alliances and services contracts

verdicts.substitutes: Owner self-managed outage organizations (Constellation runs well below industry average), NukeWorker/NRC public outage data, existing scheduling software (Primavera-type tools).
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Fleet average outage is 34-36 days (EIA 2024: 34, 2023: 35-38; fall 2025: 36.4), so 'slow half at 40' is not representative, and best outages are 17-20 days. The fee math conflated fleet-wide savings with a prime's share: 4 outages x ~8 days saved x ~$2M x 20% is about $13M, not $95-145M. Prime revenue of $100-120M is mostly pass-through with 10-15% fee ($10-18M).

picks.from_title: Signed-Off: the QA-accountable AI engineering house
picks.title: Signed-Off: fixed-price, AI-native nuclear engineering house (acquire the audit, automate the work)
picks.one_liner: Buy or white-label an approved-supplier-listed nuclear engineering boutique, rebuild its workflows AI-first under an NQA-1 software QA program, and sell finished, signed Appendix B deliverables at a fixed price with a rework guarantee.
picks.sharpened_pitch: Do not lead with the claim that AI output is unusable until a qualified organization owns it. No rule says that, and Nuclearn, Everstar and Westinghouse already sell AI to licensee engineers who verify and own the result. Lead with capacity, speed and a price guarantee in a market where capital spending is rising, about 30 uprates, three restarts and 20+ renewals queue, and the engineer pool is thin. Step 1: acquire or white-label a 30-100 person boutique already on customers' approved supplier lists, skipping the 12-24 month audit queue that blocks greenfield entrants. Step 2: rebuild its bounded, high-volume deliverables (50.59 screenings and evaluations, calculation revisions, engineering change packages) AI-first, version-locked under NQA-1 Subpart 2.7, with nuclear-qualified engineers independently verifying and signing every output. Step 3: price per deliverable class at a discount to hourly, with rework guaranteed, and sell to single-site operators and restarts first. Step 4: add developer-facing licensing (docketing completeness, RAI response, absorbing idea 8) and fleet uprate engineering (idea 7's engineering slice). Data asset: customer-accepted calculation and evaluation templates per plant design. Path: $20-25M boutique in years 1-2, about $55M by year 4 across 8-10 owners, $100M+ by year 6 with about a quarter from developers. Edge over Enercon and Sargent & Lundy is AI-native unit economics, not QA exclusivity.
picks.payer_and_signer: Contracted engineering and supplemental-staff lines in owner O&M plus project engineering in the capital budget. Signer: Director of Design Engineering or VP Engineering; Supply Chain adds the firm to the approved supplier list and the QA director accepts the software QA program. Developers: VP Licensing.
picks.path_to_100m: Outsourced nuclear engineering is a multi-$B budget (Enercon alone about $200M engineering revenue per an older figure; reported $1.25B equity deal April 2026; S&L ENR #1), so $100M is roughly 4-5% of a plausible $2-3B pool (the pool's $1.3-1.4B figure is an unverified assumption). $100M at about $250k per billable engineer is 250-400 engineers, which AI leverage of 30-40% must reduce. Mix: about 8-10 owners at $4-6M each plus 6-8 developers and restarts at $3-5M each plus uprate engineering.
picks.competitors_and_edge: AI software: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, 65+ reactors), Everstar/Gordian (DOE test), Atomic Canyon ($7M seed), Westinghouse bertha. Services: Sargent & Lundy, Enercon/Pond (2,700 professionals, PE-backed), Jensen Hughes, Framatome. Edge: fixed-price deliverables with an engineer's signature and a rework guarantee, built on AI-native workflows; incumbents bill hours, tool vendors do not carry accountability.
picks.why_now: Capital spending rose sharply in 2025 (reported +24%), uprate and restart pipeline backed by hyperscaler contracts, NRC clocks under EO 14300 raise licensing volume, DOE/INL test showed 4-6 weeks of drafting done in a day, and PE is paying up for nuclear engineering capacity.
picks.moat: Switching costs and process power: supplier-list status, per-owner acceptance of the software QA program, and a growing library of verified templates per plant design. Weak early; strengthens with signed-deliverable history.
picks.biggest_open_risk: AI may not remove 40% or more of hours on safety-related deliverables at independent-verification quality (Nuclearn's CEO told the NRC complex analysis is non-trivial). If leverage is under 20%, fixed-price undercutting loses money and the firm becomes a fourth-tier hourly shop; Enercon can also copy the model with fresh PE capital.
picks.cheapest_next_test: Paid pilot of about 20 50.59 screenings and 10 calculation revisions with 1-2 single-site operators, plant engineer signing, measuring hours versus baseline and rework rate, while interviewing 10 design-engineering directors and QA managers on what they would need to accept the software QA program and which boutiques are acquirable.

result.pool_note: Big, budgeted nuclear spend, but incumbents are consolidating (Enercon, BHI, Pelican, BWXT) and funded AI vendors already own the software wedge. Several pools were 2-10x inflated on inspection. Only the accountable, AI-enabled engineering services wedge stayed open.

verdicts.title: Badge-to-Bill: pre-payment hours integrity for T&M and cost-type labor invoices

competitors_found.name: Deltek AutoTime
competitors_found.what_they_do: DCAA-oriented timekeeping and labor costing integrated with Costpoint
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Vendor claims 80% of top-20 A&D firms use it (self-reported)

competitors_found.name: GovTime
competitors_found.what_they_do: Web timekeeping for government contractors with audit logs and multi-level approvals
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Listed at $7 per user per month

competitors_found.name: DOJ / GSA IG / DIA badge-data practice
competitors_found.what_they_do: Compare invoices and timesheets to badge swipes after the fact (Booz Allen settlement, one employee, $422,557)

verdicts.substitutes: A CO or COR can already request timesheets and badge data at no cost; DCAA sampling; OIG and TIGTA audits; DOJ and qui tam. FTC OIG found T&M invoice review is unstructured, which agencies treat as a procedure to fix, not a product to buy. No productized pre-payment hours control found, but every component exists inside ERPs, timekeeping tools and agency security offices.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: T&M pool is real ($139B FY17-21, about $28B/yr, civilians 11% vs DoD 1%), but EO 14402 exists to convert it to fixed price, so the exposed base shrinks during the ramp. The TIGTA $394,430 of $1M stat is from an Oct 2012 Recovery Act audit and extrapolated to only $927,992 on a $5.3M procurement. Agency side needs about $13.8B covered (12-13% of pool) at 0.4%; contractor side (300 x $150k = $45M) competes with embedded ERP and timekeeping vendors. Realistic total at the top is $25-45M.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) OMB or a CFO council names this a standard control: low plausibility, no sign of it. (2) Agency security offices hand PIV badge logs to a vendor: low; much IT T&M work is off-site or remote so presence evidence is partial. (3) Primes adopt it voluntarily as FCA defense at $150k per account: moderate, but then it is compliance software competing with ERPs. (4) T&M pool does not shrink under the EO: contradicted by the order's purpose.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: 31 U.S.C. 3352(i) mandates recovery audit programs, not a vendor, and the 2020 amendment removed contractor-payment language; contingency pricing is correctly ruled out. The 'collateral-duty COR' and '$6.8B FCA record FY2025' claims were not verified. Badge data raises Privacy Act and agency-security access issues.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Evidence is a 2012 audit, the EO shrinks the pool over the ramp, there is no agency data-access path or budget line, and even the upside is about $40M.

verdicts.substitutes: Prime ERPs (Deltek, Unanet, JAMIS), email and spreadsheets, factors and subcontractor-finance lenders, FAR 52.232-40 (primes must pay small-business subs within 15 days of accelerated government payment, no fees), CPARS for official past performance.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $86.4B small-business sub flow is real; at 33.34% share it implies about $259B total (my arithmetic, unsourced). At 0.45% take, $100M needs about $22B, 8.5% of all flow. Textura benchmark: about $87M revenue on about $41B/yr volume, implied take about 0.21%, after roughly 12 years, in construction. At 0.21% even 100% of $259B yields about $54M. Only early-pay margin exceeds Textura's take, and that is financing with its own balance-sheet problems.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Prime-signed portable performance records become what primes and subs ask for: low-moderate, CPARS is the official channel. (2) Sponsor bank enables early-pay without money-transmitter status: unverified. (3) Federal services subcontract flow holds up: contradicted by Booz Allen civil -23% and the EO. (4) 15-20% of all flow in 7 years: Textura needed about 12 years. Top-decile reaches about $60M, not $100M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: FSRS was retired into SAM.gov in March 2025, so the FSRS report wedge is a SAM.gov task. 8(a) suspensions are real (1,091 suspended, nearly 800 in termination) but a one-time compliance spike. No Miller Act or lien rights for services subs is accurate but does not create payment volume. Money-transmitter status unresolved.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Crowded compliance tier, a pay rail already regulated by the 15-day rule, and the Textura take-rate benchmark caps the upside near $60M.

verdicts.title: The Acceptance Rail: per-event verification for outcome-priced federal contracts

competitors_found.name: ASC Group (SeeSOR)
competitors_found.what_they_do: SaaS for QASP design, inspection workflows, scoring and dashboards
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Customers include DOE, DoD, State, NSF, USDA, GSA; small business

competitors_found.name: Contractor Performance Intelligence (patent application)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Claims to automate about 90% of COR post-award monitoring

competitors_found.name: IV&V providers (Booz Allen, SAIC, Leidos, Capgemini, American Systems)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Independent verification and validation on large IT programs; state pre-qualified pools
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Single awards of $88M-$118M ceilings; no market-size figure found

verdicts.substitutes: In-house QASPs and CORs, CPARS, contractors' own ServiceNow/Jira reporting, observability tools, IV&V contracts. Acceptance is the CO's inherently governmental call.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $200-300B outcome-priced-under-measurement pool is the idea's own assumption with no source. 0.3% fee on about $27B verified value requires 9-13% of a pool that does not yet exist, funded from a COR budget (1-2% of contract value, also an assumption) while the product is free for 90 days. CPARS timeliness stats are from a 2017 report covering 2013-2016.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) GAO or COFC decisions cite the vendor's metric format as the neutral standard: speculative, years away. (2) EO performance-incentive language is enforced rather than waived: unknown. (3) COs pay per event rather than expecting it from the contractor: low. Top-decile reaches about $35M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Acceptance and award are inherently governmental, so the rail can only inform. No regulation makes a vendor's metric spec a standard; GSA/OMB or FAR would. RFO batch 2 milestone pricing could not be confirmed; OneGov consumption pricing is confirmed (OpenAI deal).
verdicts.deciding_reason: No budget line, existing QASP tools, and a standard is not something a vendor can mandate; even the upside is small.

verdicts.title: Verified-WIP lender: control the repayment channel for fixed-price federal work

competitors_found.name: X-Caliber GovCon Capital
competitors_found.what_they_do: Contract-based advances against awarded contracts without factoring; $250k minimum draw, no maximum
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Part of X-Caliber family; lender led by ex-Live Oak banker and ex-CO

competitors_found.name: Blackstar Capital
competitors_found.what_they_do: Invoice financing for government contractors and subs

competitors_found.name: Government performance-based and progress payments (FAR 32.10 / 32.5)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Government finances fixed-price work at milestones or 80-85% of cost, preferred method

verdicts.substitutes: The government's own milestone and progress financing, bank ABL desks, factors (85-95% advances at 1-2.5% per 30 days), United Capital Funding, Porter Capital, Bay Street, Altline Sobel.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $100M of revenue at 12% yield needs about $830M outstanding plus about $100M equity; this is a specialty-finance company, not a venture software business. Median $8M is about $65M outstanding; upside $45M is about $375M outstanding. The idea itself flags this as the weakest. Unbilled WIP is the thinnest slice because milestones are either financed by the government or become invoices that existing lenders fund.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Underwriting acceptance state beats incumbents on loss rate: plausible but unproven. (2) A credit fund commits $400M+ of warehouse capital: moderate if loss history is good. (3) Milestone billing replaces T&M at scale: only partly, and FAR 32.10 already finances much of it. (4) Government credit risk stays low and dilution/offset risk stays manageable: unknown.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Assignment of Claims Act (FAR 32.8) assigns only to a bank or other financing institution with notice, and only amounts due or to become due; progress payments give the government title to work in progress; Fall 2026 ABA article says modern credit structures raise unsettled questions. Shutdown claim: 43 days confirmed; second lapse was a partial DHS shutdown reported at 75 days by one source.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Already done by contract-based advance lenders, the government's own milestone financing removes much of the need, and the model is a balance-sheet business with thin moat.

verdicts.title: The Evidence Desk: ex-auditors who cannot audit, for the 2028 DoD clean-opinion deadline

competitors_found.what_they_do: Hold FIAR and audit remediation contracts across DoD components
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: DoD spent about $4.11B FY2018-22 on remediation (government plus contractor)

competitors_found.what_they_do: Dedicated program team supporting the Comptroller's audit remediation, with AI and automation for evidence gathering

competitors_found.name: Component FIAR teams and IPAs

competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 26 material weaknesses in FY2025; eighth disclaimer

Independence rules bar the same audit firm from non-audit services on its own audited entity, not individuals who left, so ex-auditors are widely available to competitors.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea's own pool is about $1.1-1.3B/yr, so $100M is 8-12% for a boutique. The $4.11B was government plus contractor, produced minimal progress, and over $75M of FIAR funds was charged to non-remediation in FY2022; the OIG's finding is poor contract management, not missing talent. The Deloitte $78.3M contract figure was not verified.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Per-NFR-closed pricing with holdback is accepted by components: low-moderate. (2) Playbooks transfer across 29 entities: plausible. (3) Evidence engine becomes the shared platform despite Advana: low. (4) Demand holds past FY2028: unlikely. Top-decile boutique reaches about $40M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Dec 2025 result confirmed (eighth disclaimer, 26 material weaknesses). Clean opinion by Dec 31, 2028 is statutory (FY24 NDAA per DoD). GAGAS independence is a firm-level and entity-level rule; it does not stop competitors from hiring ex-auditors.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Small pool dominated by large firms, DoD building the capability in-house, no real moat, and even the upside is about $40M.

competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Booz Allen: $11.2-11.7B FY27 revenue guidance, civil down high single digits

competitors_found.what_they_do: FedRAMP High generative AI platform used inside agencies and by contractors

competitors_found.name: Leidos
competitors_found.what_they_do: Says customers are asking to convert work to fixed price and fixed-price share is rising

verdicts.substitutes: Primes' own AI programs and acquisitions, Palantir forward-deployed teams, OneGov frontier-model access at 50% usage discounts with no minimum (which makes the AI tool itself a commodity), staff augmentation. Kaizen (state/local software) and Pryzm (capture platform) are not outcome-priced delivery competitors, so the apparent gap is thin evidence.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea's math holds on its face: about $15B addressable sub revenue; $100M is 0.7% or 30 contracts at $3.3M. Booz Allen Q4 civil revenue -23% and FY27 civil guided down confirm pressure; the 2,500 layoff was May 2025 (7% of staff). The weak point is the median: a first slice on one task order, then perhaps 6-8 slices by year five, is $10-15M, below the $20M bar.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Fixed-price conversions proceed and survive a 2029 administration change: moderate. (2) Primes subcontract 30-50% of their own revenue to a startup rather than build in-house: low-moderate, their stated plan is in-house. (3) A startup can guarantee a 25-40% cost-down on regulated work: unproven. (4) 30 contracts at $3.3M with consent-to-subcontract cleared: low in the first five years. (5) Unit-cost database and authorization-boundary switching costs outlast an 18-month copy window: moderate. Top-decile probability about 5%.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: EO 14402 confirmed (April 30, 2026; fixed price default, top-10 review). FAR 52.215-23 pass-through limits apply to cost-type contracts and become less relevant as work converts to fixed price; consent-to-subcontract and limitations on subcontracting for small-business primes still bind. No legal bar found.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Largest honest upside in the pool, but primes already pursue this in-house, the median misses $20M, and the thesis depends on policy surviving 2029.

(4) No political whiplash removes the work: low. Top-decile reaches about $30M.

Uniform Guidance rewrite proposed May 29, 2026, effective date reportedly Dec 11, 2026 via CR. Award decisions and obligations are inherently governmental, so the desk cannot sign.
verdicts.deciding_reason: The bottleneck is political review, not mechanical checks, the contractor pool is smaller than assumed, and agencies have a free shared service.

result.pool_note: The 2026 fixed-price order creates urgency but no new tooling budget, so toll-on-flow ideas cap near Textura's 0.21% take. Only selling the labor itself scales, but primes, set-asides and trust block entrants. Stale stats (2012, 2013, 2017) propped up several premises. Zero picks.
